A cutting-edge approach has been developed to accurately identify genuine hadronic tau decays in the CMS detector, distinguishing them from those originating from quarks, gluons, electrons, and muons. By incorporating insights from neighboring particles, this novel method utilizes a sophisticated deep neural network to analyze complex data. As a result, it exhibits marked performance improvements over its predecessor, particularly in effectively differentiating between tau decays and quark/gluon jets, with gains in efficiency of up to 30%. Additionally, an advanced reconstruction technique has been introduced, incorporating fresh hadronic decay pathways. Validation studies have utilized real data from high-energy proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV.

Future sky surveys, notably the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), are projected to observe approximately 10 million time-varying celestial sources each night for a decade, sending real-time data streams to brokers for evaluation. Brokers will then utilize machine learning to filter these sources and select the most relevant for various scientific applications. Our investigation explores the merits and complexities of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in classification tasks, especially those requiring event selection. BNNs exhibit high accuracy as classifiers, offering the added benefit of quantifying uncertainty levels which can be leveraged to process and analyze this vast influx of upcoming data more effectively.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic crystal fibers, showcasing a substantial conversion efficiency between the HE11 and HE21 modes and reaching a peak gain coefficient of 21.4/W/km. By investigating mechanical resonances with various symmetries, we identify both mode-dependent and mode-independent interactions in intermodal Brillouin effects, which are crucial factors to consider in engineering the structures of photonic crystal fibers to boost high-order optical mode coupling through flexural mechanical resonances, as influenced by factors like squeeze film air damping and leakage.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams of Sn. Our research extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group BCN by standardizing the OGS-Coxeter-Dynkin correspondence.

Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items from a set to maximize an objective while adhering to a budget limit and a set of nonnegative item values, as well as elements weighted for coverage. We propose a novel hybridization, the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Knapsack Problem, by integrating the objectives to derive a comprehensive problem. Based on a constructed reduction, we establish the computational equivalence of BMCP, SUKP, and BMMCP from a decision perspective, also proving that BMCP and BMMCP are solvable in polynomial time if the instances are restricted to integer values. We further provide a parameterized algorithm with a guaranteed runtime of O-star(2^k • log(k) + k^2 + (c+jlog(j))k) for certain parameter values, based on the number of selected items and other instance factors.

Churn prevention in business retention is a critical concern, which this research tackles by transforming churn prediction in the online gaming industry into a binary classification task. To address this challenge, the study introduces various neural network models, which outperform traditional methods like Random Forest and XGBoost. By comparing the performance of different networks and exploring their results, the study derives business insights from an ensemble of these models. Notably, the research finds Advantage Neural Network (ANN) to be the top performer, although Linear Regression and XGBoost demonstrate competitive skills in specific areas. Meanwhile, the study reveals that machine learning methods surpass statistical methods in this domain, with the latter's performance improving significantly when combining outcomes from multiple networks, indicating potential for further improvement in chord detection for Churn prediction.

We are focusing on the Ising Field Theory, particularly at its scaling limit close to the Curie critical point, when an imaginary external magnetic field is applied, for both the electron and the magnetic versions of the magnetic field. Using the Yang-Lee representation of the scaling operator φ, we investigate a scenario where two copies of the Yang-Lee solution converge to the same fixed point, which is one of three possibilities, denoted B, C, or D. We reveal that the behavior near the Yang-Lee edge singularity is dominated by a leading singular point D. We show that points B and C, associated with the magnetic and electron version of the magnetic field, respectively, share the same leading singular behavior D. In contrast, the normal (magnetic) version of the magnetic field is characterized by a unique fixed point C, while the electron version of the magnetic field is characterized by a unique fixed point B, both with the same leading singular behavior D as the normal version. Furthermore, this D fixed point has a unique characteristic within the Ising Field Theory, as the leading singular behavior is primarily driven by the Yang-Lee edge singularity.

Our research shows that lattice calculations can be used to derive transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions, with gluons, through large-momentum effective theory. By combining perturbative calculations of gluon TMDPDFs with lattice calculations, we establish a connection between these functions and their equivalents in lattice simulations. The connection relies on a specific method for renormalizing lattice calculations to facilitate comparison and then to standardize results in the context of $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme. Furthermore, we assess the scaling behavior of ratios between moments of parton distribution functions and a specific value. The accuracy of our approach is tested through multiple comparisons. Our work provides a comprehensive approach for evaluating parton distribution functions, including those with a specific dependence on momentum transfer, enabling the precise confrontation of these functions with data.

In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced, resulting in light higgs-like particles called photon-hadron correlations. This correlation serves as a indicator of photon-photon interactions, which also produces a near-threshold enhancement observed in fixed-target experiments. Our study utilizes the STAR detector at RHIC to quantify the cross-section of this correlation in the context of QCD, focusing on data collected at mid-rapidity and an energy range corresponding to photon energies of 4-20 GeV. By studying these correlations across three different collision systems, we uncover new insights into the production mechanism and its reliance on particle multiplicity. Specifically, our analysis reveals that the enhanced production of these correlations, observed in both most and least peripheral collisions, follows a distinct trend. This correlation's behavior is also compared to theoretical predictions of contributions from electron-positron pairs generated through QCD's massless Compton scattering and electron-positron annihilation processes. By separating and examining these two predicted contributions, we derive a theoretical prediction that explains the observed dependence on collision system. Ultimately, our study achieves a precise measurement of the cross-section of this correlation in the context of both pPb and AuPb collisions at 300 GeV within an energy range corresponding to electron-positron pairs produced at masses of 1-4 GeV.

To minimize pollution, bicycle usage is experiencing a resurgence, particularly in urban environments. Despite the trend towards decreased fatalities in other traffic groups, the opposite holds true for cyclists. Therefore, tracking cyclist data is essential to improving their safety by providing city planners with data to design safer cycling routes. This study proposes an image-based approach to evaluate route safety from a cyclist's viewpoint, using visual features such as gradients and motion in video data to pinpoint hazards. The method incorporates multiple modality data fusion through a deep convolutional neural network, enabling a unified scalar risk score. The concept of dynamic risk attribution is introduced, assigning risk values to objects based on their relative distance and motion proximity to the cyclist. Evaluation data and statistical analysis indicate that the categorization of risks through object detection and deep convolutional neural network-based risk scoring enhance classifier performance. The method achieves an 8% improvement in validation accuracy over the baseline, exceeding expectations.

A novel method using the RRT algorithm is introduced to create a safety-critical path by enforcing Control Barrier Functions and robot kinodynamic constraints while minimizing computation. This path planning framework incorporates robust Control Barrier Functions to account for uncertainties, ensuring the generated path is free from obstacles and adaptable to model inaccuracies. By integrating this approach, real-time paths with a guaranteed completion time and high success rate are achieved, along with the ability to operate without restarts even when uncertainties arise during navigation. The framework also reaches a near-optimal completion time due to its non-repeating nature. This approach forms the foundation for developing uncertainty-aware and obstacle-aware Control Barrier Functions, providing a comprehensive framework for general kinodynamic systems including non-linear robots.

A collection of proper subrings that together form a ring $R$ is known as a cover of $R$.
The smallest possible size of such a cover for $R$ is referred to as the covering number $\sigma(R)$ of $R$,
and if $\sigma(R)$ is less than the covering number of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is considered $\sigma$-elementary.
For rings with a unity, the size of a minimal cover of $R$ by subrings containing $1_R$ is defined as the unital covering number $\sigma_u(R)$,
and if $\sigma_u(R)$ is less than the unital covering number of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is $\sigma_u$-elementary.
The classification of all unital rings with the smallest possible size for their covering number $\sigma(R)$ or $\sigma_u(R)$
and the size of their covering number $\sigma(R)$ or $\sigma_u(R)$ is studied in this research paper.
Using the classification of all simple artinian rings with their respective covering numbers,
alongside specific examples not part of any artinian ring classification,
the paper reaches a comprehensive conclusion by categorizing all rings with their respective covering numbers.
The definitions of the new mathematical concepts introduced in this research can be found on MathSciNet.

Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, these networks lose their capacity for constraint and consequently remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Similar reasoning can be applied to other deep neural networks featuring skip connections. Moreover, we show that a new class of deep neural networks, namely Neural ODEs, has a weaker constraint which prevents excessive deviations in the outcome, thereby providing natural resilience against malicious inputs. In addition, based on the characteristics of Neural ODEs, we develop both a stochastic defense method and a deterministic defense strategy, which successfully protect the model against various forms of attacks. Experiments conducted across multiple datasets reveal the effectiveness of these methods.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the convolution of a given kernel and a solution, extensively applied to model vehicular traffic, have a singular local limit that has been extensively studied. This singular limit is about nonlocal solutions converging to the entropy-admissible solution of a classical conservation law with a point source, essentially replacing the convolution kernel with a delta function. In recent counter-examples it was shown that this singular limit doesn't necessarily converge for all cases, yet some specific results were proven for traffic models using anisotropic kernels under stringent assumptions, like an exponential kernel which exhibits algebraic identities or with particular initial conditions. In our research, we were able to derive general results of convergence for traffic models under the condition that are natural and in-line with real-life scenarios plus a strict requirement of the kernels being convex. We developed a comprehensive test for verifying if the obtained limit is entropy-admissible along with its convergence rate and showed through an example that convexity assumption is indeed necessary for our main convergence estimates.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps of varying scale within their atlases, whereas translation surfaces remain at a fixed size. A key feature of translation surfaces is the directional flow, which becomes a significant flow on dilation surfaces and is defined by the non-singular, scale-variant components. However, the flow's singularity is inherent in dilation surfaces with a scale factor greater than one, illustrating a distinct difference between these surfaces and their translation-based counterparts. Inspired by Brin's research linking recurrent points and hyperbolic behavior, we investigate how the existence of recurrent points affects the volume of sets within this flow. Notably, the volume of a given set can either decrease or remain constant when the dilation scale increases, depending on whether the surface's exponent is above or at 1. Additionally, we establish criteria for a typical point to exhibit specific dynamics when subjected to iterated non-singular maps.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as a biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed Correlation Explanation to estimate total correlation and verified the reliability of its estimates and clustering results against established standards. Furthermore, we validated the large scale connectivity network constructed from extensive open fMRI datasets by confirming its alignment with existing neuroscientific knowledge while also revealing additional relationships between brain regions. Lastly, we highlighted the utility of connectivity graphs derived from total correlation in identifying brain diseases.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles and the 
interplay between configuration space and phase space. This study generalizes 
those concepts to functions that use Clifford algebra. It defines unitary 
isomorphisms among spaces consisting of square-integrable Clifford algebra-valued 
functions on n-dimensional space, monogenic square-integrable functions on n+1 
dimensional space, and linear functionals on symmetric tensor elements in n 
dimensional space, each space weighted by a respective Gaussian measure.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative Monte Carlo techniques to simulate posterior distributions. Traditionally, Monte Carlo methods employ Markov Chain Monte Carlo or approximate Bayesian programs to sample posterior distributions. However, these methods fall short in handling intricate log-conjugate logics inherent to Gaussian processes. This paper proposes a Monte Carlo framework based on compound priors to efficiently tackle this challenge. The proposed method yields fast convergence, especially when comparing Gaussian processes with other Bayesian models, such as variational autoencoders. The capability of this method to handle non-stationary Gaussian processes, as well as its application in hierarchical models and the estimation of regression functions, is also highlighted. Furthermore, the paper outlines various Monte Carlo techniques commonly used as baselines and demonstrates the superiority of the proposed compound priors method over these benchmarks. The method is also shown to align with frequentist inferential accounts in certain scenarios.

This research demonstrates that in outdoor settings with wireless communications employing the IEEE 802.11 protocol using dipole antennas, ground reflection is a dominant signal propagation component. Consequently, the Two-Ray model effectively forecasts signal strength with a satisfactory degree of accuracy for this environment. Notably, the study's findings are pertinent to UAVs over short distances, which exhibit narrow altitude ranges with correspondingly low heights. To illustrate this point, we utilized a BEYONDIK mini USB dipole antenna situated 10 meters above the ground with a corresponding elevation angle ranging from 5 to 35 degrees. The results showed that the Two-Ray model's error margin was approximately 3 watts over this angle range. Moreover, the study examines the feasibility of employing the Two-Ray model in UAV settings with modest altitude variations.

The last ten years have been marked by significant breakthroughs in neutrino physics. Notably, multiple studies have conclusively proven the occurrence of neutrino flavor oscillation on a global scale. In addition, while the ultimate mixing pattern of neutrino remains unclear, multiple theories attempt to explain neutrino mass restrictions. Before the upcoming explosion in data from various ongoing and future experiments, a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art findings is presented, examining both the consequences of previously mentioned findings and potential novel discoveries.

Research on top tagging has advanced rapidly due to the top quark's substantial role in studying physics that goes beyond the standard model. Recent studies have found that machine learning techniques enhance tagging capabilities. This paper examines the application of tagger training data limitations in Markov chain simulations and real jet data, utilizing the top-tagging observations of a single jet. The study focuses on tagging events featuring a single jet from $t\bar{t}$ production, employing observations from Monte Carlo data to understand the current limits of top-tagging accuracy and their potential expansion with real jet data. The study assesses two popular top-tagging observables and a graph embedding method. The results indicate that the top-tagging accuracy of a single jet reaches remarkable levels, with top-tagging accuracy exceeding 80% for events featuring a single jet from $t\bar{t}$ production, achieving specificity levels of 50% - in line with the high expected branching fractions of exclusive top-tagging observables. The study finds that the top-tagging accuracy of a single jet reaches remarkable levels. The addition of real jet data is expected to significantly expand the discovery potential of top-tagging observables in future proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement refinement, abstractions of models, and concrete instantiations. The document also examines Virtual Organizations within these contexts.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

Two supersymmetry approaches are employed to formulate quantum mechanics and recursive determinants, which are then used to generalize the supersymmetry method beyond Gaussian matrices. By adapting the first scheme developed by SIGMAN and Fyodorov for real symmetric and antisymmetric matrices, we apply it to non-Gaussian ensembles of real symmetric and antisymmetric matrices, real band matrices, and real symmetric circulant matrices. Building on the supersymmetry method's potential for expanding real-time correlation functions of unfolded Gaussian matrices, we extend its application to non-Gaussian ensembles. In addition, we present a supersymmetry method for recursive determinants, which is limited to the one-dimensional supersymmetric $\graum$ matrix and is then used to generalize the limiting soft-exponent behavior of non-Gaussian ensemble eigenvalue distributions.

This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to forecast future frames and is widely applicable. One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among successive frames exacerbates long-term forecasting difficulties. The main goal of this research is to improve the forecast accuracy by reinforcing the connection between preceding contextual information and the current state. We enhance the standard Transformer architecture by incorporating: 1) a technique that focuses on capturing relevant contextual details while discarding insignificant transformations. 2) a future frames prediction task that facilitates mutual benefits through cross-learning. These modifications complement each other, leading to notable enhancements in forecasting performance. Our proposed approach, known as PL2, outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmark datasets. Specifically, it demonstrates relatively high performance compared to other approaches on BouncingBall and Human, while closely matching the performance on Biking. Importantly, our approach exhibits consistent superiority on recent datasets (Car, Swimmer, Diver, Surfer) that heavily emphasize spatiotemporal reasoning.

This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize safety features to prevent null pointer exceptions. Our investigation applies existing type systems for address management in imperative languages, specifically those used with trivial types, to the context of Tracing C. This type system, known as STAC, is capable of reducing the frequency of garbage walks in scenarios involving pointer-chasing scenarios. Nevertheless, the approach results in pseudo-immediate garbage collection in single-heap environments. While STAC is primarily designed for Tracing C, it can be used as a framework for analogous address management systems in other imperative languages featuring tracing garbage collection.

Theoretical particles called heavy neutral leptons have the potential to resolve long-standing problems in physics, particularly those related to the behavior of neutrinos. These particles, being unable to interact with the standard model in certain ways, can interact with normal matter only through specific interactions that involve large changes. If such particles exist and are present at any level, we would expect to observe them because of their unique interaction properties, which allow for suppression of certain types of decays. Researchers have searched for signs of these particles by studying how particles interact and change into other particles under various conditions. An analysis of data from high-energy particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider was conducted, using data from 139 events totaling 79.4 trillion particle interactions. The results of this analysis, which focused on whether these particles can appear alongside other particles and contribute to certain decay processes, did not provide any evidence for their presence. In the event ranges considered, the results provided limits on the presence of these particles for the first time in experiments involving high-energy particles collisions.

Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, allowing for the efficient decoding of polar codes at lower costs, such as using binary decoders for example. The cost reduction is achieved by applying a specific permutation model to the received vector, effectively converting it into a codeword within a specific code space. Current permutations, however, rely on an ad-hoc search for an optimal match, often involving comprehensive searches of the permutation lattice. Contrary to conventional methods, this paper presents a ground-breaking, constructive approach that generates optimal permutation patterns directly from the LLR values of received symbols, leveraging the theoretical foundations of permution decodin. Furthermore, the method facilitates the pattern-specific analysis of permutation patterns, allowing for better understanding and improved generalization. When tested under fixed error rates, the method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art permution decodin schemes, including the widely-used C1 permutation pattern-based decoder.

We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield point spread functions with well-defined properties. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  (1) We demonstrate that linear co-adding processes with linear inverse mapping preserve the point spread function. Consequently, algorithms with this property include weighted mean co-adding and discrete integrals of these methods. However, these linear algorithms fail to maximise the signal to noise ratio in image data.
  (2) We introduce a new concept - convex mean image (CMI) - which represents the most effective linear convolved mean image for a given set of data. This concept allows us to establish relationships between CMI and point spread function, as well as their independence in cases where convex mean image Co-adding is well-defined and independent of the input data. 
  (3) Our research shows that convex mean image for convex means and sigmoid algorithms retain their characteristics even after the polynomial expansion of their inputs. Furthermore, this convex mean image for polynomials has a piecewise polynomial structure.
  (4) Our algorithms based on convex mean image - convolution have been found to surpass traditional means and noise reduction through convolution in terms of point spread function quality. Nonetheless, neither convex mean image - convolution nor convex mean image for polynomials noise reduction through convolution achieve the maximum signal to noise ratio of polynomial fitting algorithms like MCM or their polynomial version

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in a deforming solid is governed by the collective movement of many dislocations. Critical to this analysis is the identification of a specific energy state that remains steady, serving as a benchmark for dislocation arrangement equilibrium. As a solid undergoes deformation, its dislocations continuously form, split, and merge in a perpetual cycle of rearrangement. This process is driven by the minimization of the solid's energy, with its toughness ultimately determined by the dislocations' configuration that achieves this optimized state. Moreover, the theory also predicts that pre-existing imperfections within the crystal can act as nucleation sites for dislocations, thereby influencing its fracture toughness. By integrating these findings with the established concept of Frank-Read loops, and along with a few simplified assumptions, the theoretical framework provides accurate predictions that align with existing experimental data across various materials systems, including metals, minerals, and crystals. This theoretical framework aspires to be even more comprehensive in its scope, with its ultimate goal of forecasting the fracture toughness of wide range of solid crystals with confidence.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops pairings for the Dyson model and the end-point tangent Dyson model, demonstrating that their correlation fields constitute Gaussian free fields on the Slonoskißk complex, a region formed by mirroring specific domains and their conjugates. We establish that, for the standard Dyson model, these pairings constitute spherical imaginary surfaces, while the end-point tangent Dyson model generates multiple types of imaginary surfaces that multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution curves correspond to, depending on the starting point.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for classical verification of quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3), significantly faster than an optimal protocol with time complexity of O(2^k|C|) assumed by some researchers. However, this protocol relies on the assumption that the server possesses knowledge of the circuit. To overcome this limitation, a new authentication protocol has been developed, utilizing entanglement check and randomness exchange, which achieves a substantially faster time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|), with an additional linear factor in the number of queries. Notably, this protocol's efficiency holds regardless of whether the quantum circuit is reversible or non-reversible in nature.

A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem, where its applications extend beyond digital currencies. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, known as LC4IoT. Simulations were conducted to test the performance of LC4IoT and revealed that the proposed approach consumes minimal computational power, storage space, and processing delay.

Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a generator network to optimize this representation, we successfully generated it using a latent code. Our results demonstrate the generated levels sets accurately match given reference signals and cell growth patterns. Additionally, the signed distance function representation facilitates efficient modeling of cell growth and division. Our contributions include the development of a novel representation for cell shapes, an unsupervised generator to create synthetic cell shapes, and an evaluation framework to assess the quality of synthetic data.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized in subsequent research to insert descriptions into audio narratives. The technique we present has shown effectiveness on both digital documents and those that have been scanned from print.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including several benchmark assessments, by substantial margins.

We've developed computational models aimed at assessing the influence of stellar activity on spectroscopic analysis of exoplanet transits, particularly focusing on atmospheric characterization, in systems with both low and high resolution spectroscopy capabilities. We've analyzed models representing hot Jupiters and super Earths around active stars, identifying patterns of starpots, bowlows, and changing starpots. We've discovered that for low-resolution spectroscopy, water features in exoplanet atmospheres are difficult to detect due to stellar contamination. In contrast, high-resolution spectroscopy enables the direct separation of planetary and stellar signals, allowing us to quantify the atmospheric composition of exoplanets. Nonetheless, stellar activity still poses a challenge in obtaining accurate atmospheric composition data, particularly with relaxation times close to or exceeding the duration of observations. We've also explored the feasibility of using narrow-band photometry as an alternative to reduce the impact of stellar activity on this type of spectroscopy.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. Its low mass and the presence of fluids against its body cause movement dynamics where drag forces overcome inertia, which can be explained using theories initially based on microorganisms. These theories are applicable to larger animals like this forficatus swimmers, which helps understand how movement is coordinated in the centipede at different swimming speeds. Its swimming motion can be broken down into distinct phases, each characterized by a specific type of wave pattern - head-to-tail, tail, and head waves - that transition gradually and move in the direction of the head. An empirical model that relates the centipede's swimming speed, based on observations and measurements, also reveals the role of hydrodynamics and limb movement in the movement dynamics of this species, as well as the presence of friction and fluid drag that determines its swimming style. Which type of wave pattern and movement pattern the centipede adopts depends on its swimming speed - fast centipedes exhibit head-to-tail waves with their limbs synchronized, slower ones exhibit tail waves, and the fastest ones exhibit head waves. Which type of wave pattern and movement pattern the centipede adopts also shows a strong correlation with body flexibility in the centipedes,

The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately model tsunami behavior that is affected by dispersal over long periods. Dispersive models are crucial in situations such as a massive ocean impact from an asteroid, and they are also essential in modeling complex events that involve the interaction of ocean waves with variable depth areas, such as high-speed collisions with low-lying coastlines. High-resolution simulations featuring detailed models like bathymetry and material properties are essential but become extremely computationally intensive, making it impractical using traditional methods in models based in the ocean and coastal field of study. A deep neural network powered Eulerian approach offers an alternative by using a special tensor transformation to replace spatial derivatives with grid information, allowing for high-precision results similar to traditional methods while also reducing computational costs associated with complex simulations. However, this approach is susceptible to errors in the model coefficients, and a new deep neural network powered approach using neural coefficients has been developed to automatically determine coefficients, allowing the model to accurately model complex events like tsunami propagation and ocean behavior. This approach has been successfully tested and validated, showing excellent agreement when compared against detailed models and experimental data, and has further reduced computational costs, allowing the deep neural network powered approach to outperform traditional methods.

Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV imaging taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. These galaxies have been referred to as HST-dark due to their elusive nature. Using high-resolution near-infrared imaging taken by the NIRCam camera, we have observed and analyzed the characteristics of 33 of these galaxies. These galaxies have been found to be highly obscured by dust, very massive, and highly star-forming at redshifts of 2 to 8. This study provides the largest inspection of a particular subset of these galaxies, known as UCDS galaxies, and reveals that these galaxies have larger and more extended regions than similar galaxies that have been observed in previous studies. These galaxies have also been found to have unique features such as large, extended regions of polarized light and large regions of reprocessed dust emission. The conditions required to explain the galaxies' observed polarization are consistent with the presence of small regions of molecular clouds where dust emission and light from rapidly moving dust particles are produced. These clouds are not typically thought to be able to influence the observed polarization, but the conditions required to explain the galaxies' observed polarization indicate that they are surrounded by large regions of approximately 500 to 1000 parsecs in length. This is larger than typical regions and may be due to a particular mechanism known as turbulence which helps to spread out regions of gas within galaxies, an indication that these galaxies are large, discrete objects

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we form a novel seven-dimensional theory of gravity. Depending on the constants involved, this theory falls into either Type I or Type D classifications within the single-field Lagrangian framework. We analyze a subset of solutions that satisfy a four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space and find that static, spherically-symmetric black holes emerge. These black holes possess properties analogous to seven-dimensional topologically charged black holes and are either extremal or regular. Notably, when the theory is of Type I, it yields a black hole with an surface similar to $\RP^6$, while a type-D theory displays adherence to $\SO7$ symmetry. Additionally, we recover Bergshoeff-Köse-Samuel-Sen solution when a specific rotation is applied to the Reissner-Nordström black hole.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure all the disks come into contact with one of the container's walls when in a jammed state, resulting from a combination of external forces such as moderate pressure, gravity, and random vibrations. By dividing the disk arrangement into segments and analyzing particle motion patterns, researchers develop jamming patterns and microstates, and then use a simplified mapping to derive compact, visually interpretable expressions for pressure, potential energy, and other system characteristics at equilibrium. This analytical framework enables researchers to compare measured and calculated data for systems at different sizes and find they match under specific conditions, specifically when the disk sequence follows a particular pattern. However, it's found that random disk placement leads to significant discrepancies between measured and calculated system characteristics. Additionally, researchers observe the presence of local, temporary fluctuations within jammed systems and study the correlation between these fluctuations across the disk arrangement.

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes consistent statistical dependencies across various ENSO phases, a notion not necessarily supported. We statistically examined the likelihood of co-occurring between extreme precipitation and the occurrence of East Pacific and Central Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na across the world's landmass. Through statistical analysis and mapping, we found distinct regional patterns of strong correlations between precipitation and the occurrence of these two main ENSO flavors. The results show that East Pacific and Central Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na have unique patterns of co-occurring with extreme precipitation. We observed that East Pacific types are more likely to occur alongside La Ni\~na in eastern Africa and southern Africa, whereas central precipitation anomalies are more likely in northern Africa and southern South America with Central Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na. Moreover, East Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na are more likely to occur alongside southern Africa precipitation anomalies and central precipitation anomalies are more likely with East Pacific types of both El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na in southern Africa. These distinct regional patterns highlight the differing impacts of East Pacific and Central Pacific types on the

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to mechanical pressure, the distortion they undergo may deviate from expected behavior, even within their elastic range. The extent of nonaffine behavior, a concept observed in various numerical models, poses a significant challenge to experimental studies due to its low amplitude and localized nature within the material's complex network. A new technique has been developed to analyze this nonaffine contribution through changes in frequency within certain tests. The technique involved analyzing two types of systems, solid rods and glass beads, using two distinct methods: one based on patterns of cracking and the other on patterns of congestion. The results from these studies provided insights consistent with theoretical predictions regarding nonaffine behavior's effect on material consistency, the effect of geometric characteristics on nonaffine behavior, and the role of nonaffine behavior in determining the material's overall properties.

This research investigates a population model, factoring in the effects of age and environmental pollution, comprising a single population with distinct larval and adult stages. The model uses logistic functions, influenced by the per capita growth rate and environmental toxicity, and is relaxed to an almost periodic class. Relying on the Schauder fixed point theorem and Lyapunov's direct method, we demonstrate the existence of single-species larval and adult coexistence equilibria, and show their uniqueness under specific conditions. Furthermore, we examine the impact of environmental pollution on adult populations and derive sufficient criteria for their asymptotic behavior using the theory of almost periodic functions. Building on these findings, we extend our analysis to a two-population competition model and derive conditions for the long-term coexistence of both species and the dominance of an adult population, assuming the environment is uniform.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, which is a type of mathematical logic system. This logic system, which focuses on the structure of language, is proven to be completely rational, meaning it is both strongly finite and has a unique model characteristically. This achievement is made possible by first establishing a correspondence between cut-free derivations in the extensions and labeled proof trees, and then developing model-theoretic criteria that can be used to assess the rationality of these derivations. This breakthrough extends the researchers' previous work on a smaller subset of the extensions, which was found to be capable of forming a strictly developing sequence.

Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value but maintaining their integrity is a difficult task due to constant updates. Current methods often employ Euclidean metric topology, but this is not a natural fit as it is better suited to representing geographical data. Hyperbolic geometry more naturally models hierarchical relationships, yet few systems utilize this metric for taxonomy maintenance. We developed HyperLeR, an innovative approach that leverages negative sampling to generate graph embeddings in hyperbolic space, making it particularly well-suited for hierarchical taxonomies. When compared to state-of-the-art techniques applied on both Euclidean and hyperbolic taxonomies, HyperLeR demonstrated superior performance in query tasks, as measured by MRR. Additionally, HyperLeR's integration with existing taxonomy enhancement methods enhanced subsystem performance.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the dipole electric properties of molecular dimers in the S66 dataset using a highly advanced theoretical framework, namely CCSD(T)-F12b/aug-cc-pVDZ-F12 as a reference. When the external electric field is applied, the dipole electric properties of molecular dimers primarily experience two main influences: the polarization and hyper-polarization effects. The polarization effect manifests itself through significant dipole moments when the molecules' dipoles are aligned parallel to the intermolecular axis. Hyper-polarization effects, on the other other hand, arise due to the coupling between the monomer dipoles and high-order electric multipoles. By examining the contribution of nine types of hyper-polarization effects, it has been found that the rotationally induced effects in polar and, to a lesser extent, in charge-transfer complexes exhibit the most pronounced effects. Charge-transfer diels-alder (CTDA) and hydrogen-bonding complexes, however, were found to have weaker hyper-polarization effects which can be attributed to the restricted mobility of monomer charge transfer sites. Furthermore, the obtained results have been validated by comparing them with the levels of theory of CCSD(aug-cc-pVDZ).

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and efficiency, incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems for enhanced planning and scheduling. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in environmental factors and dynamic demand often cause discrepancies in initial schedule estimations. Insufficient real-time updates of schedule adjustments resulting from varying uncertainty levels across processing stages contribute to increased non-productive storage, delaying shipments and necessitating on-line adjustment of internal schedules to maintain agility and competitiveness. To tackle these challenges, we propose a context-aware learning-based approach for real-time navigation in complex industrial networks, incorporating a level of fuzziness to account for uncertain environmental factors and dynamic task adaptations. Our method combines two decision-making components: the first handles uncertainty using fuzzy numbers and probabilistic learning, while the second incorporates learned expectations for task adaptations. Our approach was tested using two real-world scenarios, with successful results demonstrating an average improvement of 8% for navigating network paths and up to a 25% reduction in shipment delays.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated through the use of case studies, marking a breakthrough in understanding multi-dimensional resiliency semantics.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and axion quark nuggets, employing accelerometers in a network configuration and discusses how atomic interferometry-based networks might enhance these searches.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t is given by \[ \Delta u - \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla u = (au + b) \log u \] where a, b, and \phi are smooth, positive functions on the manifold, and \phi satisfies specific growth conditions based on the Lagrange bound with parameters s and p. Our estimate reveals the influence of the external potential \phi and the parameter a on the behavior of u. Notably, when a = 1, we obtain an anisotropic version of Hamilton's estimate, while for general a, we establish a generalized version of Li-Ni's estimate for the fundamental solution of the heat equation.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a broad class of mathematical models, widely used for analyzing sequential data in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and signal processing. HMMs consist of an unobservable state sequence, observed data, and state transition probabilities. The Markov property restricts the influence of states to the immediate previous state. We developed two novel HMM variants: the "path-restricted" HMM, limiting state transitions to a predefined path, and the "cluster-markov," grouping states with limited transitions and allowing inter-group transitions. We introduced advanced training algorithms for these modified HMMs using the EM algorithm and derived specialized inference formulas for each model type. Our approach bypasses complex Bayesian network calculations, yielding straightforward solutions. We validated our approach with synthetic data, creating HMMs from individual states, paths, or clusters, and observed accurate model reconstruction in most cases. However, the accuracy depended on various factors, including the model type, state number, observed data sequence length, and noise level. In cases far beyond typical HMM applications, our approach demonstrated resilience and provided straightforward solutions.

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field is represented as a continuous non-linear Markov process. Unlike regular white noise, the stochastic force relies on the local turbulent transport coefficient. Our work confirms various statistical characteristics of turbulent transport, including the zero-mean and local balance properties, as well as the establishment of an expression for the turbulent transport coefficient related to the correlation function of the velocity field at a scale larger than the turbulent intermittency parameter. Our approach also enables the exploration of turbulent diffusion in inhomogeneous conditions and their implications on the statistical properties of turbulent transport. Our theory aligns with the observations from numerical simulations and experimental data on turbulent transport in various applications, including turbulent convection, turbulent diffusion, and turbulent intermittency.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a complete understanding of the dynamics behind nucleon-nucleus and
nucleus-nucleus scattering. When phenomenological models are limited, they
often end up with a degree of ambiguity. We suggest that nuclear folding
models can more effectively assess the reliability of the nuclear density and
ground state wave function derived from the investment of energy in the 32Si+32Si
system. Furthermore, the conventional method for calculating the Iwata et al.
potential at zero distance may cause model uncertainties, which can be
mitigated by utilizing the microscopic density to calculate the potential at
close proximity.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation behavior in a thin conductor plate separated by two large parallel walls at a temperature $T$, where the plate's area is $A$ and the distance between the walls and plate's thickness is much smaller than $T$. It contrasts the radiation behavior with that of an ideal gas at low temperatures ($T_{gas}$) by deriving the number of radiation particles ($N$) using a single particle Schrödinger-Planck equation and applying the Dirac-Boltzmann distribution, both at high and low temperatures. At high temperatures, $N$ is directly proportional to $T_{gas}^3$ (as for an ideal gas) and increases as the slab distance ($d$) raises to the fourth power. Conversely, at low temperatures ($T_{low}=\hbar\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{2}}$), $N$ is independently proportional to both $T_{low}$ and $A$, indicating that the radiation particles are non-diverging at low temperatures ($N_{low}$) and suggesting a quantum liquid where no thermal expansion occurs. Moreover, $N_{low}$ is also independently proportional to $d^3$. Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework demonstrates that strong relationships between locations significantly increase privacy costs, such as those found in public transportation routes from multiple users. Our approach, therefore, enables informed decisions on relationships between locations and the relative anonymity of users in location-based services.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves as a crucial component in lidar-based mapping and navigation systems. The development of effective place recognition systems relies heavily on the utilization of relevant datasets. The existing datasets, however, predominantly comprise recordings from urban environments, leaving a need for a dataset specifically designed to facilitate the development of place recognition algorithms tailored to rural and camping settings. The CamLoc dataset, comprising 12,000 3D point clouds, provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on rural and camping place recognition tasks. The integrated CamLoc+RGB-D dataset, comprising 20,000 point clouds and corresponding color images, offers a substantial resource for researchers and practitioners to further refine their methods. The CamLoc dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/ciepiteso/CamLoc_Dataset.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in subsequent data analysis. In this research, we studied how multisite study design affects our ability to detect significant differences in functional connectivity between two groups when using statistical tests. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we discovered that multisite studies actually increase our ability to detect meaningful group differences, contrary to our initial assumptions. By utilizing data collection efficiencies and statistical methods that account for within-site variability, we are now capable of identifying group disparities at a significance level equivalent to that of single-site studies, while also enhancing our overall analysis power. This is made possible through the implementation of a novel statistical metric, called the sensitivity index, which serves as a comprehensive performance evaluator and can be used to guide optimal data collection strategies within a general framework applicable to various research contexts.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language mixing in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are unable to efficiently capture the characteristics of code-mixed languages 
due to insufficient training data, necessitating novel research directions. 
Aggressive and conservative methods currently offer the best available 
solutions; however, multiple alternative approaches remain unexplored. 
Code-mixed language processing poses significant challenges in relation to 
word embedding technology, particularly when compared to processing languages 
with consistent patterns of mixing and matching words. On the other hand, 
code-mixed languages present opportunities for innovation due to their 
unique characteristics. In this paper, we focus on understanding the nature of 
code-mixed language switch points and explore novel representations in this 
area. Our findings are derived from extensive experiments with over 310 million 
word pairs extracted from mixed Hindi-English and Bengali-English language tweets.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly alters the predicted critical temperature, decreasing it by up to 30% compared to previous studies. Furthermore, we found that the density of states plays a crucial role in determining the rate of superconducting gap coefficient at low energies, which is influenced by phonon frequencies at the 40-60 meV gap. This finding implies that the superconducting gap has the potential to split into multiple components near the Fermi surface holes with different curvatures.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are often unsuccessful without pre-compiled maps or when real-time mapping is challenging due to limited sensor data, high processing costs, and uncertainty in map metrics. In response to these limitations, we introduce a learning-based method to generate map data using an MDP model. This approach employs an encoder-decoder structure to derive a spatial boundary strategy for navigation, requiring minimal training data to generate a search space for navigation in dynamic environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel learning-based map data generator through successful navigation of the Akara dataset, outperforming a state-of-the-art method in this domain.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve high accuracy under both real-world and simulated scenarios.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also exhibits uniform convergence to a conditioned ergodic distribution, which in turn converges to a quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific local interactions.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise total invariant interpretation for its order n=1 mod 2 case; whereas its occurrence at an odd order n case involves the framing ambiguity that characterizes it. Moreover, we've proven that, for its odd order n case, the direct cocycle integration results in a variant of the Chern-Simons invariant, with the determinant factor included explicitly.

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models and considers how upcoming measurements of the SM-like Higgs and Z-pole may influence allowed model parameters. Based on a global analysis of two Higgs doublet models using the GAMBIT tool, our study takes into account numerous recent experimental constraints. We find that for certain model input parameters, future precision measurements could significantly restrict the model's parameter space, with some scenarios potentially being already at the limit of acceptability according to the LHC experiments' 95% confidence criteria.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles with tailored hydrophobic sections, allowing them to trigger surface assembly and form complex structures within aqueous environments. Evolutionary optimization enables novel particle designs capable of producing robust, long-lasting surfaces on spherical templates to generate hydrophobically bound helical structures, whereas previously designed particles were limited to either one of these assembly outcomes. What's more, our results reveal a previously unexplored area within the particle design space where certain particles trigger rapid, explosive surface assembly, resulting in persistent structures with exceptionally high energies.

Our research appears to suggest a dynamical-Higgs-phase outcome in a broad range of chiral gauge theories, particularly those that are strongly-coupled. In contrast, a different scenario featuring flavor symmetric vacuums with massless baryonlike composite fermions does not seem as likely. The possibility of formulating a strong-anomaly effective action, similar to one applied to QCD, could also be involved in the dynamical-Higgs-phase outcome. This could potentially be achieved with an modified QCD equation that incorporates an auxiliary Higgs field that has a non-zero value. Similarly, using a different type of equation that incorporates a non-zero F-term ferromagnetic correlation may also be possible. These modified equation of motion operators could be viewed as a type of sigma-model dual description, providing an alternative to the more conventional scenario featuring flavor symmetric massless composite fermions.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input forces and output velocities in stationary Navier-Stokes equations and derive some functional analysis conclusions. These findings imply that the Navier-Stokes equation is well-established for cases where the spatial dimension is 3 or higher and the frequency is greater than the dimension divided by 2. In contrast, we demonstrate that the equation loses its stability in cases where the frequency is less than one-half the spatial dimension. Notably, our methods show that the equation's sensitivity to input forces is directly related to the properties of the involved operator when the frequency is subcritical, whereas when the frequency is critical or supersymmetric, the equation enters a state of parameter independence, rendering its stability certain, which partially validates a conjecture put forth by Tsurumi.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now susceptible to a polynomial-time key recovery attack under certain circumstances. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest employing subcodes to conceal the secret codes in Modification 1. Meanwhile, in Modification 2, we combine the secret matrix with a randomly selected low column rank matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Theoretical analysis confirms that both alterations offer resistance to the current range of structural attacks. Moreover, we utilize the systematic generator matrix for the public code, resulting in a public-key size reduction, as well as greater resistance to attacks, more compact public keys and higher information transmission rates.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations of
infrequent words. This paper investigates a novel method to address this issue by
leveraging dictionaries like Wiktionary to define rare words. The rare word's
definition is added to the input text, along with two novel tasks: word and
sentence alignment. This enhanced model, Dict-BERT, is evaluated on various NLP
benchmarks and shows significant improvement in processing rare words and
overall performance on NLP tasks.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight convergence. In this work, we investigate the distribution of weights of a minimum spanning acycle when only partial data is available. Our findings include that the empirical distribution of acycle weights is connected to the structure that results when complementary parts are analyzed and that expected convergence holds even with partial data. Additionally, we observe that the structure that results from combining independent graphs also leads to the same distribution of weights. In the process of these mathematical advancements, we reveal a connection between submodular libraries and the well-known modular lattice of partitions, and we also show the relationship between the multi-dimensional generalized hat graph and the minimum spanning acycle in certain complexes, further extending the known "hat theorem" to these higher dimensions.

In this context, we explore the concept of federated learning (FEL), a decentralized form of machine learning (ML) that addresses the issues associated with data localization. FEL allows multiple participants, each with their own datasets, to train a high-quality machine learning model without needing the actual training data to be present in the same location. There are primarily two approaches to FEL: horizontal and vertical federated learning. In horizontal FEL, participants contribute the same data distribution to the training process. In vertical FEL, multiple participants contribute individual attributes of the training data, creating a unified distribution. Given these varying approaches and the uniqueness of the field, research on vertical FEL and horizontal FEL are relatively isolated from each other. Nonetheless, there are concepts that apply equally across the board. One such concept is the training-test data imbalance, which can have far-reaching effects by influencing model parameters. Balancing the learning process, therefore, becomes paramount. This work aims to become a comprehensive reference on balancing the learning process in FEL by integrating established concepts with cutting-edge solutions, with an emphasis on test-data imbalance. By reviewing and exploring mitigation strategies in the context of single and double federated learning, this work aims to highlight current limitations and identify promising areas for further study. Moreover, this work aims to identify and discuss key challenges and opportunities within the broader FEL imbalance framework, opening doors for future research.

Baryogenesis via R-parity violating supersymmetry is referred to as $B$-Mesogenesis. A novel $CP$-violating mode where a $B$ meson decomposes into a proton and a $\pi^-$. The associated amplitude is evaluated and found to be highly sensitive to the $B$-$\Lambda$ transition matrix element, demonstrating its potential to contribute significantly to $CP$ asymmetry with a large magnitude and being in line with theoretical constraints on the related phase.

In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interconnected cyber and social layers, safeguarding public safety is becoming increasingly complex. To address this challenge, this study develops a sophisticated mathematical model that simulates the interactions and resource allocations between agencies when faced with terrorist attacks on both physical and cyber-social targets. The proposed model, Smart City Defense Game, considers the interactions among three players, each having a limited budget, as they defend their territories from a common enemy, the Terrorist Organization. Each layer includes multiple targets, and the defense outcome depends on the relative allocation of resources by the respective agency and the Terrorist Organization. Players can share resources, but there are shared risks involved. We have shown the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium for this game, and the defense outcome depends on several factors, including the relative budgets of the agencies and the Terrorist Organization's strategy. The model includes two utility functions for each agency: one that maximizes the number of targets defended and another that accounts for the risk involved in the defense effort. Our analysis reveals that certain conditions must be met for certain properties to hold true. A practical implementation of this model is demonstrated using Seattle as a Smart City example. The model's accuracy was verified through field testing of its application in Defense of Seattle.

Researchers examined the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe. They considered these black holes within a container-like space and analyzed their physical properties under varying pressure and volume to determine thermodynamic stability. Through an advanced phase transition technique, a phase diagram was created and a pivotal temperature was identified for black holes at a critical point. This temperature was found to be in line with previously established results and was further generalized to include electric charge. A parametric study of the critical temperatures was also conducted and the findings were validated by matching thermodynamic equations with established black hole thermodynamics. Ultimately, this research explored the relationship between Einstein's and Maxwell's equations and the underlying physical principles of black holes and their connection to cosmic phenomena.

Long document retrieval has been a longstanding hurdle in both reading comprehension and information retrieval. Recent pre-training models have shown potential in addressing this challenge, particularly in the retrieval and ranking stages of long documents. Nonetheless, issues persist in the realm of long document ranking, such as the presence of noisy labels and the challenges posed by unbalanced sampling of long documents. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach comprising a bag-based sampling method and the group-wise listwise ranking model GGCLST. The latter builds upon leading listwise ranking models by introducing a multi-group convolutional layer. Through thorough experiments on two benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach in outperforming the state-of-the-art by nearly 7% in terms of precision at 5th position.
