Our investigation involved the use of muon spin relaxation and specific heat measurements to study the magnetic properties of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ systems in the range of $x = 0.3-0.7$. The results indicated that this series exhibits ferromagnetic properties above a certain temperature threshold. Based on the phase transition behavior, a T$_{MI}$ model was applied, revealing a critical temperature ($T_{MI}$) of 0.026 $\mu_B$. The data also showed that for compositions over $x \approx 0.6$, CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ exhibits intermediate magnetic properties, with a saturation magnetization ($M_{sat}$) increasing nearly proportional to $x$. In contrast, the low-field muon spin relaxation rate ($\frac{1}{T_{1}}$) showed a marked decline with increasing $x$. These findings suggest the occurrence of electronic spin diffusion and slow magnetic fluctuations at lower temperatures in the range of $x = 0.3-0.7$. Additionally, we found that $T_{1}$ is influenced by dynamic spin fluctuations of the Ce ions. Our analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of combining muon spin relaxation and specific heat measurements in the study of magnetic properties.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, 20cm spectral line observations were conducted across 86 high-mass star-forming regions, yielding a total of 57 radio detection of HI narrow-line self-absorption. The study found that about 64% of upper-mass stellar objects were associated with such regions, revealing that HI narrow-line self-absorption is prevalent in regions driven by high-mass stars. It was also discovered that HI narrow-line self-absorption is more frequently found towards regions with larger hydrogen density gradients. The study further indicates that high-mass star-forming regions generally have lower velocities of ~1.12 km/s and wider velocity spreads of ~42.56 km/s. The observed scatter in specific observed measures can be largely accounted for by both region size and velocity spread. It was also discovered that there is a moderate correlation between linearly extended regions and certain velocity characteristics.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. Specifically, we've developed an explicit local characteization of these transformations, revealing the conditions under which they correspond to actual beta-transformations. Building upon this, we've gained new insights into the behavior of beta-transformations with a hole at zero, including how they fit into the larger landscape of transformation maps.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 1/fb of pp collision data gathered at a 7 TeV energy level by the LHCb detector, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on the obtained data. As a result, phi_s was estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, in alignment with the Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, their findings revealed no indication of direct CP violation.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation.

In finite fields of dimension 2, an arc is a subset where no 3 points share a line. To determine the total number of such arcs, a specific counting method is employed, involving the intersection of 3 distinct lines. For a fixed set of points, we calculate a logarithmic correction to the main term in an enumeration of intersections with 3 distinct lines, also accounting for double counting due to collinear points. Beyond its application in counting arcs, this correction term has implications for a range of related problems in combinatorial geometry.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by illustrating the triangle corresponding to the subset $\{4, 5, 8, 11\}$ when $n$ is $10$.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations for groups of cases (e.g., graphs of the same class). To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel explainer for GNNs, PGExplainer, which parameterizes explanation generation using a deep neural network to explain multiple instances collectively and displays superior performance on three benchmark datasets compared to the state-of-the-art on graph classification and regression tasks, while also improving interpretability of more complex GNN models.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in linear time complexity. We further propose a universal postsynaptic function for several types of neural networks, including transformers, where a single parameter controls the risk of information overflow in the hidden state. Our improved Legendre model achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex datasets such as IMDB movie reviews and Amazon product metadata while utilizing significantly fewer parameters and undergoing at least five fewer matrix multiplications.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's implicit structure, and the fundamental forces of nature.  A new class of experiments, including particle observatories and laboratory-based research projects, is being developed to detect the signs of feebly interacting particles such as dark matter and new fundamental components of physics.  These experiments and the underlying research initiatives are described below, focusing on their potential to contribute to the discoveries anticipated in the field of fundamental physics and cosmology.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's framework, and language learning occurs within geographical locations where the language is spoken. This study develops a theory by which languages spread and monolingual individuals isolate themselves in specific areas, and we have formulated this theory into a mathematical model. Our primary findings are that the migration of individuals triggers an exponential growth of languages in each location at their beginning, but this eventually becomes slow and stable over time. When individual migration rates vary, one language dominates while the others fade away. Our research also reveals that if each location initially has multiple languages, homogeneous languages will form and isolate themselves within that location. Our mathematical findings match real-world patterns and the Aztec boomerang graph model provides a suitable method for analyzing this language spread model.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal results, particularly when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have investigated how PINNs train these functions. Our findings indicate that network width plays a crucial role in PINN convergence, with larger widths allowing the network to capture the target function's high-frequency features. However, this comes at the cost of increased training instability. Our study further reveals that using regularization can help in PINN training by mitigating complexity-related issues. However, this method's effectiveness diminishes with higher target function frequencies. Moreover, our research shows that wider neural networks with regularization can converge to the optimal solution for functions containing low-frequency patterns, but this is not possible for functions with high-frequency patterns. To overcome this limitation, we have explored an alternative method of enhancing PINN sensitivity by employing higher-order finite difference derivatives based on sampling patterns. This method allows us to accurately approximate derivative values even with a low number of samples, particularly for functions with high-frequency patterns. We have successfully applied this technique to train neural networks in conjunction with finite difference derivatives. Our results demonstrate that this hybrid approach enables the training of wider neural networks to capture high-frequency patterns, thereby surpassing the limitations of conventional PINN algorithms.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping in the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly due to the waves being coupled and the damping only being in one part of the domain, resulting in a exponential decay of the system's energy with a decay constant dependent on the frequency. By applying the Riesz potential inverse method to the frequency domain equation, we obtain an equation describing the decay rate of the system's energy which has a decay constant $\gamma(\nu)$. We use the behavior of this function as $\nu$ approaches infinity to determine that the system's energy decays at a rate greater than $t^{-\frac{1}{6}}$.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs underscore the importance of efficiency, while improved transparency via more interpretable models fosters trust from users. In this research, we present a novel hierarchical approach to deep RL by combining symbolic methods, leveraging a symbolic state model to enhance data-efficiency and introduce policy interpretability. The proposed framework includes a high-level agent, task solver, and symbolic state model. Through the development of a new symbolic RL algorithm using inductive logic programming, we achieve policy interpretability through the transformation of the deep policy network into logical rules that govern state transitions and action taking. Experimental results showcase the transparency benefits of our approach while remaining competitive in terms of efficiency with original deep methods.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes and a 2.25π efficiency in quasi-circulators. We also demonstrated the ability of our method to direct optical power within multiplex applications. The ability to operate at ambient conditions, combined with the exceptional performance, makes our method an excellent solution for nonreciprocal optical applications.

We expand upon the research initiated by P. L. Bellman in the 1950s and 1960s, specifically his work on concave kernel functions, to address a broader category of reticulated functions defined as products of multiple kernel functions. This generalization is applied to the fields of real analysis, geometry, and topology, with implications for (a) identifying optimal solutions and understanding local maxima in extremal problems, (b) forming a framework with modified Lévy-Khinchin and Bochner theorems for reticulated entire functions, and (c) developing an innovative method to construct general homology and extremal problems as reticulated with convex kernel functions. This new technique is capable of providing alternative solutions to K. Köhler's Extremal Problems and is compatible with reticulated semigroups of operators.

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than an GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li protons and neutrons, made feasible through updated nuclear matrix calculations for this specific lithium isotope. By utilizing data collected by a CRESST prototype using LiAlO$_2$ and tested above ground in Munich, Germany, we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations to improve our detection of spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and neutrons, particularly significant for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ where improvements of over two orders of magnitude are seen compared to previously published results with the same data.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. This is achieved by controlling the number of Gaussian kernels in the blend, resulting in a complex objective function. Theoretical evaluations demonstrate that as the number of kernels increases, closed-form estimates for certain function characteristics improve. This is accompanied by tighter lower bounds for estimation error. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this method for restoring blurred images.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation with weight -1 can be embedded in a pre-Lie module under specific conditions. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-algebras based on different Rota-Baxter operators of degree 1 and and also derive a natural extension of the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of second order from a covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and the development
of strong reasoning frameworks for logic and function declarations provide a
solid foundation for effectively applying Hoare logic through symbolic manipulation.
This research showcases a case where Hoare logic was utilized to securely test
a Smart Contract using DeepHoare, a novel tool combining semantic parsing and
automatic reasoning. The results obtained through testing demonstrate that
DeepHoare can efficiently process logic-based smart contract declarations and
perform sound and comprehensive Hoare verification.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and ensure the consistent, fault-tolerant agreement of values across the network.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs before presenting novel research findings where we utilize neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods to determine the lateral mobility of cholesterol within lipid bilayers. Furthermore, we utilize the soft-particle model to calculate the effective viscosity and elastic constant of the cholesterol, finding that cholesterol has a minimal impact on the bending modulus but substantial effect on the viscosity of the lipid bilayer.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model's, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_c}{4}$, indicating that quantum gravity effects begin earlier than previously thought and also that a larger phase space volume exists at the bounce than previously anticipated. Furthermore, the model presents a Mottola-Schwartz mode that remains smooth across the bounce, with its node's location dependent on the matter density within the system.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles at the energy 
frontier, spanning $8.7-19.3$ EeV. Analyzing these events, 34 of which were 
captured on camera, allows for accurate measurement of the area where the 
protons entering Earth's atmosphere interact, spanning approximately $35$ 
metric acres. By correlating a $3\sigma$ circle around each shower with $20$ 
point measurements, researchers can precisely map the projection of the 
proton shower's direction entering Earth's atmosphere. Our comprehensive 
analysis, combining contextual information, detector readings, and thorough 
 inspections of the event sites, along with an in-depth examination of eight 
"bright" events with exceptionally well-defined signatures, including a six-fold 
replay of the same shower, recorded at the energy $18.3$ EeV. Our findings 
suggest an exceptionally concentrated area for the projection of the proton 
shower's direction, spanning approximately $35$ metric acres in diameter, with 
a focus radius of around $45.5$ meters, thus shedding new light on an old 
enigma of high-energy physics and reinforcing the hypothesis of the "probe" 
model of extragalactic sources of cosmic rays.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of precision in their output predictions, which hinders the performance of downstream tasks such as robotic control and robotic surgery. This issue is particularly severe when the predictions involve spatial data with high dimensionality, such as the position of bones during surgery. This research develops an output refinement module to enhance the accuracy of predictive spatial data by utilizing a sequence of reference points derived from a 3D mesh model of an object. The model represents these reference points as a set of interdependent latent variables and learns their underlying distribution through a sequence-to-sequence generative neural network. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this module using a realistic simulation of laparoscopic surgery and showcases its practical application in a medical robotics project.

The traffic estimation field heavily relies on using traffic sensor data to develop models that anticipate future traffic. Breaking down test data into smaller overlapping sections allows traffic forecasting models to produce predictions at specific locations and time points. However, using these segments has a drawback - it limits the model's ability to generalize when it's subjected to a test involving traffic from a entirely different location, which is precisely what happens when traffic from one city is used to test a model trained on data from another city. In this research, we investigate how using partially overlapping sections impacts the accuracy of our traffic predictions, and propose resampling test data so that only non-overlapping sections are preserved to improve the performance of our models under these challenging conditions. Our proposal was put to the test against three different traffic estimation methods which included Feed-Forward NNs, Bidirectional LSTM networks, and Bidirectional GRUs. The results of our trials both in the laboratory and in real-life conditions involving two different cities have shown a notable enhancement in the performance of our models. Specifically, we achieved an average improvement of around 4% across all the evaluation metrics we used, including Mean Square Error and Mean Absolute Error.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical moves, called'red' equations, and an infinite set of 'black' equations. We've also discovered a link between the concept of 'asymptotic coherence' in strict $n$-categories and what we're calling 'weak asymptotic coherence' in Gray categories. To prove coherence in Gray categories, which may not be strict, we use a specific type of coherent rewriting system, which generates an infinite set of red equations and an infinite set of black equations.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about performance when applied to other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We developed and validated a domain-adadaptation technique using uncertainty-based mapping to improve segmentation when data distributions significantly change. We tested it on a epilepsy dataset, with the added constraint of partial domain labeling, presenting an unusual challenge in epilepsy due to data scarcity and significant shifts between training and testing distributions. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with improved performance on epilepsy data. We also incorporated the uncertainty map into a patch-based alignment framework, resulting in further enhanced segmentation performance.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry bears no quantitative significance in distinguishing the quantum pigeonhole effect from classical scenarios.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is developed for protons within the proton radiation belt, taking into account proton interactions with the Earth's magnetic field and atmospheric penetration to model loss rates. This is complemented by a steady-state model that balances proton generation and loss rates to obtain the spatial distribution of protons at different energies. Utilizing a Monte Carlo method, the proton radiation distribution is simulated for various energy ranges and at different spatial locations. Our findings, which are compared with existing data, demonstrate that the CRAND source model can accurately capture the general distribution of proton radiation. Consequently, this model provides a reliable basis for designing space missions operating at low Earth orbit and below.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks and 
predicting their performance capabilities. Research has demonstrated a positive 
correlation between expressivity and the achievable accuracy of neural networks 
and other complex models. Building on existing research, a new framework has been 
developed to quantify the expressivity limitations of neural networks and identify 
the optimal trade-off between expressivity and computational cost. By balancing 
these factors, a new optimization method is proposed, yielding faster convergence 
when testing different hidden layer configurations in kinetic neural networks.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, the performance
of this Huber mechanism is evaluated systematically along with two established
noise-based approaches in matrix completion. Experimental findings indicate that
the Huber mechanism surpasses the other methods while exhibiting features of
robust estimation. Furthermore, an exploration of the trade-offs between noise
addition and performance degradation reveals that the Huber mechanism yields
more favorable outcomes with substantially reduced amount of added noise.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research.

Research on exoplanets has led to groundbreaking discoveries surrounding low-mass stars, like TRAPPIST-1, which holds the record for most planets discovered, with eight, and orbits an ultracool dwarf star in the habitable zone. To understand planetary orbit radii and masses, researchers have analyzed data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and the American Space Agency's (NASA) existing astronomical databases for transiting and non-transiting planets, including those around low-mass stars. Based on their findings, scientists now estimate that planets with minimum masses between 2.6 and 21.1 times that of Earth likely orbit within 20.4 astronomical units of their host stars, with an 80% chance of this range extending up to 50 astronomical units. While our current data reveals no planets around low-mass stars with orbital periods below 10 days, it appears unlikely that any such planets could exist, given our current understanding of astrophysical laws. With our detection of planets around host stars weighing just 0.08 times that of the sun having masses over 2.6 times that of Earth, we have effectively expanded the known range of planetary orbit radii by at least 50%. Our analysis also indicates that planets with orbital periods above 50 days likely lie outside an existing observational boundary, suggesting that planets with minimum masses between 0.25 and 0.08 times that of the sun likely do not exist around stars

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem (MCPT) with a specific scenario: a full grid graph with n squared cells. A competitor of the winner will have taken the most clicks for each light arrangement. Our work on the MCPT reveals the exact number of clicks needed to solve any given grid of lights, which is n squared minus n. This ideal sequence of clicks, known as an optimal sequence of moves, has been described as well.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly for blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models.

Program analysis employing abstract interpretation involves two sequential steps: upward flow (exploration of the program's domains) and downward flow (computation of the least fixed point). This presentation focuses on the underlying mathematical framework of abstract interpretation; specifically, it examines the different phases of fixed point computation and the various frameworks (continuous, discrete) that have been developed to represent these phases.

A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties that contribute to a variety of technological applications. Topological phonons, encompassing nodal rings, lines, and points, are found in different oxide perovskite systems, encompassing structural forms (tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral), compounds (BaTiO3, PbTiO3, SrTiO3), and external influences (photoexcitation, strain, temperature). Notably, tetragonal perovskite structures with a variety of chemical compositions demonstrate both topological phonons and external tunability. Our work aims to provide an overview of topological phonons in perovskite oxides and explore their controllable aspects.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle distance-based outlier detection effectively, given the growing availability of powerful computational environments. Building a parallel algorithmic strategy for the distance-based outlier detection problem is challenging due to the inherent sequential steps in the process and the need for accurate evaluation of data objects. Research has shown that implementing parallelism in the distance computation phase can lead to inconsistent results, thereby limiting the efficiency of the detection process. In an effort to develop high-speed solutions for this critical problem, we have developed two innovative algorithms utilizing graphics processing units. Our experimental results have proven the effectiveness and superiority of these algorithms over existing methods.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission within a laser-induced absorption/suppression process is being studied for an atom emitting dipole radiation, placed near a perfectly conducting surface mirror. Considerations for this analysis include the atom's excited state $|1\rangle$, which emits a dipole wave of specific amplitude; unabsorbed reflected pulses may potentially excite the atom's ground state $|0\rangle$, resulting in spontaneous emission; this emission can lead to a photoelectric effect where the atom's radiation causes electron excitation in the metal (though this effect is generally negligible at visible wavelengths); to accurately model this system, we must also account for energy conservation, as well as energy absorbed from and emitted to the electron gas in the metal (though these effects are generally negligible at visible wavelengths); to accurately model this system, we must also account for energy conservation, as well as energy absorbed from and emitted to the electron gas in the metal (though these effects are generally negligible at visible wavelengths); to accurately model this system, we must also account for energy conservation, as well as energy absorbed from and emitted to the electron gas in the metal (though these effects are generally negligible at visible wavelengths).

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for a set of nodes, and the second allows for the filtering of these neighborhoods based on specific criteria. We establish formal guarantees for the efficacy of our framework and demonstrate its practical utility through the development of two seamless integration mechanisms - one combining equitable neighborhoods with cost-sensitivity and adaptive risk scoring, and the other combining equitable neighborhoods with cost-sensitivity and adaptive downweighting. Our empirical findings reveal superior node-level fairness for various benchmark and real-world datasets.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final stages through collaboration between ATLAS and CMS, utilizing 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV. Leveraging the large and homogeneous statistics, researchers investigate SUSY scenarios with the most optimistic discovery potential. When the LHC generates squark antiparticles, it probes gluino masses up to 2.5 TeV for production involving two squarks and one gluino. Additionally, they examine production involving three gluinos, exploring various stages of squark coverage and probing the mass of 5.5 TeV gluino. Also, they investigate pure gluino scenarios at a mass of 2.75 TeV and tailor their SUSY analyses to match discovery potential of heavy neutralinos and simplify the interpretation of searches for acoupled SUSY particles. Moreover, searching for evidence of SUSY particles decaying into multiple jets, including possible hidden states of neutralinos, they explore the lower limits of masses of 1.4 TeV and 1.2 TeV for charginos and neutralinos respectively. Also, they investigate the lower limits of masses of 235 GeV and 187.5 GeV for charginos and neutralinos respectively in scenarios with split SUSY.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble formation and survival depend on the interaction of two factors - the variety of opinions among arbitrageurs and the duration of the positive feedback loop. Unlike earlier theories, these models reveal a complex relationship where the optimal bubble size doesn't always decrease with increased variety of opinions, and highlight the significance of arbitrageur heterogeneity in the stability of financial bubbles.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items, where each review contributes differently to modeling user/item preferences. To overcome these challenges, a new approach called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) has been proposed for review-based item recommendations. The method starts by encoding user/item reviews using BERT and introduces a lightweight sentiment extractor to capture review semantics. A sentiment prediction task guides this sentiment extractor to identify relevant features. A rating regression task follows, which integrates a rating prediction model and an interactive fusion network. The interactive fusion network allows reviews to interact with items/users in different ways, where each review, item, and user can share and distinguish their features. Experimental results on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed SIFN method.

Developing CS NLP systems poses significant challenges, primarily caused by the current shortage of CS data, exacerbated by the difficulty of acquiring raw data, necessary for training models. Traditional data collection methods, such as crowdsource-driven ones, have the drawback of being expensive and time-consuming. This paper presents an innovative approach to efficiently generate data for CS NLP tasks. By utilizing a pre-trained cross-lingual language model as a guide, we focus on uncommon words from a vocabulary more frequently encountered during sentence generation. This methodology enables the production of informative samples at a fraction of the cost associated with traditional data collection methods. We test and validate our data generation technique across two code-switching language pairs, Hu-Zh (Hindi-Urdu) and Ma-En (Malayalam-English), and observe that models trained on curated data produced better results on fundamental NLP benchmarks at a fraction of the original data set cost, when compared to models trained on traditionally collected data sets. This study further reveals that the data we generate yields comparable performance even when trained from shorter, more affordable data sets, allowing for efficient model development even with limited resources available.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Consequently, this subgroup cannot be embedded within any locally compact topological group. We also demonstrate that a specific subgroup of homeomorphisms of the disk, which are not simply elliptic, is not relatively compact in the compact-open topology.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that correspond to conformal brane geometries of (1+1)-d. These boundary conditions are known to be linked with numerous high-level field theory and quantum gravity scenarios, and we're exploring their connection with gauge theory and holographic scenarios. The notes serve as a detailed examination of the requirements for an integrable boundary to exist in (1+1)-d conformal field theory, and we're discussing cases involving sine-Liouville theory and its interactions with D-branes within a strung-out context. The discussion also involves a model derived from Liouville quantum gravity and an in-depth analysis of its relationship with string theory. The notes conclude by reiterating, through a (1+1)-d perspective, prior conjectures regarding a connection between AdS/CFT and Wess-Zumino-West theorem.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental component for solving these problems efficiently is a carefully designed and accurate numerical mesh-based scheme. In this study, we explore the advantages and limitations of hexahedral elements, also known as hexahedra, in three-dimensional mesh models. Since hexahedra have the highest spatial accuracy among element types, they are well-suited for various numerical computations. However, their hexahedral layout often complicates tasks involving geometric transformations, rendering them less commonly found in practical meshes than other types. To bridge this gap, we develop an innovative method for creating symplectic meshes composed of hexahedra from more flexible element structures. The proposed technique is efficient, easy to implement, and flexible enough to handle various foundational hexahedra types. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical benefits of hexahedral meshes by showcasing applications in computational dynamics and image-based processing. The algorithm's validity and performance are verified through numerical tests conducted in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional settings. The open-source code for this study, including the mesh processing library, is also made available for the research community to access and use.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. This study shows that this
function can be learned under certain conditions without assuming certain decision-making
characteristics. Instead, we focus on certain conditions of the decision-making process
and develop a new approach to learning the decision-making model using a type of
calm constraint optimization method. Our results show that this method works well even if
the conditions of decision-making are only approximately correct. We also demonstrate
the method's effectiveness using a type of simulation known as the traffic planning problem.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, particularly when approximating complex characteristics. This necessitates an efficient, adaptive post-processing solution that can accurately estimate essential problem parameters like concentration profiles and temperature distributions. Our proposed approach employs a novel, robust, and locally refined analysis, underpinned by the piecewise linear linear spline framework. We develop and integrate an optimized error estimator based on the L2 norm, which effectively identifies areas requiring increased refinement. Our refinement strategy involves selectively targeting spatial locations with the greatest approximation inaccuracy. Additionally, we incorporate a robust edge-correcting method to mitigate errors near element boundaries. Through rigorous testing on a range of benchmark problems, our refined error estimator demonstrates its ability to locally evaluate approximation accuracy and efficiently direct the refinement process. Notably, our method achieves satisfactory results on challenging problems like the inviscid heat transport problem, where it successfully mitigates Gibbs oscillations through local refinement.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency varied between 2.1 to 3.3 Hz, and then sharply increased to ~9 Hz. This phenomenon is associated with the evolution of corona size and feedback fraction. When correlated with radio observations and spectral types, these findings suggest that the morphology of the corona changes from a layered state to a uniform state and eventually becomes compact, as the source transitions from the hard-intermediate to hard state.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt their policies to take advantage of specific partner behaviors instead of truly learning cooperative strategies. To address this issue, we developed a novel framework called Cooperative Policy Sharing (CoPoS) that enables MARL agents to effectively learn and represent cooperative strategies while facilitating seamless policy exchanges among them. Through our theory and experiments, it was shown that our approach enables agents to achieve stable cooperation by facilitating cooperative strategy sharing and testing. To the best of our knowledge, CoPoS is the first MARL method for achieving cooperative representation learning through policy sharing. Our evaluation of the approach involved three existing cooperative settings and compared its performance to established baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in enabling cooperative representations and robust cooperation in both static and dynamic environments.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or 
multiple examples. Visual material recognition is a crucial element in 
several industries such as food processing, agriculture, and industrial 
production. Our work involves leveraging vast resources commonly used 
by computer graphics artists to develop a CGI network capable of training 
a fully autonomous agent to simulate a variety of materials and textures. 
Using MatSim, we achieve state-of-the-art results in material state transfer 
and propose a visual material classification system, outperforming existing 
models in top-1 accuracy by 19, 25, and 36 percent on the three materials 
tested. The dataset and CGI network are openly accessible for further 
research and development at https://matsim-dataset.org/.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on a Lie groupoid. The Lie 2-algebra structure of a quantized symplectic manifold is also investigated in detail.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we rely on the powerful transformer model to enable detailed refinement of matches across the feature space. Our approach yields superior results on large-scale datasets, particularly in textureless regions. Additionally, by combining it with previous local-to-global feature matching techniques, we achieve the highest accuracy in extensive benchmark tests, breaking through the 50% threshold for the challenging KITTI dataset. Our code and datasets are publicly available at github.com/jingjinghong/AduFlow.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly regarding the determination of the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight. It identifies the underlying issue as an ill-posed mathematical problem, which may cause the introduction of noise during the reconstruction process. By applying mixed Gaussian and binary noise models to the line-of-sight component, the study derives the minimum-mean-square-error solution. This component is then combined with other magnetic field elements in the Rosseland diffusion equation to retrieve the elements of the Stokes vector, which in turn enables the retrieval of the magnetic field. Through numerical experiments with synthetic data and real data, the study's findings on correcting bias in the field maps hold true, while its predictions about the precision of the reconstruction remain to be validated.

This research paper explores real-time pricing (RTP) policies that encourage load shifting, providing consumers with incentives to reschedule their energy usage from peak to off-peak hours. By rescheduling energy usage, peak-hour demand is reduced, making energy more readily available during peak hours and potentially increasing supply to meet peak-hour demands. The paper examines non-competitive, repeated game models between consumers and an energy provider, with the energy provider seeking to reschedule peak-hour demand by offering rebates for off-peak hours usage and higher rates for peak-hour usage. However, the study finds that even though the energy provider reschedules peak demand, it remains a Stackelberg leader, controlling the game and its own costs. The paper provides closed-form expressions for the equilibrium payoffs and analysis of the impact of connectivity among consumers, showing that connected consumers reschedule more peak-hour energy than consumers without connectivity, who prefer fixed pricing. The study also examines how pricing policies and connectivity influence consumers and energy providers, with energy providers considering customer satisfaction in addition to profit. The paper compares the findings of two scenarios: a scenario where energy usage is constant across all hours and a scenario where energy usage is non-uniform, revealing that connectivity among consumers reschedules more peak-hour energy than consumers without connectivity, who reschedule no peak-hour energy. The study further highlights the benefits and limitations of real-time pricing under specific connectivity scenarios and illustrates the potential impact of connectivity on consumer and energy provider payoffs and satisfaction. The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory context. Next, we investigate thermodynamic properties, such as Hawking temperature, for these black strings and study their graphical representations with respect to event horizons. Additionally, we examine the impact of Rastall theory on these black string properties.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -5.0. Recent data release from Gaia, which covers 219 million sources, presents an immense opportunity to identify metal-poor stars. This study employs low-resolution spectra from Gaia's BP/RP photometers to identify metal-poor stars, focusing particularly on enriching the metallicity distribution function of the Galaxy's stellar halo. To achieve this goal, a method using synthetic spectra has been developed to assign metallicity readings in the range of -5 to +1 with an accuracy of about 1 dex. Through a simulation, it has been estimated that this method can accurately identify metal-poor stars with a metal content below -3. They are then ranked by their luminosity and proximity to the Galaxy's center, resulting in a list of 82 metal-poor stars with magnitudes brighter than 18. To further verify the existence of these stars, their light curves have been analyzed, and  54 have been confirmed, along with an additional 28 candidates awaiting confirmation. Among the confirmed metal-poor stars, nine possess an ancient age categorization, and five possess a metal content below -5. One metal-poor star with a metal content below -5 also possesses a mass estimated to be less than 0.9 solar mass.

This research aims to offer flexible, downloadable, and up-to-date data regarding the start and duration of fire seasons worldwide. Utilizing a sophisticated machine learning technique, we developed a global fire season dataset, which employs a unique multi-repeated regression strategy to accommodate varying time periods. By segmenting the 1981-2018 time series into consecutive windows of 28 days, and analyzing them separately, we generated precise probability maps to determine the commencement and termination dates of fire seasons. According to our analysis, the majority of global regions experience fire seasons lasting no more than seven months, while only a few regions experience seasons exceeding eight months in duration. Our data is unique in incorporating probabilistic information, which allows for the representation of uncertainty associated with model predictions. Moreover, by distinctively labeling southern hemisphere and tropical regions, we achieved better performance in these areas. Overall, our data can be invaluable for researchers conducting regional-level assessments, exploring relationships between climate change and fire seasons, or conducting spatially based risk assessments.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These methods have never before been compared in a meta-analysis. We selected 30 languages with complete data for each of these metrics. Our analysis revealed that some measures correlate somewhat with each other, while others primarily capture unique aspects of morphological complexity. We used principal component analysis to identify patterns and reduce dimensionality, and this analysis revealed that some measures of morphological complexity are essentially equivalent. One of these measures, based on word length, accounts for over 70% of the data, suggesting it's a reliable indicator of morphological complexity. Another measure, also related to word length, is also a good representation of the data. Permutation testing revealed that four other measures share similarities with the first principal component. These findings imply that these seven measures provide little new information when considered individually. In contrast, two measures correlated with separate components, representing distinct aspects of morphological complexity. One measure, based on word length, captures over 50% of the data, and another, Edelman's c2, also correlates strongly with the second principal component. 

To test the external validity of these findings, we analyzed the rankings of languages according to their morphological complexity using these metrics. The measures that track down similar signals, like word length, tend to produce similar rankings. In contrast, the c2 metric yields a different ranking, one more closely aligned with measures of lexical complexity.
