Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge. This method builds on previous work by removing the necessity for object-pose-labelled data or category-specific 3D models during both training and testing phases. Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, we define the concept of zero-shot, category-based pose estimation and frame it in a manner that is both probabilistic and orientation-sensitive. Secondly, we leverage a large, easily accessible image dataset to provide an accurate baseline for our approach. Thirdly, we demonstrate that our framework achieves this benchmark without requiring data with labelled poses or utilising 3D models of the objects in question. Our results show that the framework performs positively in both cases, and we anticipate that our approach will pave the way for a more unified method of object detection and pose estimation that is not influenced by prior knowledge.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at https://github.com/c-lyu/Traffic4Cast2022-TSE.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, we apply VACA to assess counterfactual fairness in classification tasks, as well as train fair classifiers that maintain high performance standards.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing high-quality data that spans an extensive frequency range and vast areas of the sky. At these levels, even small changes are difficult to measure accurately, requiring the incorporation of sophisticated statistical tools to assess data quality and make reliable observations. To address this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive and efficient data analysis approach, describing in detail the methods used to calculate the uncertainty of data values and providing an overview of the data analysis pipeline. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to mock data, sharing the results in order to facilitate future analyses using comparable software tools. Additionally, we demonstrate the approach's capabilities in real-world settings through a specific analysis of data collected from the Germanlofar, a facility located in Germany, during observations of strong radio sources and atmospheric interference. These experiments allow us to accurately measure the data analysis uncertainty at deep levels and provide insight into the environmental interference visible at these frequencies, such as interferences from the Sun and synthetic aperture radar technology.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, with photovallic technologies playing a significant role. Advancements in understanding light-matter interaction and in using light for various applications rely heavily on advancements in photonic technologies. Traditional design methods for photovallic devices, including photodiodes, phototransistors, and photovoltaics, are often hindered by limitations in modeling and understanding light interaction with micro and nano structures. With the onset of the "Fourth Industrial Revolution" and advancements in the "System-on-Chip" era, there is heightened interest in developing innovative photonic solutions, with the potential to revolutionize various fields and stay aligned with sustainable development goals. By leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning, researchers can streamline device design, manufacturing, and optimization processes, leading to breakthroughs in photonic technology. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how artificial intelligence and machine learning drive photovallic technology innovations, highlighting the significance, applications, and methodologies in this field. It reviews various numerical models and machine learning techniques for photovallic device design, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. The study also classifies and assesses the potential of 50 different machine learning applications in photovallic devices. Furthermore, the paper outlines future directions for machine learning and artificial intelligence in photovallic devices, emphasizing the role of simulations, the need for more advanced machine learning methods, and the importance of incorporating artificial intelligence in

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses, the film industry relies heavily on the opinions of studio executives as they make decisions about which movies to produce, a clearly subjective process. This study takes a more informed approach by leveraging the capabilities of machine learning to analyze box office data and identify which film attributes contribute to a movie's revenue. A dataset was compiled from the IMDb Pro database, enabling the analysis of production costs and global grosses, and allowing the exploration of various data splitting strategies to ensure reliable results. In the end, this study identified which film characteristics are most likely to contribute to a movie's revenue, and provided recommendations for mitigating the risks associated with filmmaking.

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
guarantees the stable operation of the power grid within a wider parameter range 
than previously thought, particularly regarding voltage stability. Nevertheless, 
there is an inherent trade-off between the role of secondary and primary control, 
as these processes compete to correct grid imbalances, which manifests as potential 
instabilities and significant residual frequencies or voltage distortions when the 
two control mechanisms are not properly coordinated.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units, allowing systems to function in harmony, leading to the emergence of new features that combine digital and physical elements. By integrating various systems, a unified approach can be achieved, enabling a system of systems design that incorporates a scalable framework. This paper illustrates the system of systems concept by outlining a domain model for the automotive sector. Specifically, the author focuses on developing a system of systems for the road transportation network, incorporating components such as drivers, passengers, owners, and road users. Using the Ontology Web Language, the author codifies a domain model that enables a unified understanding of system of systems concepts, including interdependencies and functional threads.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are made about the polarization characteristics that polarimetry missions should detect for two specific blazars: AO 0235+164 and 3C 279.

In our study of intricate multi-dimensional environments, also known as complex landscapes, we explored various aspects of approximation techniques for determining the stability of stationary points. Our research reveals that approximations based on localized Taylor expansions, referred to as Stokes expansions, determine the stability of these points with absolute accuracy despite our approximation method's limitations. Our findings identify the conditions under which these approximations enhance or degrade the accuracy of stability assessment; these conditions are tied to the analytic properties of exponential factors in the Taylor series expansion. We defined Stokes sectors where these approximations excel and determined that these sectors cover the entire real line in order to guarantee the stability assessment of stationary points. Ultimately, our work provides a foundational understanding of our approximation technique but falls short of achieving a practical global non-approximate stability determination; this remains a challenging problem for future investigation.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for analyzing multiple state copies in real-time.  These methods involve initially selecting specific measurement types to employ, followed by a direct comparison of obtained results for each copy.  By focusing only on real-valued correlations among the system's observables, the set of possible state discrimination methods becomes substantially reduced.  By showing that the optimal global measurement for any correlation value is a family of locally indistinguishable, commutative observables, we resolve a key question and demonstrate the sufficiency of focusing on real-valued correlations even for real-valued outputs.  Moreover, we find that the set of these optimal local measurements for various correlation values is closed under weak operator product, providing insight into entanglement detection.  By generalizing the concept of real-valued correlations, we also examine the case of qubit states, which involves categorizing the set of correlations according to whether they can be achieved by mixing two states or applying SU(2) rotations on a specific state.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass spectrum of light mesons, can replicate the masses of light baryons.

In the study of the sun's interior using sound waves, the speed of these waves when moving along the same meridian in opposite directions helps scientists understand the movement of the sun's fluid surface horizontally from the north to the south. The daily fluctuations in this speed are likely influenced by the movement of the sun's fluid directly underneath the active solar regions. The data from the SOHO space telescope shows a daily pattern in the sun's fluid movement which sees a daily peak in the north-solar region in the months of May and June, interestingly this daily movement around the active regions of the sun shows a strong annual cycle which has a daily peak in the north-solar region in the months of November to February. The daily fluctuations in the movement of the sun's fluid around the active regions of the sun are predicted to strengthen as the sun approaches its annual maximum in the months of November to February. The daily movement around the active regions of the sun are predicted to be more frequent in the south-solar region in the months of May to August, interestingly this daily movement around the active regions of the sun shows a annual reverse cycle which has a daily peak in the north-solar region in the months of May to August.
