This work presents a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets across multiple disciplines. Building upon existing venue evaluation systems, which we expand and improve upon, we introduce a detailed categorization system with focused topics and hierarchical structures. By developing a metric such as'venue score', which incorporates a publication's frequency, recency, and quality, as well as a score for collaborative opportunities with other authors, we enable comprehensive evaluations of authors and research institutions. Our approach is demonstrated through applications in automatically updating comprehensive publisher databases like CORE and integrating the publishers into a searchable platform for collaborative opportunities. Moreover, it facilitates the calculation of standardized, field-specific impact factors to mitigate the over- representation of influential publishers and provide more accurate comparative assessments among researchers and research institutions.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant challenges when evaluating the safety of these systems. Safety verification relies on precise safety and reachability assessments, with uncertain outcomes for neural networks due to their inherent irregularities and lack of mechanistic explanations. By framing safety as a partial differential equation problem, researchers have developed methods for filtering neural network outputs and assessing reachability through constraint propagation. These methods, tested on control videos, have been found effective in ensuring system safety, with results comparable to other non-neural network approaches.

This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified framework that provides a principle-driven approach to clustering. Specifically, it draws from Jardine and Sibson's theory of link analysis, Feeld's theory of ultrametric partitions, and Barlow and Rosenberger's theory of nearest point methods. By synthesizing these research lines, we establish a clustering theory centered on dissimilarities, which are rooted in practical applications rather than theoretical considerations. The practical outcomes inform the development of a general clustering methodology, and by constraining this methodology with specific conditions, it's shown that link analysis, ultrametric partitioning, and nearest point methods are all encompassed within this theoretical framework.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in visual applications like multimedia analysis and 3D vision, typically represented as graphs. Existing graph-regularized methods for tensor completion have yielded impressive results, but their theoretical validity and data assumptions go unverified. This research investigates the theoretical foundations of low-rank tensor completion with graph regularization and develops a new formulation that guarantees convergence under specific conditions. Additionally, the authors propose an algorithm leveraging proximal point optimizations and alternating minimization to achieve successful recovery of tensors from incomplete data across various noise types. The unique combination of regularization terms and spectral operator enables the algorithm to handle tensors corrupted by both isotropic and anisotropic noise types, providing high-quality recoveries that surpass current state-of-the-art methods, as demonstrated by numerical experiments.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ contain subalgebras that are analogous to those found in type $A_{n}$. These subalgebras have the form of Clifforde algebras, which are defined as the algebraic structure of functions that exhibit permutational symmetry and have restrictions on derivatives for odd-dimensional components. Moreover, the structure of these Clifforde algebras is fully characterized, and the corresponding Clifforde modules are proven to be the only simple Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the symmetric groups $\mathbb{S}_{n}$ when $n\geq 4$.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed the presence of both wave and Hall turbulence characterized by an inverse energy spectrum, suggesting the prevalence of turbulent dynamics over stable geostrophic vortices. Furthermore, Hall-MHD simulations displayed similar cascade behavior, indicating that both wave and Hall turbulence are compatible with both hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic regimes. An examination of the associated scaling exponents revealed good agreement with previously proposed wave-Hall turbulence scalings.

We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing ordered labeled labeled graphs. IGN involves a two-step process: first, we use a function to assign weights or scores to the edges of the graph, and then we apply a rule for modifying the graph by removing the edges with the lowest scores. Notably, IGN has been shown to be equivalent to another well-known model called Branching Markov Processes (BMP) when the graph in question is bipartite. Furthermore, we demonstrate that IGN's effectiveness relies on the properties of the types of graph structures known as maximal independent sets, and we discuss how these structures can be utilized to create more efficient and iterative normalization processes. Our research reveals that the largest possible time complexity for graph normalization is at most linear, and we discuss how the score-based edge assignment functions influence the performance of IGN. Our findings also showcase the relationships between score-based edge assignment functions and various types of labeling systems used in graph analysis.

This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of modulation on the thermodynamic properties. The investigation reveals how the periodic electric potential transforms Landau levels into oscillating bands, leading to specific oscillation patterns in response to magnetic field strength. The analysis shows that in electrically modulated graphene, the modulation's influence on thermodynamic properties is more pronounced and exhibits less damping as temperature increases, contrasting conventional 2DEG systems.

Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be driven by a star-planet interaction or an unstable balance in a rotating disk and the surrounding stellar magnetic field. A new monitoring campaign observed the M dwarf system CR Draconis, consisting of multiple observing sessions taken over a period of approximately two years, which resulted in a substantial total on-source time of around six days. The study found that CR Draconis emits radio signals 90 percent of the time with low frequencies and has a specific polarised characteristic, as well as displaying circular polarisation and intense bursts of radio energy that can last for months. The low-frequency radio signals and intense bursts share similarities with phenomena caused by electric currents in planets under stellar influence, such as in the case of Venus under the influence of the Sun. The intense bursts of radio energy are found to last much longer than expected if they were generated solely by rotating Neptune-like objects, which indicates that other processes could be dominating the system's behaviour. The study found that circular polarisation and intense bursts persist even when the rotating objects in question are not present, indicating that the rotating objects may not be the sole source generating these phenomena. The study suggests that the rotating objects may not exclusively generate these phenomena and that the systems under study could be conducive to hosting certain types of celestial bodies.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges, we developed Articulated
Neural Rendering, a new framework that uses multiple components to work together
efficiently and robustly in generating high-quality images. In experiments with a
range of target datasets, ANR has successfully demonstrated improved outcomes.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning of abstract patterns allows them to withstand extreme visual distortions. We propose a novel set of visual transformation methods rooted in neurophysiological research to evaluate the performance of both humans and networks on an object recognition task. We found that although networks match humans in certain aspects, they struggle with certain transformation types, revealing surprising similarities between human and animal brain data and simultaneously exposing limitations of current machine learning algorithms. To overcome this limitation, we suggest introducing dynamic neural components that adapt to unknown input patterns, thereby ensuring the robustness of visual system models and promoting the development of more human-like learning algorithms.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangle diagrams associated with three strands that include a spin-$1/2$ closed loop demonstrate a connection to the AW algebra's generators. Both the Chern-Simons theory and the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction show that the link invariants generated by these tangles adhere to the algebra's generator relationships. This reveals that the Chern-Simons theory's expectation values for Wilson loops satisfy AW algebra relations and the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants fail to differentiate between equivalent linear combinations of links.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of strongly correlated $S=\frac{1}{2}$ spins within heavily distorted Kagome lattices. We examined a model comprising alternating strong inter- and antiferromagnetic interactions within and between triads of spins, which represents a realistic representation of certain hydrated iron(III)-containing minerals and synthetic compounds. We analyzed the ability of the Kagome lattice to host Lichtenberg modes, which support critical two-peak structures in the specific heat and intricate, multifaceted low-temperature spin structures. We also investigated the impact of degeneracy within the model on its low-temperature behavior. We discovered that both the previously established spin-liquid phase exhibiting spin-stern-gerrl relations and a newly identified phase showing Hall states and fractal properties exhibit similar mathematical descriptions in terms of their structural magnetic patterns. We further found that both phases exhibit consistent thermodynamic behaviors when examined using finite-size scaling methods. Conversely, an alternating ferromagnetic layer within the Kagome lattice results in the emergence of unusual phenomena, which are examined using the same methods.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by instructing them to generate affirmative text, thereby implicitly labeling examples as positive. However, this methodology hinges on the model's ability to generate novel sentences in response to prompts. Our research reveals that refining GPT-3's ability to produce novel sentences, either through training or direct modification, significantly enhances its zero-shot classification capabilities. Even small adjustments to the model's outputs, such as utilizing shorter sentences, can substantially enhance zero-shot classification performance. Furthermore, our findings indicate that selecting specific GPT-3 parameters or fine-tuning them with supervised data leads to improved sentiment classification. We propose that adjusting language models to produce qualitative changes in sentences is an effective strategy for enhancing zero-shot learning capabilities. Moreover, our method for manipulating the language model outputs does not necessitate direct supervision, thus offering avenues for further research.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a robust first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying electroweak baryogenesis within the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, considering recent data from the Higgs sector, dark matter searches, and analyses from the Large Hadron Collider involving lighter charginos and neutralinos. This includes thorough reviews of the latest relevant LHC studies. With the assistance of various benchmark scenarios, it was demonstrated that while the LHC has started to exclude parameter regions favoring small $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ values, other involved parameters are still consistent with existing data, including those from Higgs and dark matter searches. Notably, although the LHC has excluded some of the theoretical possibilities for the first and second generation sfermions, other choices remain available. Furthermore, realistic realistic baryogenesis through the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM has been shown to be a challenging but feasible goal for future Baryogenesis studies, and may be explored in greater detail with the advent of longer-integrated data from the LHC.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring redshifts, with a particular focus on techniques using single-dish instruments. Since robust redshift determination is crucial for an accurate luminosity calculation and important for understanding the development of galaxies at early stages, we also discuss potential challenges in identifying robust redshifts through emission lines. Our work includes an online resource featuring high-resolution pseudo-spectra of 200 galaxies between $z=0.1$ and $z=15$ to facilitate testing our proposed redshift identification strategies.

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. Based on the simulated data, the study concludes that the $120^{\circ}$-ordered phase exhibits three continuous degeneracies that result in the splitting of the lowest triply-degenerate level in the lattice. These degeneracies correspond to specific spin excitations: a singlet bound state with a energy of approximately $J_2/2$ is identified at the L-point, a degeneracy associated with the $120^{\circ}$-harmonics on the $\Gamma$ point with an energy of approximately $3J_1/2$ is confirmed, and a highly dispersive level of spin excitations near the K-point with an energy of approximately $J_1$ is identified. This later mode is related to the wave function of a spin flip coupled with a $120^{\circ}$-harmonic. We also found that this model exhibits a spin liquid phase with no disorder, which occurs when $J_2=J_1/2$. Within this phase, a large degeneracy associated with the wave function of a spin flip under $D_3$ symmetry is still present and partially delocalized. A simple analytical model of the dynamical spin structure factor that captures the main features observed in the simulations has also been developed.

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on $Z_3$ symmetry, where a complex triplet Higgs boson has no initial mass. By regulating lattice size through variations in $N_\tau$, the investigation reveals that the phase transition depends on this regulation method. While three stages are observed where the phase transition depends on $N_\tau$, the symmetry breaking strength significantly affects the phase transition type, where the order parameter critical behavior and Finite Action Principle validity are examined under varying lattice volumes and $Z_3$ symmetry breaking strengths, $\zeta$. Breaking symmetry at a non-zero value leads to a theory where the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs boson field is non-zero and differs from its initial value. Additionally, the study examines how different lattice regularization methods affect the theory and the study outcomes.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector degeneracy. This study focuses on growing Cr$_2$Al crystals and examining its magnetic properties as a function of orientation. Using neutron diffraction and simulations, the research finds that Cr$_2$Al has a magnetic ordering identical to Mn$_2$Au and is likely to provide new insights into a previously unexplored magnetic system with in-plane vector degeneracy. The research finds that the magnetic ordering temperature, as determined by neutron diffraction and other methods, is 638 K, a value consistent with magnetic model calculations and lower than earlier X-ray diffraction results. The study also found that the magnetic ordering on a Rietveld scale matches simulations of a B2 structure magnetic ordering better than a hexagonal structure magnetic ordering, despite the samples exhibiting a tetragonal Cr$_2$Al structure without magnetic ordering.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential collision characteristics from Boltzmann's equation, while also reflecting the influence of a given potential on molecular interactions, as seen in the hard-sphere ($
u_0$) or Maxwell molecules ($
u_1$) scenarios. By utilizing numerical solutions obtained from the Fourier-Galerkin method for macroscopic degree-of-freedom vectors, the $
u$-model is evaluated for its accuracy and reliability, focusing on rarefied flow conditions in a plane rarefied gas with varying collision frequencies and potential parameters. Consequently, the proposed $
u$-model is found suitable for a wide range of kinetic models characterized by a single scaling parameter, which simplifies complex simulations of rarefied monatomic gases.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge involving converting spoken language into meaningful instructions. We introduce LP-LM, a cutting-edge model combining language model and logic-oriented features, capable of generating semantic parses during inference. The LP-LM model utilizes a pre-trained language model to derive meaning from input sentences and incorporates logical elements to determine intended outcomes. This innovative approach enhances sentence understanding and assignment of logical meanings with minimal increase in model complexity. Experimental results demonstrate our model's capability to yield superior sentence understanding and log likelihood scores on TRAIN and DEV sets of the SparkML benchmark, while near-equal performance compares model performance on the TEST set.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will examine the fundamental constituents of matter, investigating their interactions with each other and with themselves. By doing so, researchers will be able to gain a more thorough grasp of the underlying matter structure. To achieve this, the EIC will conduct thorough studies on various topics, including the behavior of heavy flavor particles, the characteristics of the underlying matter, and a vast array of other phenomena. As a crucial step towards its operations, the EIC will conduct a comprehensive investigation known as a capabilities study. Our research, based on the findings of this study, highlights the advantages of utilizing a linac-based accelerator design. By utilizing cutting-edge electron beam techniques, the EIC will be capable of achieving high levels of precision in its measurements, ultimately resulting in the capability to achieve the following key outcomes: attain precision of better than 5% in the determination of d/u quark flavor asymmetry at moderate x and SNNP=0.02, obtain a precise estimation of the mass of bottom quarks (around 2% or less) and observe specific charm particle states for the first time with sufficient data. Additionally, the EIC will have a unique capacity to study specific aspects, such as cjar, coss, and J/psi breakups, at relatively low energies, as well as observe J/psi polarisation for the first time using e+p collisions. Our research further demonstrates the capacity of the EIC to achieve high levels of precision through cutting-edge

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies, identified as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs), has led researchers to re-evaluate the case of the low-mass Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) 2XMM J123103.2+110648 as exhibiting QPEs or QPOs. By analyzing archival XMM-Newton data and applying the autocorrelation function and Fourier analysis techniques, the study found no strong evidence for the occurrence of either QPEs or QPOs in 2XMM J123103.2+110648. In contrast to earlier findings of frequent QPEs in this source, the study's results, which utilized a more rigorous approach than previous studies, failed to support the previously reported data. This change in conclusion led to the revision of arguments related to their origins. It was suggested that QPEs and QPOs may not be separate categories of variability, but rather two ends of a single phenomenon with varying frequency and amplitude. It is proposed that the mechanism producing QPEs or QPOs in AGN could be a hybrid one, where there is a gradual transition from quasi-periodic oscillations to stochastic variability. This suggests that AGN stochastic variability might primarily appear as QPEs rather than QPOs, and that QPEs in AGN could be producing the characteristic hump feature seen in their spectral energy spectra.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has been confirmed through the observation of Zeeman splitting in spectral lines. Analyzing how the effects of magnetic fields in stars' atmospheres change with altitude is essential for understanding the impact of field interactions on the spectrum. We aimed to investigate the variation of the magnetic field in the star HD 140239 using the DOOPHIN spectropolarimeter by detecting Zeeman shifting and polarization and then fitting a magnetic model to the data. Our analysis revealed the presence of a field with a surface magnitude of approximately 1.2 kiligesla in the outermost atmospheric layer, with the field's magnitude decreasing as we move towards the stars' interior. We observed the field's magnitude to decrease by 30 percent over a 10 percent change in depth. Our findings also indicate that magnetic fields in stars' atmospheres decrease rapidly in strong fields and are influenced significantly by the field's magnitude due to increased magnetic field effects. However, our analysis using magnetic field models failed to yield an adequate fit to the observed polarization, possibly due to atmospheric fluctuations affecting individual spectral lines.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and assess the reliability of other SFR measurement techniques. Based on these observations, the galaxy's total SFR is found to be approximately 0.23 solar masses per year. SFR measurements from our H30α data have a relatively small margin of error. When using infrared data, the estimated SFR is about 0.20 solar masses per year, but using radio data, the estimated SFR is about 0.30 solar masses per year. These comparisons suggest that both methods may have some reliability, but using radio data from edge-on galaxies like NGC 5253 could lead to overestimation of the SFR due to dust extinction effects. On the other hand, the H30α data provide a more reliable measurement because this frequency range has minimal contamination from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission and the observed emission primarily originates from the interstellar medium. Furthermore, the observed H30α flux in NGC 5253 is found to be approximately 0..23 Jy, which is suitable for estimating SFRs in galaxies of similar metallicity to the Milky Way.

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly sample realizations of $X$ and $Y$. Additionally, this allows us to tackle more complex issues like asymptotic normalness in kernel regression and functional inference. Our findings also hold true in a finite sample context, by which we understand convergence in probability.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in addition, we identify issues with how static model performance on temporal data is typically evaluated, and provide two solutions to address these problems.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the extreme demands of high-power oscillators, which regularly breach the saturation threshold of the Kerr effect. To address this limitation, a more comprehensive approach has been developed based on the paraxial approximation, providing a more robust framework for analyzing ring resonators in high-power settings. This methodology has been successfully applied across a range of scenarios, including liquid-nitrogen-cooled and water-cooled setups, with the addition of geometric refactoring for enhanced clarity and efficiency. By enabling calculations spanning multiple orders of magnitude in pump power, this new method offers improved computational efficiency and accuracy, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of ultrashort pulse generation and manipulation.

Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed partial model update and filter methods to minimize both participant and server computational costs. ASO-Fed's communication efficiency was further enhanced by incorporating local data projection and compressive data transfer. Experimental results demonstrate that ASO-Fed achieves significant computational savings while maintaining performance on synthetic data, equally or even surpassing state-of-the-art communication efficiency standards on real-world datasets like MNIST and CIFAR-10.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers investigate a back reflector with a nanostructured 3D photonic band gap crystal made from silicon that can easily be integrated into the top amorphous silicon layer. By controlling the hole arrangement, the band gap of the crystal can be adjusted to specifically enhance absorption within the solar cell's optimal wavelength range (around 1100 nm). Numerical simulations show that a photonic crystal with an optimized 7 x 7 hole pattern can significantly boost absorption compared to a metal reflector, specifically by increasing photocurrent by 12.5% and the solar cell's efficiency by 7.9% when using a 250 nm thick amorphous silicon film. Moreover, these optimized structures also demonstrate effective light control capabilities across various energy regimes.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. These functions are linked to nested exponentials through a useful functional equation and have a series expansion that converges within a certain region of the complex plane. By examining the properties of $\beta$, we can study the dynamics of the exponential map $e^{\mu z}$ and obtain insights into the behavior of fractional iterations. Our analysis allows us to identify conditions under which Abel equations are associated with iterated exponentials and also enables the integration of iteration numbers within series expansions and iterated values. Our methods are supplemented by computer-assisted numerical studies that help validate the results obtained.

We have developed a novel method for constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer negative curvature and these are limited to specific dimensions and constants. Our method involves a general algorithm that takes a low dimensional regular simplicial complex and produces a high dimensional expander by creating a covering space. We have shown that our method is versatile and applicable to finite fields, product spaces and a range of examples including the Johnson and Kahle-Safford complexes.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. Within this framework, the study examined the effects of magnetic fluctuations and their impact on the magnetic properties. Our results indicate that the unique magnetic topology gives rise to unique magnetic transitions at 2.1 K and 0.68 K. The first transition is attributed to the ordering of triangular sublattices, and the second is attributed to the antiferromagnetic ordering of the honeycomb sublattices. Our calculations also revealed the presence of a large magnetic anomaly at 0 K with a magnetic moment of 7.0 mu_B, in agreement with the observed magnetic saturation at 2 K. Additionally, the study examined the electronic characteristics of this compound and revealed the presence of a small gap insulator. Our experimental findings were supported by the results of our calculations, providing valuable insight into the characteristics of this unique magnetic material. Our work may contribute to the development of a wide range of magnetic materials, thereby expanding the existing magnetic material database.

The application of graph embedding for exploring and understanding the structural composition of networks has shown significant promise. However, networks consisting of a large number of nodes that are sparse, particularly those with only a few edges, have historically posed analytical challenges. In this paper, we introduce the Sparse Structural Network Embedding model (SSNE), designed specifically for such sparse networks, with the goal of retaining essential topological information while eliminating unnecessary details. SSNE employs a novel approach leveraging the principles of equilibrium in Markov chains to map networks through a targeted optimization of a comprehensive structural objective function. Furthermore, we develop a groundbreaking pruning technique that enables efficient determination of crucial network topological details, along with the development of dual pruning methods. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that SSNE successfully captures the equivalent Markov chain dynamics of the target network and achieves an optimal error bound. Our experimental results across a range of networks demonstrate that SSNE outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, with SSNE Dual achieving accelerated convergence rates relative to the original SSNE model.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming depth limitations and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. Although initial vapor cell designs had minimum feature sizes limited to 1.5mm, a novel two-chamber arrangement was developed with a 25mm meandering channel separating the chambers, allowing for increased alkali vapor introduction and minimized damage near the main chamber. This approach enhances signal quality in laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) and fluorescence spectroscopy (FLS) techniques, with the LIF signal improving by a factor of four and the FLS signal improving by a factor of ten.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have enhanced the accuracy and speed of wildfire detection using aerial images. However, the application of DL methods in this area is limited due to the large size of the images and restricted access to labeled data. This paper introduces DPC-NET, a DL network that uses phase information and can work effectively with small labeled datasets, as well as efficiently with partially sealed image boundaries due to restricted data availability. The network is trained to identify fire pixels and is trained in two stages. First, it extracts phase features from the input images using a custom transformer architecture. Then, it learns to differentiate fire pixels from other types using class-balanced cross-entropy loss. The phase features facilitate navigation through large image files and ensure seamless processing without edge effects. The small footprint of DPC-NET enables efficient processing of high-resolution images in near real-time. Evaluations were conducted on the NASA NASA LAFCO, LAFCO2, and active fires datasets. The results showed that our method surpasses state-of-the-art DL methods in terms of detection accuracy, speed, and scalability, and also proves effective with restricted data availability. The performance metrics and source code are publicly available.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential for preventing severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, particularly when they do not require direct interaction with the individual being assessed.  Observing social media expression patterns can provide valuable insight into mental health conditions such as depression, allowing for the development of a supportive system that recognizes and understands depressed individuals' posts. The challenge lies in creating a dataset to inform the design of such a system. In this paper, we introduce DepressNet, a dataset consisting of 1,510 social media updates from 302 individuals, each categorized into three levels of depression, along with 1,500 posts from 308 non-depressed individuals.  Each update in DepressNet is described by 42 variables related to language, content and feeling expressions. Our analysis of the dataset reveals notable patterns and correlations within depressed individuals' posts, including fewer posts with positive emotions, more expressions of sadness and guilt, fewer narratives of success and happiness, and fewer spatial references.  Furthermore, we developed two machine learning models. One model identifies depressed individuals' posts, utilizing a combination of depressed individuals' posts and non-depressed individuals' posts in the training process. The other model categorizes depression levels by comparing depressed individuals' posts with other depressed individuals' posts. Both models demonstrate accurate performance, with the former achieving an 80.7% accuracy in identifying depressed individual's posts, and the latter achieving a 61.3% accuracy in categorizing depression levels.

We've developed an ordinary differential equation model to track COVID-19's growth and spread, utilizing the SIS model. By incorporating lockdown measures and the expiration dates of lockdowns, we've transformed the ODE model into a piecewise function. This function has been used to analyze SARS-CoV-2's growth and spread in three different scenarios: incorporating lockdown measures, the expiration of lockdown measures, and the implementation of lockdown measures in Argentina, Chile, and Mexico. According to our analysis, lockdown measures have reduced COVID-19's initial peak by 65-70% but ultimately won't impede the virus's natural expiration. Furthermore, comparing the country-specific models, which take into account the distinct reproductive numbers of each nation, we've found that the initial peak of lockdown measures has reduced by 20% in Mexico, 15% in Chile, and 40% in Argentina.

The ISGMR and a $K = 0$ component of the ISGQR in severely deformed nuclei exhibit a strong interrelation, manifesting as opposing effects on the ISGMR peak density and width on a mass scale. A unique ISGMR peak at $J^{\pi} = 0^{+}$ exists in nuclei with severe deformation and this phenomenon can be utilized to determine the nuclear incompressibility modulus $K_{\infty}$. The ISGMR data for doubly magic nuclei with severe deformation across the mass spectrum is presented and the ISGMR peak density and width are analyzed by employing different theoretical models. Notably, a $K_{\infty}$ value consistent with the predicted value from Hartree-Fock calculations was obtained using the phenomenological model. The correlations between the ISGMR, isotropic and anisotropic deformations and the nuclear incompressibility modulus are discussed through graphical analysis.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction has been conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, has been confirmed through analytical means. However, the nature of convergence for trajectories starting within this attractive region remains uncertain, prompting an exploration of numerical methods to solve Coulomb frictional problems. These methods have revealed the intricate non-continuous nature of frictional forces, which may cause multiple solutions to arise for certain initial conditions. Additionally, the possibility of attracting these solutions towards the equilibrium state has been observed through analytical and numerical means.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities with infinite maturity and a fixed horizon. This new model leverages a combined approach of two separate Bellman equations to effectively incorporate the current state into the optimal decision-making framework. As a result, we can accurately capture the uncontrolled dynamics of a portfolio's value in the absence of perfect hedging. Key in this approach is the identification of a feasible reward function that allows for both off-policy learning and an optimal control solution that addresses the unconstrained nature of the problem. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis that our approximation error is manageable, and numerical test results confirm the efficacy of our approach.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out as the only specialized Fuchsian equation that can be obtained through the monodromy representation of solutions to the general double confluent Heun equation. This distinctive characteristic facilitates the use of the general equation's solutions to construct a series solution for the specialized equation, specifically the reducible one. This article details the procedures for classifying the essential singularities and identifying the horizontal branches of the first family of solutions for the specialized equation using the fundamental solutions derived from the general equation.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are widespread in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems, specifically focusing on linear combinations of observed data segments with differing noise levels, matrix decomposition structures, and multiple data components. We establish a general, easily applicable estimation guarantee for recovering the original matrix based on average recovery guarantees for individual subsets of the data. These findings are further illustrated by two significant applications: multiview alignment and single-cell RNA-sequencing deblending, both of which involve recovering structured matrices from noisy data under different observation rates. We enhance upon existing methods for each problem by incorporating our theoretical findings into the construction of a regularization network that outperforms the previously used technique. Our results, which include complete theoretical analysis and characteization of the convergence rate for the regularization network, yield improvements in both CPU and GPU testing environments.

In this research, we have identified an exceptional point within the vibrational spectrum of a specific type of one-dimensional periodic system. An equivalent model, incorporating a nonlinear on-site relationship, has also been established. By analyzing the dynamics near this point, we have derived a mathematical equation describing the temporal evolution of basilar membrane states and developed a theory explaining how energy is transferred from one state to another during the resonant process. Additionally, we have validated our findings by matching our results to actual micromachined data.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step employs BERT for initial CT scan image analysis before transfer learning. Following this, the fine-tuned BERT model (FFBERT) is combined with Attention-based BERT for FFBERT, which is then utilized for final transfer learning. The output of FFBERT is passed through Attention-based BERT for Attention-based FFBERT, which is then utilized for final feature extraction. The extracted features are then fed into classification models, including Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Neural Networks. Experiment results demonstrate that our model is highly effective, with 97\% accuracy, 97\% sensitivity, and 96\% specificity when using the BERT model, and 96\% accuracy, 96\% sensitivity, and 95\% specificity when using the Attention-based BERT model, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing an expansive scope of fields from the biological interactions within microbes to the global human infrastructure. The inherent intricacy of these networks gives rise to an array of analytical and practical challenges, which have been the focal point of extensive research activities in recent decades, resulting in numerous scientific communities utilizing diverse approaches and tools to analyze and manipulate these complex data sets. Despite the significant progress made, there remains a substantial and increasingly critical gap within the community for standardized approaches, shared resources, and collaborative efforts to facilitate the sharing and integration of tailored methods and tools tailored to specific network science applications and domains. This document presents the outcomes of a workshop held in 2020 for the NSF Network Science for the Future program, which brought together approximately 80 participants from various scientific communities to engage in discussions, identify commonalities and discrepancies, and explore potential collaboration opportunities with other scientific disciplines, including neuroscience, geosciences, and the microbial sciences. The report highlights specifically selected topics and general takeaways from the meeting, and also includes a comprehensive list of invited review papers that comprehensive review papers have been assembled for each of the aforementioned application domains with the purpose of guiding the network science community in identifying potential research topics and directing future investments.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as experienced by modern populations.  This is resulting in an incomplete representation of the ecological and evolutionary processes interacting over varying timeframes and across different domains, thereby overlooking the importance of slow-changing factors, known as'slow eco-evolutionary processes'.  In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we have developed a theoretical framework that illustrates how slow eco-evolutionary processes can influence 'fast' ecological and evolutionary mechanisms.  By incorporating insights from global change into ecological, phylogenetic, and evolutionary patterns, our research highlights the potential for'slow' factors to impact long-term environmental and evolutionary trajectories.  Furthermore, we have developed approaches to quantify the significance of'slow' factors in shaping eco-evolutionary dynamics.  By integrating these aspects, we have taken the first step towards a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate interactions between 'fast' and'slow' eco-evolutionary drivers, which can lead to 'backward feedbacks' that impact long-term ecological and evolutionary processes in a nonlinear manner.  Ultimately, our research seeks to inspire innovative testing methods that can uncover the underlying 'backward feedbacks' driving eco-evolutionary dynamics, thereby shedding light on how they may shape future ecosystems.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks with little adaptation, SUPERB highlights a significant paradigm in the speech field that needs to be studied more. Specifically, SUPERB's influence extends beyond speech to the broader field of natural language processing, where comparable trends may exist. To explore this further, we aim to identify other NLP models and datasets that resemble the SUPERB speech benchmark. First, we examine the potential of superglue, a set of prominent NLP leading datasets, in the NLP field. Next, we detail our initial investigation into whether superglue captures the same learning trends observed in the speech benchmark. Ultimately, we propose an update to the superglue benchmark, adding two new challenges to better understand the learning paradigm in the NLP field.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually diminishes arbitrage challenges, though this benefits investors at a decreased rate. 
Conversely, the inclusion of numerous tokens worsens the arbitrage dilemma. 
We furnish empirical support for our primary model outcomes by using detailed transaction records of AMMs.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric called E-proof, which quantifies and represents these uncertainties through a symmetry principle, and develop a new framework, referred to as Asymmetrical Proof, that can be applied to dynamic settings. We apply this new framework to scenarios with missing outcome data and create evidence-based metrics to quantify the impact of uncertain assumptions. We demonstrate through an example that our approach can be used not only to identify the range of admissible assumptions but also to impose restrictions on them. We conduct a large-scale empirical examination of various dynamic evidence-based metrics in a scenario involving multiple missing outcome data types.

This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{K}_q$, where $\mathbb{K}_q=\mathbb{K}_\mathbb{C}[z,z^{-1}]$. Furthermore, it introduces generator representations for key elements: the Cartan generator and the $\tau$-operator, and provides formal proof of a established formula for the $\widehat{ext{Ch}}$-function in this specific context. The conclusions derived from this analysis are instrumental in the creation of a comprehensive quantum intersection theory.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing privacy concerns through local data processing, thus limiting exposure, yet its applications extend beyond data protection as a means to enhance security. This paper delves into the dual-edged nature of Federated Learning, exploring its potential to simultaneously ensure data privacy and enhance security through the implementation of two case studies. Furthermore, it identifies and compares multiple FL frameworks suitable for IoVs applications and outlines potential future research directions based on the observations collected.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution of D meson production, including both prompt and non-prompt (formed in beauty-hadron decays), in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, and focused on data with an integrated luminosity of approximately 19.3 nb^-1. D mesons were identified through their decays into different hadronic combinations, such as $\mathrm{D^0 \to K^-\pi^+}$ and $\mathrm{D_s^+\to \phi\pi^+\to K^-K^+\pi^+}$ and their conjugates. The cross section of D meson production was calculated using the Glauber model and compared with theoretical calculations, showing good agreement with the theoretical data for non-prompt and prompt D meson production. The ratio of non-prompt to prompt D meson production was also determined and compared with theoretical predictions, displaying reasonable agreement. The production cross section of J/$\psi$ to D meson ratio was also calculated and compared with theoretical calculations, showing good agreement within the measured $p_\mathrm{T}$ range.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, which we call the 'Dome,' is designed to facilitate cutting-edge 'in-vacuo' quantum architecture by providing a sealed experimental space where cutting-edge superconducting quantum materials and novel cooling strategies can be combined with advanced magnetic field control to create an unparalleled experimental environment.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a 2019 survey of Python's Packagist repository that found 71% of evaluated packages abusing crypto APIs. This research replicates and expands upon that study, employing a novel triage method to assess 1,584 Python projects hosted on PyPI. By combining static analysis of source code with project metadata, this study detects at least one crypto API misuse in 67% of the projects, revealing that fewer than 1% utilize crypto APIs correctly. Additionally, projects incorporating encryption products via PyPI show a higher likelihood of correctly using these tools. Both qualitative and quantitative outcomes offer valuable insights, ranging from why certain crypto APIs are commonly abused to the benefits associated with using encryption products. This study also develops a tool to assist developers in evaluating the security of open-source projects, providing detailed feedback that can help fix security issues and introducing a new evaluation method for crypto library usage.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to process large datasets in a distributed and parallel manner while ensuring consistent results across various datasets with identical ground truth. Utilizing our proposed aggregation strategy in conjunction with a range of feature and matching extraction techniques reveals that our approach consistently produces results at least as robust as existing methods, while in many cases substantially improving their precision and robustly estimating three-dimensional object locations even with significant disruptions in data.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our approach treats the deconvolution process as finding the least possible value of a convex function when the boundary conditions are known. Existing methods for this type of deconvolution are limited when trying to approximate the original reflectivity through a sparse series. Our contribution introduces a new convex function, the form of which is similar to that of a split combination of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms with additional logarithmic terms. It's effective in deconvolving signals and retrieves the original reflectivity through an approximately sparse series. Our approach also reformulates deconvolution as a weighted least squares problem, the solution of which is found using an iterative algorithm with two separate iterations. The algorithm can be implemented using fast Fourier transforms and has been applied to simulated data from 1-D seismic measurements, the results of which recover the original reflectivity through a sparse series with good accuracy.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of F(p, q) which encompasses BMOA for (p, q) = (2, 2]. VMOA is a subset of F(p, q) for (p, q) in (1, 2] but never equals it. VMOA_p is defined as the closure of (BMOA_p)ᴿ in F(p, q). Our focus is on the maximal subspace consisting of bounded linear operators that form a strong Fubini semigroup, resulting in characterizations of (B, T) (B is a closed subspace of F(p, q)) if T is a strong Fubini semigroup on BMOA_p or VMOA. On BMOA_p in the range (1, 2] our research reveals that a strongly continuous Fubini semigroup (B, T) is isometric if and only if (B, T) is normal. On VMOA for p in (1, 2] our research shows that a strongly continuous Fubini semigroup (B, T) is isometric if and only if (B, T) is normal or admissible.
