Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory (CFT), including operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients, which describe how operators combine at renormalization group fixed points. We have calculated the second moments of operator product expansion coefficients within the compact XXZ spin chain model. This model, which is an example of a integrable quantum field theory, allows us to find general expressions for our parameters of interest using free fermions, even at non-zero temperature. By decomposing non-thermal states into thermal/vacuum contributions, we have determined the central charge and the ratio of the stress-energy central charge to the identity operator's second moment. Our results for the compact XXZ spin chain support our general formula for c/c_{\phi} and validate previously proposed values for c and c_{phi}.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial component in numerous NLP tasks. Although many languages have been POS-tagged, few have been tagged accurately for historical and low-resource languages due to label shortages and unclear category definitions. To address the challenges in tagging languages like Ancient Greek, this study offers two new POS models based on character n-gram issues from 18th and 19th century English, providing a potential solution for tagging languages with limited resources. An external dataset was used to verify the accuracy of the models, and it was found that one model achieved an average accuracy of 73.15% and the other, 65.87% (with p-values of 0.9997 and 0.2292, respectively, indicating no significant difference between the models and the standard dataset). An existing character-based model was also tested and achieved an accuracy of 57.46%, significantly different from the best POS model (with a p-value of 0.0172).

We seek to develop a comprehensive framework for evaluating the reliability of proposed demand functions. Our primary goal is to identify all quadratic polynomial demand functions, and in the process, we establish the necessary and sufficient requirements for a candidate demand function to be considered valid and separable. In addition to our analytical approach, we utilize convex optimization to verify our findings and uncover novel insights into symmetric equilibrium single-parameter auctions.

As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into machine-readable specifications. However, human specifications often lack clarity, causing misunderstandings in communication. Introducing CitySpec, a novel system utilizing neural networks to interpret ambiguous requirements and generate specifications with clarity, based on knowledge-based input. CitySpec enables real-time, non-verbal specification interpretation, allowing for seamless interaction between humans and machines. Utilizing a pre-trained transformer model and a specially crafted knowledge graph, CitySpec surpasses existing performance standards on requirement parsing, while also enhancing its ability to handle unknown vocabulary and robustness against unseen data. Additionally, CitySpec effectively generates specifications with minimal semantic irregularities. You can access CitySpec on GitHub at https://github.com/ku21ca/CitySpec.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly effective in overcoming the ring approximation's limitations in these algorithms. As a result, we anticipate substantial speed gains, specifically in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm, where this acceleration can lead to significantly reduced total time complexity. Moreover, we discover that this acceleration is consistent with an additional classical optimization stage following the quantum circuit. To confirm the practical benefits of this innovation, we tested the technique on a simulated quantum computer using the variational quantum eigensolver and the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. Our simulation data show that hidden inverse methods can yield error mitigation without augmentation, while further enhancing performance with the augmentation strategy, we achieve an impressive 32 times faster convergence rate compared to the standard approach. This finding solidifies the hidden inverse method as a versatile tool for enhancing the resilience and efficacy of quantum algorithms.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category, given the same underlying set as the original. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of the cofibered image of preorders and develops criteria for determining when the partial order is the least upper bound. In the broader category of categories and functors, these conditions also imply the existence of suprema in applicable cases.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model that accounts for non-linear relationships between variables, this study investigates the stochastic connections between wind speed, wave height, and storm tracks in the North East Atlantic between 2003-2018. It finds a significantly inverse correlation between wind speed and wave height during high wave conditions in the region, which has significant practical implications for wave and wind energy industries in the UK and Ireland.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text representations through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn universal visual concepts. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual concept learning, we introduce Cross-domain Contrastive Learning to bridge the semantic gap between image and text domains through multi-cross-domain contrastive learning, thereby enhancing visual-text alignment. By expanding the contrastive learning space from two to multiple domains, we facilitate tighter image-text alignment and improved generalizability across various scenes. Since pre-trained models are inherently flawed, we introduce a fine-tuning strategy utilizing pseudo-labels to correct visual-text alignment. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method against state-of-the-art approaches on seven benchmark datasets, demonstrating substantial enhancement in image-text matching performance. Our method's efficacy is further validated through robust and abductive testing on multiple scenarios. Notably, our method's image-text matching performance consistently surpasses state-of-the-art models by a significant margin on commonly used evaluation metrics.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting framework, we extend this concept to nonsymmetric matrices. Our innovation lies in the development of an operator shifting technique for matrix inverses, which is akin to the James-Stein estimator. Our analysis demonstrates that the shifted inverse of a nonsymmetric matrix yields a more robust estimator than its conventional counterpart. Utilizing this theory, we derive our pioneering shrinking estimator, which outperforms existing alternatives. Interestingly, our algorithm can be viewed as a black-box implementation of a recent shrinking estimator proposed in a related study. Our experimental results showcase the efficacy of the shifting estimator, highlighting its potential to significantly reduce error without extensive computational knowledge.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. In the process, we compute the Mackey functors for $\underline{\pi}_{k\rho} H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial coefficient and a relation between the Hilbert series and the Frobenius map. These conditions contribute to a better understanding of tight ideal series and their connection to Frobenius splitting. Moreover, when the local ring is equidimensional and Cohen-Macaulay, we establish that rationality and $F$-rationality are equivalent, providing a significant generalization of prior work in this area.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within medical contexts involves the direct use of DICOM image data, with information regarding image characteristics, patient details, and examination purposes encoded within tags. Standardizing the sharing of data between various applications and institutions, DICOM enables the seamless integration of ML models across the entire healthcare system. However, the standardization comes with the cost of making data that was previously private or difficult to access now easily accessible. Concerns are rising regarding the need for ethical data annotation when working with DICOM, specifically regarding sensitive information such as patient ages and demographic data. This paper outlines the requirements for ethical data annotation in the process of training ML models using DICOM data.

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, when evaluated on the horizon. The entropy can also be calculated using a Virasoro algebra and Cardy formula approach, in which we identify relevant diffeomorphisms based on a simple physical principle that maintains the horizon structure's invariance. Our method complements earlier research and utilizes the York-Gibbons-Hawking surface term to reach a similar conclusion, thereby providing technical and physical advancements.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation for long and variable DNA sequences of varying lengths. The resulting latent representation demonstrates its utility in both supervised and unsupervised tasks and achieves comparable performance in similar tasks. A key advantage of our proposed model is its ability to achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple tasks including classification, clustering, and link prediction on DNA sequence datasets.

The manner in which the surface finish of thin films impacts their electronic characteristics has significant implications for their utility in future devices. 
It is well established that the bulk properties of V$_2$O$_3$ thin films undergo a transition from metal to insulator when the atomic ratio is adjusted. 
Our study of photoemission spectroscopy across different V$_2$O$_3$ surface preparations reveals that this metal-insulator transition has distinct metal and insulating surface preparations. 
This implies the presence of unique electronic properties near the surface of these films. 
High-resolution photoemission spectra show that the metal-insulating transition is characterized by the migration of 3d bands from the surface to the film's interior as the atomic ratio changes. 
This phenomenon allows for a distinct metal-insulating phase transition at the surface regardless of the metal-insulating phase transition in the bulk. 
Our calculation also indicates that the surface completion of the bonding band occurs in conjunction with the metal-insulating phase transition in the bulk. 
This finding highlights the significance of surface finish in governing the metal-insulating phase transition in V$_2$O$_3$ thin films. 
This research provides an understanding of how metal-insulating phase transitions are influenced by surface finish and could potentially be applied in the development of devices from transition metal monolayers.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed for converting Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method. Furthermore, we identified two types of Clebsch canonizations, labeled as fully canonical and partially canonical, depending on whether all momentum map components are utilized. We exemplify the technique with two well-known Lie-Poisson systems and derive the corresponding canonized equations using both algebraic and geometric approaches.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018, identifying 37 novel planets or stellar boundaries and 19 previously known planets or stellar boundaries with updated data. Following a thorough examination, 33 novel planets and 16 previously known planets had their data reliably established. With a significant number of newly identified planets, this study greatly expands the understanding of microlensing planets, particularly in the mass-ratio analysis segment of the parameter space, providing ten new data points above the critical mass-ratio threshold - a fivefold increase from previous research. These new findings reveal a consistent pattern of flattening in the mass-ratio spectral distribution above the critical mass-ratio threshold, indicating a scarcity of observed planets in this area. Moreover, this study determines an average inner slope of approximately 1.30 for the mass-ratio parameter at or above the critical mass-ratio threshold, incorporating the previously known seven such systems, with an estimated total sample of fourteen systems - resulting in a somewhat larger average value of 1.50. Several planets, including some potentially habitable systems, were located in the Galactic bulge area, with several others situated in the disk population, showcasing a notable difference in their angular momentum characteristics as evident from their semi-major axes and eccentricities distributions.

To address a category of optimal control issues within hyperbolic conservation law systems, we develop a suitable variational formulation of the problem. This is accomplished through a Lagrangean perspective, which necessitates the introduction of boundary terms in the Euler equations due to the presence of boundary conditions. The resulting reduced problem is then tackled via a suitable Galerkin approximation in the context of the Euler-Lagrange equation. This approach is specifically applied to the case of the Euler equation as a canonical example. The corresponding numerical results are provided to validate the theoretical findings.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client loan repayment histories and demographic data.
This study compares the performance of several machine learning models – including Random Forest, Decision tree, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost – using data from a private Ethiopian bank, to determine which model excels on KMeans SMOTE over-sampled data.
Upon conducting the evaluation, XGBoost emerged as the top performer, securing a 89.75% ROC score.
Coupled with the analysis, the research investigates the relative importance of borrower characteristics, including age, with observations, to inform industry practice and lending policies.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally observed by Guay-Paquet-Matsumoto, are extended to more detailed results, notably involving the h-vector of Dyck paths and the DF-algebra. Additionally, analogous relationships are established for non-attacking rooks placed within Dyck paths.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform OCFs, while competing models are nearly equivalent in terms of performance. Additionally, our OCNs have been successfully applied to orientational invariant object recognition, achieving accurate results on challenging datasets, particularly the STL-10, CIFAR-10, and Stanford Cars datasets.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the spectral isolation technique pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we derive comparisons of the elliptic aspects of the involved relative trace formulas, ultimately yielding novel outcomes that extend Waldspurger's theorem to the scenario where n is equal to 1.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass for a heavy quark, specifically with a mass greater than 100 GeV, through virtual effects from light degrees of freedom. Our method involves virtual quarks with a complementary lighter flavor, and we apply it to have the virtual quark mass close to its light counterpart. To minimize the influence of the virtual quark mass on renormalization, we use momentum-scale and mass-scale separation, and apply smooth threshold matching to remove scale dependence between the two methods. Our technique allows for the calculation of pole mass systematic errors by removing unwanted scale variations using renormalization group techniques. Our technique is tested with two and three flavors and our results show significant scale variations in pole mass, up to 50 MeV, around experimental values and this technique is essential for the accurate determination of the quark mass in mesons.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $V(G)$.  A specific edge coloring of $G$ with colors from 1 to $t$ is referred to as an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring when each vertex $v$ in $R$ is connected to $v$ with the color sequence $abbb...b$ where $a$ corresponds to the edge between $v$ and a non-$R$ vertex, and the remaining connections of $v$ to vertices in $R$ are of the color $b$. The goal of this paper is to investigate the concept of $R$-sequential edge coloring and to provide tight bounds on the minimum number of colors needed for this type of coloring in specific graph configurations such as order-embeddings, Cartesian products, and strong line graphs.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 1 < q < 2.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
requiring multiple scans. To address this issue, we studied low-dose and ultra-low-
dose CT scan images, which minimize radiation levels while maintaining diagnostic
effectiveness. By comparing visual features with standard-dose CT scans, we were
able to develop a machine learning model that accurately identifies COVID-19 from
these low-radiation images. Through thorough testing, we found our model to be
extremely reliable, achieving a high accuracy rate of 91% even when using
ultra-low-dose images, which significantly minimizes radiation levels during the
diagnostic process. This model has the potential to provide rapid and reliable
diagnoses while keeping patients safe from radiation. Moreover, we analyzed the
effectiveness of different imaging modalities and denominators used in diagnosis
to rule out COVID-19. To support COVID-19 research and provide valuable insights,
we publicly share our dataset, which consists of reprocessed standard, low-dose, and
ultra-low-dose CT scan images, along with the corresponding metadata.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent satellite collisions and maximize functionality.  The space occupancy (SO) concept, crucial in planning satellite trajectories, involves designing orbits with minimal overlap, thereby optimizing space and ground positions for a given set of satellites.  Given the constraints of SO, this research introduces the first set of SO-compatible solutions for large-scale mega-constellations in low-Earth orbit by employing the evolutionary dynamics of their two-dimensional Keplerian orbits.  The study demonstrates that SO solutions, depending on the configuration and number of satellites, can have ranges of stable equilibrium positions, and provides analytical predictions for the boundaries of these ranges based on the values of specific parameters.  Additionally, the study expands the existing theory of stable SO solutions to accommodate the realistic conditions of these mega-constellations, and demonstrates that the phase space structure allows for the detection of an integer relationship between the values of specific parameters, which is crucial in planning and maintaining these mega-constellations.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes within complex computational domains, we develop an automated approach using an simplified geometric representation. This method initially divides the domain into smooth segments using carefully chosen control points, ensuring a precise domain polytope containment. Employing an optimization technique, we then refine the position of control points to create highly accurate mesh interpolations. The outcome is a set of high-order quadrilateral meshes that are both geometrically accurate and efficiently computed, suitable for computational analysis on various domain types, including those with internal boundaries and boundary feature captures.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value calculation involves a quadratic form derived from a correlation matrix, making it suitable for analysis even under non-normal data with specific constraints. Building upon this, a new test statistic has been proposed for assessing correlation in multivariate settings, utilizing principal components to accommodate data with a large number of variables. The method maintains sensitivity to correlation, is robust to outliers, and remains sensitive to extreme values, retaining power to detect correlations. The performance of this new approach is compared to the original by estimating false positive rates under diverse data conditions, with results indicating the test's efficacy in non-normal settings, a lack of significant differences in performance under normal data assumptions, and the test's robustness to categorical data, though potentially losing power in exploratory data analysis where not designed to capture complex interactions.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) in three dimensions. This research setting has substantial implications as the uncontrolled dynamics in these spaces lead to solutions that lose regularity as they develop singularities. In these spaces, it has been demonstrated that the Navier-Stokes equations have multiple possible solutions, and the persistence of these solutions depends on the size of the finite dimensional feedback control used. By extending methods previously employed in Hilbert spaces, our study provides the first proof of stability in these critical spaces and over two- or three-dimensional domains with no-slip boundary conditions. This research was supported by the Mathematical Treatment of Fluids Workshop: Recent Developments and Challenges in Mathematical Fluid Dynamics, held at the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute in Oakland, California.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the Categorical Vocabulary Learning dictionary, a web-
based dictionary platform that utilizes a generative dictionary to describe word 
meanings. By incorporating contextualized embeddings, the generative dictionary 
addresses the problem of context-dependent definitions and provides more dynamic 
meaning representations. Experimental results from a small-scale user study among 
English learners demonstrate that the proposed dictionary boosts vocabulary 
recognition and understanding compared to a standard dictionary.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus falling short in guaranteeing the accuracy of generated explanations.

Quantum devices based on self-assembled InAs islands in a Si substrate have shown promising properties. A particular focus has been on the geometric characteristics of these islands and their material quality in the context of developing high-speed quantum bits. Although the size of these islands is small and the thickness varies laterally, a uniform thickness across different regions has been observed, which is crucial for optimal electronic behavior within these areas. Additionally, the perpendicular alignment of these islands relative to the substrate interface is crucial for the electrical properties of these islands. Our study examines the surface morphology of these InAs islands using a scanning tunneling microscope and electron microscopy. Along with these results, electron mobility measurements were carried out across a range of InAs well samples with varying thicknesses. These thicknesses ranged from 1.5 to 6.0 nm, which was determined using a method that measures the thickness of these islands indirectly. These data indicated a threshold thickness beyond which the islands began to grow in a layer-like fashion, resulting in significantly enhanced electronic properties. This finding holds promising implications for the development of these InAs islands as the basis for next-generation quantum bits.

Research has shown great promise for locally learnable models, which rely on local membership queries (LMQs) to determine whether a given input belongs to a specified set. However, a pivotal challenge has arisen, with many studies demonstrating the inability to establish robust distance approximators (RDA) using LMQs alone. On the other hand, we've successfully developed an RDA using non-adaptive LMQs, which can handle any dimension and provide an accurate $\epsilon$ estimate with high probability by applying our new upper bound. This breakthrough builds upon our previous work, where we established robustness conditions for LDAs, expanded on Kothari's LDA robustness bounds, and contributed robust distance approximators for $L_2$-norm and the metric ball. Our studies also reveal that an RDA using LMQs requires at least $O(1/\epsilon)$ queries in any dimension, and present an application in learning robust $L_2$-distance norms. Additionally, we've developed an anti-concentration inequality applicable to any subgroup of the vector space and established robustness criteria for any locally learnable models.

Our previous study revealed that any matrix resulting from the lower/upper completion of a complex symmetric/Hermitian matrix, along with specific structured matrices, can be efficiently computed using linear-time complexity for essential operations such as inversion, solving linear equations, and calculating the matrix product, thus facilitating straightforward implementations of iterative methods like the conjugate gradient and minimal residual algorithms. This current research extends that findings to "generalized L/U-block tridiagonal" matrices, including scenarios with internal block entries being identity matrices. We demonstrate that a direct inverse existence criterion is applicable and facilitates the explicit matrix inversion, linear solving, and matrix product computations in linear time complexity, with a key factor being the ability to efficiently compute "energetic Schur matrices" of relevant submatrices. Building upon these findings, we introduce a straightforward, linear-time algorithm for the LDST method, thus generalizing and simplifying existing methods that computed the Schur complement of suitable submatrices.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planetary candidates with masses equivalent to those of Neptune and Earth, can provide insight into how its radiation impacts exoplanet atmospheres. AU Mic's space weather was extensively studied using multiple space observatories during a 16-day orbit over the AU Mic system. Results from the XMM-Newton telescope indicate X-rays remained below the detection threshold of its cameras for most of the period, while solar particle events detected by the Parker Solar Probe's WISP instrument likely influenced AU Mic's interplanetary space, albeit not significantly. Upper bounds on particle flux were set at 20 per second per square centimeter for high-energy events and 10 per cent per square centimeter for low-energy events. Analyzing the AU Mic system with various telescope configurations failed to detect specific emission lines, likely due to either absent signals or superior detection thresholds, which restrict understanding of how extreme stellar events affect exoplanet atmospheres and their chemistry.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an open-source computer program in C++ that calculates the energy loss of charged particles traversing a variety of media with both radiation and mechanical friction at play. As an example of its utility, we use this program to estimate the total, non-relativistic energy loss of high-speed protons passing through common types of tissue at a range of speeds. We also determine the ratio of energy lost due to mechanical vs. radiative friction in such cases.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves simple and efficient balancing of data without adding new points. Its utility is demonstrated through Bayesian analysis and practical application, also highlighting its capacity for expansion to other classifiers to mitigate the issue of dominant classes.

We employ photometry data from Sloan Digital Sky Survey to determine the luminosity function of a quasar population over a redshift range from 3 to approximately 5.  Using advanced luminosity estimator methods, we calculate mean parameters for a specific luminosity model, resulting in the observation of an upturn in the quasar luminosity function's slope at high redshifts.  Specifically, we calculate a slope of approximately -3. for quasars at z approximately 3, and a slope of approximately -4.5 for quasars at z greater than 4.  These findings align with research on nearby galaxies indicating a similar shape in the luminosity function but shifted to brighter magnitudes as redshift increases, and also corroborate previous studies showing the luminosity function's slope to be steeper at higher redshifts.  Furthermore, we locate the luminosity peak at a specific absolute magnitude of approximately 45.5 (in AB mag system), which is consistent with research in neighboring galaxies.  Furthermore, we verify that the luminosity function is accurately represented by a single parameter and is not affected by the luminosity estimation technique or data selection.  We also verified that the distribution of specific physical properties does not cause the observed shape of the luminosity function.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements. Our research has also enabled us to map out the quantum dot's interaction with nearby charges and observe the impact of this interaction on the tunneling events. Our findings offer valuable insights for the development of future devices based on superconducting islands and quantum dots that can be used for sensitive measurements in complex electrical systems, as well as for the detection of paraelectric phase transitions.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a more comprehensive set of criteria and introduce new concepts of "approximate conservation" and "approximate convexity". These conditions are utilized to evaluate the behavior of shocks in various models, including some that describe fluid flow. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of stable shockwaves in a particular system of equations, determining the boundaries beyond which shocks become unstable.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel perspectives by combining traditional style transfer models with a novel, efficient motion model specifically designed for image-conditioned diffusion models, unlike more common GAN-based methods which we find to have higher training complexities and less accurate results for distant perspectives. Our results demonstrate superior quality and a broader scope of applications in comparison to existing solutions, particularly for generating distant, unseen views, and we observe a notable increase in the scope of our generated predictions -- up to a 2-fold improvement.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex collective behaviors. While recent research has found connections between these networks and mathematical structures known as non-linear stochastics, a clear theoretical foundation for such relationships remains lacking. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we employ tools from algebra and category theory to establish a theoretical framework for relationships between simple network structures and mathematical mathematical structures known as probabilistic non-linear Markov chains. Our work provides a clear understanding of how these theoretical objects can be viewed as generalizations of traditional random walks and Markov chains, while also revealing how these theoretical concepts can be used to analyze and model complex collective behaviors arising from network interactions.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber with a finite radius. The new model has been applied to analyze the instability of a cylindrical film subjected to a periodic pressure difference. The findings indicate that slip at the liquid-solid interface weakens the film's stability, causing more rapidly growing perturbations. Interestingly, this increased instability leads to a greater preference for specific wavelengths in the resulting patterns of periodic ridges and grooves on the film's surface. The new theory has been verified by comparing its predictions to experimental results, including measurements of the critical stress required to sustain a stable film. This validation has produced highly accurate predictions for a particular chemical mixture and a range of fiber radii.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable results both within and between evaluators, with minimal difference compared to the manual approach in terms of coronal deformity angles. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibited accurate intra-rater consistency, with the mean absolute deviation within robotic scanning being only 1.8 degrees compared to 4.7 degrees for manual scanning. This study indicates that robotic scanning is a reliable and efficient alternative for measuring scoliosis deformity angles with ultrasound. Its precision and reliability make it particularly suitable for monitoring scoliosis progression in patients with mild curvature.

This paper presents an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by generating voice rates as trimmed samples from a pre-trained normalising flow. A key feature of this approach is its ability to produce natural-sounding durations, allowing for more accurate modelling of variability around mean duration estimates. As median-based estimation is less susceptible to outliers than mean-based methods, we select this averaging technique for our duration modelling framework. To further improve modelling, we incorporate a loss function designed to regulate output trimmer probability distributions, enabling the flow to accurately capture both short and extended voice segments. Our model leverages a vast dataset of spoken sentences, enabling robust evaluation on diverse datasets, including out-of-domain text from chat logs with unprecedented domain disparity for speech synthesis. Comprehensive evaluation assesses the efficacy of our duration modelling approach in terms of speech quality, using perceptual optimisation to tailor tone and style, and has achieved state-of-the-art results in speech quality on SS3M, ACAR, VCC2018 and Baidu8HDSB datasets, with further insights provided by underlying analysis.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. In this research, we conducted a broad experiment using 102K unique phrases to classify hate speech into its various forms, employing both neural and traditional machine learning models that utilize contextual information. Our analysis reveals that the best model, combining the strengths of multiple classifiers, achieves high levels of accuracy across every type of hate speech, exceeding 90%, and demonstrates significant improvements over single-classifier models and ensemble methods that rely solely on n-gram features. Additionally, we found that certain phrases associated with hate groups are often indirect and subtle, such as using coded words or symbols, which makes hate speech detection even more challenging than initially thought.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets relevant to the analysis of historical documents to identify gaps and areas where new datasets are urgently needed to facilitate research progress. The research involves document image recognition tasks such as identification, translation, restoration, and other related tasks including document structure and layout organization. The study conducts a systematic review of 349 significant studies published between the years of 2009 and 2021, using specific search terms related to dataset construction and document image analysis. The research examines datasets in terms of their language, period of creation, size, and the tasks they cover, and also evaluates the key areas of expertise required to create such datasets based on the studied tasks and relevant areas of expertise. The research further highlights critical points and proposes future directions to support research progress in document image analysis and improve the quality of document-related research through the establishment of new datasets.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a single-reduction gear train with timing belts. Following the development of the model, a feed-forward controller is designed using the flatness theory to enable precise trajectory reproduction, and subsequently, the trajectory adjustment method is developed to compensate for parameters that are not readily available. Finally, the stability and convergence of the closed-loop system are verified through analytical linearization and gain scheduling, ultimately leading to the implementation of a robust controller on the robot via an additional actuator. Experimental results indicate that this control strategy enables precise path planning, with maximum position errors of less than 0.5 mm and a settlement rate of approximately 1 mm per minute.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which involve analyzing changes in various aspects of a person's social life, a new research method is proposed that utilizes multiple time-related health data to create categories of life course health patterns. Similar to social pattern types, these new categories, known as health transition patterns, are identified through a clustering analysis of early life and later life health indicators. The methodology is demonstrated using data from two sources: administrative health records from approximately 350,000 children in England and a South Korean cohort study following approximately 248,000 children from 2001 to 2013. The aim is to demonstrate the potential applications of this new method in both clinical and administrative settings, highlighting its capacity to analyze data that may or may not contain continuous health information. Additionally, this method is proposed as a means to recognize and act on an individual's unique set of early life risks that may have long-term health implications.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping cell calculations to break down integrals, which can then be evaluated efficiently using centralised and peripheral groups. Although the original implementation by Aalders and Feenstra is customised for atoms and numerically-based methods, our version optimises performance for molecular applications using a combination of periodic tables, efficient indexing, and spherical harmonics, tailored for use with the PySCF package. We demonstrate our improved method outperforms the original implementation by Aalders and Feenstra across a range of test cases involving various basis sets.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with APSP easily computable via an $O(n^{2.373})$ algorithm by Curto-Isakovic and Williams. For specific graph classes however, the problem can be solved efficiently. One such class is that of chordal graphs, where a new algorithm was introduced in this study, building on existing solutions. The newly designed algorithm is modelled after Gil's $O(k\cdot n^{2})$-time solution for general graphs, applying it to chordal bipartite graphs. Additionally, the study utilises Kuratowski's theorem to derive a boundary for the size of resolving sets in graphs with a particular obstruction number of three.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space via an abstract representation theorem.  Additionally, this paper demonstrates that these spaces have natural Scott-continuous monoidal closures, and establishes a meaningful domain-like structure to replace directed spaces in existing context-domains semantics, allowing for a straightforward interpretation of callaces in the lambda-tilde calculus.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have been efficiently categorized into distinct classes based on vital characteristics including energy input, surface temperature, and hydrologic cycle activity. Although, in stable climate conditions, this hydrologic cycle displays regular periodic behavior and can be accurately represented by established mathematical models, in extreme climate environments characterized by 'hothouse' climates, this model's reliability is greatly compromised. In such environments, abrupt onsets of change, oscillations, multiple states, and interactions with the boundaries of these systems are common and can lead to an incorrect conclusion that the hydrologic cycle in these environments is randomly fluctuating, thus precluding effective application of mathematical techniques used in less chaotic regimes. Yet, in the case of 'hothouse' climates, this cycle manifests as distinct phases displaying slow dynamics, alternating between states of low and high water content on land. This phase-dependent behavior indicates that using time averages from these systems is not an effective method to describe their behavior and, consequently, using energy conservation principles in this manner is also not valid. This conclusion has broader implications including the feasibility of using these principles in extreme climates characterized by'superhothouse' and'megahothouse' environments, an assessment that supports the notion that even in these environments the hydrologic cycle is not completely random. This cycle's behavior is influenced by its own past history, and this interaction can be quantified using a specific mathematical model which enables prediction of future behavior, ultimately allowing for comparison of two types of cycles, one

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a curved space to solve Riemannian manifolds. The spin-off variant's twistor space representation reveals its link to higher-spin gauge theory, expounding on the full gauge theory's underlying geometric structure. We also discovered that self-dual Yang-Mills theory encompasses a subtler higher-spin field, contrasting the conventional higher-spin theory model. Furthermore, the spin-off variant's associated null geodesic Lagrangian offers fresh insights into its three-dimensional counterparts, mirroring the findings of the established twistor space representation of topological self-dual Yang-Mills theory. We also derived the spin-off variant's associated null geodesic Lagrangian using the established inverse Penrose transform method.

The application of deep neural networks in the automatic classification of thoracic lesions has gained significant momentum in the medical imaging community thanks to advanced deep learning techniques. Despite their success, these models are often trained on imperfectly annotated data, which can be corrupted by both systematic errors (such as incorrect label information) and random noise (arising from imperfect annotation processes). To mitigate the adverse effects of noisy labels, we propose a robust deep learning training method called LTL (Label Quality-aware Training and Optimization for Neural Networks) that emphasizes eliminating errors based on model-predicted probabilities and selects high-confidence samples for validation. Our experimental results, conducted using real-world data from the Artificial Adversarial Neural Network challenge, demonstrate that LTL is an effective countermeasure against adversarial noise, further indicating its potential benefits in scenarios affected by labelling noise, including those involving medical image classification tasks.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This is exemplified in the cases of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, the CRW is considered within the framework of the reverse hyperbolic law, and the distribution of its stationary states is investigated.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of a well-established model for the Reynolds number dependence of drag at the wall in certain types of flow has been confirmed. This model, developed by Moser, Kim, and Vallato, describes the rate at which certain characteristics of flow patterns, known as eigenfunctions, near the wall in a given flow environment, increase as the flow rate increases. This model applied to the part of the flow where the flow changes direction from upward to downward and onward from downward to upward, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate for the whole of the flow. This model applied to the part of the frictional energy loss and other related flow properties, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate. This model applied to other types of flow properties, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate. This model applied to other related flow properties, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate. This model, developed by Gatti, and Vallato also describes the rate at which certain characteristics of flow properties, known as derivatives of eigenfunctions, near the wall in a given flow environment, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate. This model, developed by Wang and Calderer, also describes the rate at which certain characteristics of flow properties, known as derivatives of velocity field, near the wall in a given flow environment, and it was confirmed that this model is accurate.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to the topological charge of the Skyrme field, thereby being quantized. Conversely, the overall magnetic flux is a nonquantized entity. Additionally, this model accommodates three types of self-dual solitons profiles, characterized by a compacton, a Gaussian decay, and a power-law decay, respectively. Furthermore, we execute numerical computations to determine solutions to the self-dual equations, thereby visualizing soliton profiles under varying nonlinearity parameter conditions.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under minimal crystalline symmetry. The results showed the existence of various phases: phases containing multiple Weyl nodes with surface Fermi arcs; a Chern insulating phase featuring gapless surface states despite bulk gapping; a unique phase combining gapped, flat surfaces with gapless, fermionic states; and a newly discovered phase characterized by non-Abelian magnetic texturing on the surface, where surface magnetic flux is $p/q$. We found that the points $p=1$ and $q=2$ correspond to previously studied phases: a Weyl semimetal and a Chern insulator, respectively. In our discussions, we focused on the numerical values $p=1$ and $q=2$ as well as $p=2$ and $q=3$, providing clear descriptions of the $p/q$ Arabi-Majid composite particles formed on the surface. Additionally, we outlined the general quantitative rules governing the surface Chern numbers and discussed the transport properties of the new textured phase, revealing a unique quantized Hall effect with non-Abelian characteristics.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional light. Our results, derived from extensive finite-different-time-domain simulations, reveal that this hybrid nanoantenna optimises light emission from the quantum dots by enhancing light absorption within the silicon nanoring, thereby producing a highly directional and powerful near-field radiation. Our novel QD-array nanoantenna device achieves significant advancements, including a nearly complete suppression of spontaneous emission into the substrate, a maximised directional radiation efficiency, and a highly variable and tunable directionality of the emitted radiation. These advancements offer significant potential for leading roles in future light-emitting technologies.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation of defects, scars and folds in curved crystals and nanomaterials examples of mechanical strains that exhibit screening.  Although extensively studied in crystalline structures, its presence and behavior in amorphous solids have not been extensively researched.  A molecular-dynamic simulation involving a gold wire embedded in a silica matrix discovered the absence of elastic response near a crack tip during a bending event for amorphous material.  Notably, strain localization at specific planes along with folding of the material near the crack edge were observed during the event.  Notably, this set of the "strong screening" characteristics of mechanical strains in amorphous materials.  Analysis using a discrete dislocation dynamics model revealed that a discrete dislocation crack model could accurately describe the observed folding event in the amorphous wire.  Analysis of the gold wire's stress during bending events revealed that a mechanical strain gap existed between the material and the silica matrix.  Notably, this set of the "weak screening" characteristics of mechanical strains in amorphous materials.  A simple theoretical model could accurately predict the observed bending events in the amorphous wire for both the "strong screening" and "weak screening" scenarios.  A disordered material lacks the long-range elastic structure found in crystalline materials, however, exhibits a long-range elastic structure associated with specific parameters such as shear modulus, density and sound velocity relevant to folding

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in proximity to hexagonal boron nitride from the viewpoint of theoretical modeling. We compare silicene's electronic characteristics on hBN to those on metallic substrates (Pt(111) and MoS(2)). By tweaking an input parameter without employing work function correction, our results indicate that silicene's electronic properties on hBN are notably distinct from those on metallic substrates. On hBN, our calculations reveal a higher bandgap, s-p hybridization, and bandgap width in silicene, whereas on metallic substrates, our results show minimal bandgap formation. Utilizing density functional perturbation theory, our linear response analysis of silicene on hBN yields vibrational frequencies that are in agreement with experimental data, suggesting that silicene's properties on hBN are accurate and reliable. We propose that silicene on hBN is an attractive system for modeling and studying two-dimensional silicene systems.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses intriguing mysteries. This article explores the aging process of Sgr A East, a supernova remnant, by analyzing key characteristics such as size, morphology, central star formation, and comparison with similar 2nd generation cloud complexes like the Central Molecular Complex. This comparison is made to determine whether Sgr A East is believed to be a supernova remnant or an obscuring cloud complex. If the upper age limit for Sgr A East is 5-15 million years and it is compared with the 2nd generation cloud complexes, then it may be considered as a supernova remnant candidate. However, if the aging process of Sgr A East were to extend up to 10-20 million years, then it might be an active star-forming region. This dual identity of Sgr A East might be attributed to a 'pre-supernova' phase, a previously recognized phenomenon in the development of supernova remnants. This pre-supernova phase refers to a situation where a region may meet all criteria for a supernova remnant, yet its lifespan precedes the expiration of its star-forming potential. This phenomenon, however, does not necessarily mean the star-forming potential is replaced with an even longer lifespan of star-forming potential.
