The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of KNN and SVM algorithms is heavily influenced by class imbalance issues, whereas neural networks show resilience against it.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID-19 coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID-19 more heavily in areas with lower national death rates but over time this trend reversed. We also found that local news outlets typically focused on regional developments but occasionally prioritized national updates, which correlated with recent COVID-19 death rates in viewers' areas. Additionally, our results indicate that local news outlets tended to overcover certain regions with high case counts and undercover areas with high death rates, suggesting a broader information gap driven by disparities in local news coverage capacity and audience engagement.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds specifically within the Lagrangian framework. Although most existing algorithms are derived from the Lagrangian formulation, some researchers also develop Eulerian-based methods. These alternative methods can still maintain conservation of energy and linear momentum, provided they integrate total mass precisely, but come with inherent limitations that restrict arbitrary motion and velocity. In contrast, preserving angular momentum and energy is largely dependent on the choice of discretization method. While SPH naturally allows for the computation of total (kinetic plus potential) energy, separating kinetic and potential energies requires additional calculations, which is particularly important in applications such as thermal analysis. An innovative, computationally efficient SPH approach has been designed to accurately track the conservation of mass and to facilitate the use of a compact scheme to calculate the discrete angular velocity and its derivative, which, when integrated with the Valencian method, is shown to effectively conserve angular momentum and energy. When paired with compact differentiation and an innovative temperature calculation method that our group previously developed, this new algorithm is capable of conserving both kinetic and potential energies. We test the algorithm's performance in a series of experiments.

Numerical studies have been conducted to investigate the $Q^2$ dependence of the ratio $R=\frac{G_E}{G_M}$ in semi-inclusive in-line polarization transfer experiments, using a proton target and a linearly polarized lepton beam. We've calculated the double-polarization transfer observables $A_{xx}$ and $A_{xx}'$ and analyzed their response to variations in $R$ and $R'$, focusing on $A_{xx}$ and its differences with world data. Additionally, the study's findings on the sensitivity of $A_{xx}$ and $A_{xx}'$ to $R$ and $R'$ provide valuable insights for measuring these polarization transfer observables via in-line experiments.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for enhancing learning with limited data, which is highly effective in both imitation and reinforcement learning settings. The challenge of learning from limited data is well-documented, although the use of curiosity-driven methods often results in expensive environmental interactions. Our solution lies in leveraging the teacher's expertise by utilizing their knowledge to generate synthetic data, which is combined with real data for joint training. This simulated experience is then combined with real-world training to enhance the agent's performance. Our proposed approach is versatile, suitable for both imitation and reinforcement learning, making it a promising solution for various challenges, which is demonstrated through our experiments in simulated environments, showcasing improved performance with the addition of synthetic data generated by the teacher.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been conducted. This study utilized 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research targeted final states containing two electrons, two muons, two $b$-quark jets, and one or two detected leptons or jets. Through dominant $b\bar{b}hh$ production, $gg$-mediated background control samples were established. Observed upper limits at 95% confidence level on non-resonant $hh$ production and vector boson pair production were set at 1.72 pb and 6.9 pb, respectively. These limits are the initial of their kind and exceed theoretical predictions for non-resonant $hh$ production in the standard model. Furthermore, when combining all $hh$ modes, the observed lower limit on the branching fraction of the $b\bar{b}hh$ process was found to be 0.0068, which is three standard deviations higher than the standard model's predicted value.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integration, minimizing the necessity for intricate optical design within the maser structure.
Using a compact cell filled with 84mmTm/100mT NOVAS gas cells, we have successfully achieved a level of sensitivity at micro-Gauss levels over an extended range of magnetic fields.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension of the MSSM sector with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ symmetry, where the neutralino's lifetime is lengthened by the mixing with the hidden sector's neutralino due to the $R$-charge splitting. The $Z'$ bosons in this model are missing at the linear dilaton point but can be made heavy with appropriate $R$-charge adjustments, staying beneath the LHC bounds. The existence of these long-lived neutralinos can be investigated through simplified models with the correct signatures for the CMB observation's relic density requirement.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface 1-norm or 2-norm in relation to the vertices of an input closed polyhedron, as well as introducing a similar scheme for the weighted version of the Delaunay subdivision, which is derived from the weighted alpha-hull of a set of points. These computational methods are essential for a recent theoretical framework proposed by Auzinger et al. in 2018. Additionally, the study provides proof that decision problems associated with the general (unweighted) surface 1-norm and 2-norm are computationally challenging for continuous optimization, as well as showing that finding the optimal weighted alpha-hull of a set of points is also a computationally challenging problem for certain situations.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian information, while the central controller aggregates and analyzes the received data to establish a tentative solution. Convergence is guaranteed without requiring communication between the controller and machines, thus allowing for a fully decentralized system. Additionally, decentralized optimization is studied in practical contexts, including parallel computation based on a decentralized cluster, comprised of a central controller and peripheral machines, and parallel computation on a parallel data storage system, featuring multiple processing units and shared memory.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional detection by employing the ionization topography to determine the recoil direction. We present a new analytical framework that effectively relates the readout resolution to the acceptable uncertainty in recoil direction for these detectors. Utilizing simulations, we evaluate the effectiveness of this approach in detecting WIMPs utilizing an $Ar-CH_4$ TPC and a pixelated micro-pattern gaseous detector. Furthermore, we investigate how readout resolution influences the WIMP sensitivity by considering both signal interpretation methods.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results if the factors influencing driving behavior are inadequately addressed. In this study, a novel dataset featuring 1 billion rows of commercial drivers' behavior records and related personal characteristics and contextual information is introduced. Furthermore, a methodical examination of the dataset is conducted to identify key factors and evaluate their impact on road safety. Finally, a deep-learning based model is proposed to address data imbalance and generate predictive models for different groups, each modeled based on the estimated posterior probabilities of their underlying latent attributes.

This study addresses the challenge of unseen scene text instances in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) by providing an accurate text detection and recognition result for images containing rare or unseen text moments. Our contribution lies in the preprocessing of synthetic data through a style transfer operation using the Star-GAN-DCGAN framework, which enables the generation of synthetic images along with their detection and recognition ground truths based on the PreAct-ResNet model. This allows the model to learn text representations that can generalize to unseen scene text instances. Additionally, the study takes an innovative approach by incorporating real-world images containing rare and unseen text instances for training, rather than simply augmenting the training data. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the ICDAR 2013 and Visual Genome datasets, achieving a recall of 80.9% and word accuracy of 80.2%.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how correlated field parameters are at different locations, used extensively in various scientific disciplines such as statistics, engineering, and physics. Since the 1970s, researchers have employed Gaussian fields as a standard for spatial and temporal correlations. The recent resurgence of these fields is attributed to advancements in computational algebraic statistics and random field theory. This paper outlines the foundations of these fields, presents methodologies for constructing them, and reviews their applications, ultimately providing a framework for analyzing recent developments and leveraging computational tools.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and find that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar result also holds for the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying narrow and tall shapes on the device geometry on spin polarization oscillations. The findings reveal that in graphene nanoribbons with significant band gaps, prominent spin polarization oscillations can be perceived, which is in line with systems featuring strong spin-orbit interactions. The spin polarization ratio reaches a maximum of approximately 80% and exhibits periodic increases with varying barrier heights, coinciding with predicted spin-orbit coupling behaviors.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a pancyclic structure.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, pressure variations, and radial movement along a specific axis, finding significant relationships among these elements. By comparing data on specific particles to laboratory collisions, researchers discovered that a particular Nucleon matrix element that indicates interaction with the anti-nucleus displays unevenness. Furthermore, the study shows that a particular nuclear matrix element that indicates interaction with the anti-nucleus, $2\hat{S}_{CH}$, is unchanged in all three collision types, indicating that it is a robust physical property.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous research applications across diverse fields. Despite time integration method versatility, traditional techniques are often hindered by computational complexity as a square of the number of dimensions for accurate solution representation. Our proposed ASK method utilizes sparse grid approaches to significantly minimize computational demands while still achieving precise results even at high dimensions. By leveraging the speed of sparse grid collocation combined with spectral methods, we enhance the method's efficiency, demonstrating the ability to handle 20-dimensional systems nearly 200 times faster than an adaptive Chebyshev tabular array method. Furthermore, we expand the ASK method to include non-uniform systems, showcasing its efficiency through comparisons with time-stepping solvers of different orders. Our investigations into the method's capabilities, performance, and accuracy are further solidified through demonstrations in number theoretical systems, synchronization of oscillators, control theory, and fluid dynamics modeling.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, and the exterior complex scaling method for extracting resonance parameters through the use of numerical solutions to the Schrodinger equation is elaborated upon. Our results include new model results for the two-dimensional Schrodinger equation to facilitate testing our proposed theory. We compare our theory with existing literature on the one-dimensional Schrodinger problem and also apply our theory to understand the photoionization of H2 using the variational principle.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. At its core, this algorithm relies on a series of cancellative transport operations between negative and non-negative functions. These operations involve a single switch between two scenarios: either scaling a function or multiplying by another. As a result, these operations can lead to two key issues that cause the algorithm to stall: a degenerate case where functions remain unchanged, and another situation where functions become completely irrelevant. In other words, this algorithm can become stuck in a state where it performs the same calculations indefinitely or, alternatively, ignores key information and makes no further progress. In this article, we identify these potential bottlenecks, develop strategies to bypass them, and provide alternative approaches to the original algorithm. Specifically, we introduce the concept of balancing functions and a modified version of the Sinkhorn algorithm that incorporates this concept. Interestingly, this modified algorithm is linked to a second mass transportation problem that involves concave functions. Importantly, we show that this modified algorithm is capable of using sample information from both source and target distributions, thus making the most out of available data. Moreover, when the target function is known, our algorithm becomes equivalent to a standard iterative approach that involves push-forward and push-back transformations of functions, which is also used in the field of pullback isomorphisms. The ATLAS detector at the LHC recorded 257 pb-1 of data during a proton-proton collision at an energy of 5.02 TeV in 2017. Analyzing this data, the focus was on top-quark pair production alone, yielding a measured cross-sectional value of 67.5 pb, aligned with theoretical predictions in perturbative QCD. Additionally, this measurement accounted for systematics, including statistical, statistical uncertainty in jet modulation, and instrumentation-related factors, providing a refined estimate of $G(5.02~\text{TeV}) = 66.2^{+10.2}_{-9.6} ~\text{pb}$. This result holds a relative accuracy of 12.5% and provides the most accurate top-quark pair production measurement thus far at this energy level, with this finding being submitted for review to the journal Journal of High Energy Physics.

Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this phenomenon in the context of systems that inhibit certain phenomena associated with the surrounding environment. They utilized an exact mathematical technique to analyze what happens when a fundamental oscillator, which stores energy in its simplest form, is linked to an disordered solid-like system able to inhibit certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment. The results reveal that the fundamental oscillator exhibits a mix of two distinct types of fluctuations that typically indicate either the occurrence of certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment or its inhibition. The results also show that there are specific conditions in which these two types of fluctuations simultaneously indicate the occurrence and inhibition of certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment. The results further reveal that the fundamental oscillator can transition between different patterns of oscillation that typically indicate the occurrence of certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment or its inhibition alone. The results align theoretically expected boundaries between these different patterns of oscillation with calculations that simplify to a different mathematical technique based on these types of phenomena and the boundaries between these different patterns of oscillation also indicate the occurrence and inhibition alone of certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment. The results show that the fundamental mechanism of energy transfer between these types of phenomena and the boundaries between these different patterns of oscillation is based on the occurrence and inhibition alone of certain types of phenomena associated with the surrounding environment. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19 pandemic-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 12% to 30%) in face-to-face distance encounters during the pandemic. Interestingly, a notable trend emerged, as individuals from lower-socioeconomic backgrounds experienced an increased average proximity to others during shopping and dining activities, often within close ranges (under 3 feet). Conversely, in higher-socioeconomic areas, such proximity decreased by 3.5 times during the same activities. This social distancing divergence, driven by economic status and urban lifestyle, tends to persist even as the pandemic recedes. It suggests that the COVID-19 pandemic may leave a lasting legacy of increased social segmentation across different areas of income levels.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied at the preconditioned state via system linearization.
Using demanding case studies, the FSMSN approach is compared against established
methods including MSPIN and conventional strategies like Sequential Fully Implicit
and Fully Implicit Methods. Notably, the analysis underscores the significance of
sub-problem tolerance adaptation in accordance with the underlying preconditioning

Our analysis connects the actions and amplitudes of a two-dimensional string theory with Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, revealing a strong similarity. We also investigate an exact factorization in the non-perturbative theory, encompassing both the Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity and a quantum cosmology action, which results in a unified action. This action, although bounded below, exhibits an unbounded above, hinting at a dual description using a Euclidean path integral. Furthermore, incorporating a Euclidean time sector in the dual description can potentially be connected to the original time parameter, thus gaining a new understanding of the bound. We also explore connections with T-duality, as well as with Chern-Simons theory, which has a natural connection with T-duality, in our discussion.

In the Alcubierre warp drive model of spacetime, a novel approach to resolving singularities arises from modifying the warp drive metric by incorporating a shift vector, achieving regular solutions to the Einstein equations. This study examines warp drive spacetimes with a novel form of singularities inspired by Ho\v{r}ava-Penrose discontinuities, where the shift vector's radial component is tied to the warp drive's geometry radius. Additionally, the study investigates the warp drive spacetime's properties as a Ho\v{r}ava-Penrose singularity pair and explores the boundary conditions on its event horizon.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process data for underground infrastructure systems. This enables a wide range of users - administrators, workers, and the general public - to make data-driven decisions by accessing integrated and digitized information. This demo paper outlines GUIDES' architecture and highlights its core components: (i) the creation of underground infrastructure maps and (ii) the fusion of various types of geospatial data.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interactions between optical dipole traps located at the focus of lenses and at the focus of a broadcast lens configuration. By calculating the trap's potential distribution, we determined its non-uniformity to be approximately one percent. This allowed us to measure the dispersion of momentum distributions from which we calculated diffusion rates in the x and y planes. We investigated the impact of laser cooling, the effects of quadratic radio-frequency modulation on the ion's motion, and the influence of the external electric field on the ion's motion. By combining these individual diffusion rates and assuming isotropic diffusion, we calculated the overall diffusion rate. From the total diffusion rate, we determined the overall temperature of the ions, which in a specific instance matched the expected temperature obtained from the uniformity of the trap potential. This method can be applied for determining the temperature of collections of ions in complex three-dimensional arrays, especially useful for optimizing the placement of photons in ion quantum gates.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single quantum simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip, a focal point of many mechanistic studies. Conversely, the chemical interaction accounts for the cross-interaction between the plasmonic field and electrons on the sample under the condition of a stationary state, typically manifesting as resonance Raman-like signals. Our simulations focus on a SnP3O10 scarab structure exposed to 784 nm light and are evaluated against experimental data, demonstrating that this approach offers deep insight into the underlying sample analysis.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find excess emission due to AME beyond the expected thermal and synchrotron components. Instead of a detection, our research yielded only upper limits for AME, which when combined with similar upper limits found in the literature are insufficient to provide a strong indication for or against the'spinning dust' hypothesis. Future observations with the Sardinia Radio Telescope could include an in-depth study of the AME emission in M 31, its standard candle alternative NGC 4254, and local spiral galaxies with high star formation rates such as NGC 4736.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model predicting two separate transition stages, it is now understood that the significant entropy change arises from the extensive breakdown of bonds in pairs of ammonium ions at around 240K as part of the primary phase transition. Furthermore, it is noted that previously reported stage 2, corresponding to around 270K, was, in fact, an artifact resulting from imperfect polarization orientation within the crystal structure. Although the ammonium ion's bond breaking/disappearance is anticipated to result in ferroelectric properties, it is notable that the ammonium ion's associated vibrational modes are only incidentally affected by this process. Moreover, it is observed that, at around 120K, additional modes (described as being related to tunneling) emerge, providing substantial contributions to the material's electrocaloric properties at low temperatures. Lastly, it is observed that both tunneling and entropy generated by bond disruption complement one another to produce substantial entropy for ammonium sulfate, but this synergy only becomes apparent when considering both contributing factors.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes execute a 'probability-matching' strategy, which means choosing an option with a likelihood equal to its relative reward on average, whereas they sometimes opt for an 'extremity strategy', which involves consistently choosing the same option, with performance being optimised by incorporating both approaches. Experimental data suggests that both stress and motivation can impact how frequently these strategies are employed, with effects being particularly pronounced on the extremity strategy in a motor task involving a bird pecking for food. Consequently, a theoretical model was developed to explain these observations using a common cognitive mechanism - a noisy decision-making process. Theoretical results confirm that this mechanism can indeed lead to the coexistence of both learning strategies, which agrees with experimental findings. Moreover, the model shows that stress and motivation can alter how frequently these strategies are utilized by affecting the optimal trade-offs involved in a trade-off between following an instinctive path and optimal probabilistic learning patterns.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could form a basis for a Witting-like configuration of 120 simple roots associated with the E_8 Lie algebra. This is based on a group of 29 elements generated by reflections within a sub-space of H_3, where the scalar product is positively orthogonally curved. The E_8 root system can be reproduced by applying these reflections to a set of 16 distinct simple roots. Eight of the elements in the group consist of repetitions of the element a, while 21 elements are g_0 as defined by J. Witting. Additionally, 16 elements can be represented as the product of a reflection g_i for i=1,2,...,16, where all these elements have a modulus of 1. It is also possible to form a configuration with 121 simple roots within a three-dimensional hyperbolic space by using a fundmental group generated by the reflections g_1, g_2,...,g_16, where the moduli of these elements are all 1.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the previously best result for an improved approximation factor while also reaching the previously best result with reduced query complexity. Additionally, lower bounds on the data structure's efficiency were derived using the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing strategies. We introduce a new class of mitigators that proactively minimize errors with optimal experiments, followed by a corresponding postprocessing approach. By pre-emptively adapting to the measurement process, our approach optimizes the preparation of quantum states. We demonstrate that optimal preadaption is computationally feasible for small systems from the eigenvalues of the noise matrix. Furthermore, we show that by accurately estimating the noise model, our postprocessing technique achieves the same scaling as the standard maximum likelihood one, but with fewer assumptions. Our method is shown to perform well on real quantum processors, with an average postprocessing gain of 13.3% for simple qubits. Despite dealing with complex noise patterns, our method is successful in discovering the underlying noise model for noisy qubits.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focus on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. We acknowledge that robots sometimes make mistakes in their interpretation, resulting in suboptimal assistant behavior. To address this, we propose that robots take an active role in educating users about their interpretation methods and how the robot chooses the most suitable task. By providing this explanation, the robot enables the user to directly guide the robot's decision and work in harmony towards a single goal. We conduct an online experiment to understand how the robot's explanation affects user knowledge and decision-making during assistive teleoperation and discover that the robot's explanation significantly enhances the user's understanding of its decision process. Moreover, we find that the user is more inclined to direct the robot when the user understands the robot's interpretation methods, though we also observe that the user becomes overwhelmed when presented with an excessively detailed explanation. To leverage this finding, we suggest displaying explanation details only when the user demonstrates an understanding of the robot's underlying conventions through their actions following the initial explanation. As such, we design a shared control framework incorporating (i) an initial explanation phase where the robot outlines its decision process, (ii) a wait period allowing the user to utilize the robot's arms, and (iii) a secondary explanation phase where the robot identifies the user's lack of understanding and provides

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a frontier saliency metric to prioritize detection. A straightforward algorithm detects these frontiers by identifying the most prominent points in the octree representation and blends the frontier detection and representation updates. The effectiveness of HiTMap is demonstrated through simulation and field tests showing its ability to efficiently and locally navigate around obstacles without deviating and regardless of the starting location, while also facilitating robust frontier detection to improve exploration capabilities.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultrasonic, magnetic, optical, and encryption technologies. This paper presents a novel method to directly create two-dimensional zero-delay affine phase-shifts using one-dimensional minimum power phase inversions within a specific frequency range. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that affine phase-shift sequences exhibit uniform displacement properties and are found to adhere to certain constant values related to the minimum power of the phase inversion. Utilizing affine phase-shift sequences, we are able to derive two-dimensional zero-delay correlation sequences with properties analogous to two-dimensional Walsh sequences under certain conditions. Our findings reveal that the maximum values of two-dimensional correlation sequences are directly proportional to the minimum power of the phase inversion.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures in objects and individuals. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of various energies, corresponding to different photon energies, the process of CT imaging involves not only reconstructing images but also compensating for variations in attenuation based on energy. If this correction is overlooked, it can lead to notable effects known as beam hardening and photon scattering, which result in distorted images due to varying attenuation across different energies. In this study, a newly proposed inverse radiative transfer line integral model has been applied for beam hardening correction in CT. By considering variations in photon attenuation and scattering across different energies, this model provides more accurate results, especially when scattering effects become apparent at lower X-ray energies. Simulated experiments confirmed the model's effectiveness in its intended application, which involves both cases with and without photon scattering. Additionally, beam hardening effects were quantified by comparing reconstructed densities with their actual counterparts, which demonstrated the model's performance in accurately reconstructing CT densities. This study's findings can be adapted for use in CT scanning procedures.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather user feedback to dynamically construct a class-based index for extracting entity data. Our exploration focuses on List QA, which entails gathering user feedback to refine a list of candidate answers via a series of questions and selections. By combining these two processes, we developed a new CNER user interaction paradigm that first presents a set of terms and asks users to mark the context-sensitive terms and rank them in order of relevance. Using CNET (a collection of user feedback on entity data) and LB1BOSUB (a movie script containing annotations), we found through analysis that pinpointing context-sensitive terms alone yields substantial enhancements over non-contextual IR. Furthermore, asking users to rank the terms additionally yields further substantial improvements when applied to a DRUG semantic search application involving medical professionals. Our research suggests that more effective context-sensitive retrieval systems can be developed by asking users to identify both the context-sensitive terms and their relative importance.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, and it appears ubiquitously in both everyday life and geophysical phenomena. Recent advancements in multivariate time series analysis have focused primarily on the development of new methods for high-dimensional data, which is expected to exhibit non-stationarity, non-linearity, and irregularities in different dimensions. Unfortunately, existing research has only marginally explored the relationships between these properties and the practical applications of multivariate time series. Our study delves into the relationships between these properties and the practical applications of multavarite time series by investigating the domains where these properties are most relevant. We compiled a database of 110+ multivariate time series, each with distinct characteristics, and selected 50+ real-world examples from various domains like environmental monitoring, disease analysis, and news headlines. Our database is hosted online at https://multivarate-timeseries.github.io. Our investigation centers around two core questions: 1) What practical applications can be achieved using existing time series analysis techniques in combination? 2) What time series analysis challenges persist despite the use of existing techniques. Our analysis reveals that while existing techniques can tackle simple tasks such as trend detection and correlation, more complex tasks including the identification of relationships between multiple variables and the preservation of privacy of time series remain unresolved. We outline potential research directions and propose the MUTCAT challenge to advance the field of practical multivariate time series analysis.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can utilize clinical data to enhance healthcare quality by identifying patients at risk, making predictions, and discovering patterns. However, concerns surrounding data privacy have significant implications for the development of these learning models. In this context, research into Private Active Learning (PAL) has gained momentum as a strategy to address data privacy issues. PAL is an iterative process involving data collection from the patient, which is both time-consuming and expensive. Therefore, optimizing PAL to minimize both the quality loss and the number of samples required has become a pressing research need. We present PAC-PAL, a novel algorithm that efficiently handles high-dimensional data including images and text. This approach employs a fast approximation technique to ensure real-time decision-making at the patient level, which significantly improves the quality of the learning process by up to 300%. Additionally, our algorithm reduces sample complexity by accelerating convergence and decreasing the number of required samples by 25%. Our comprehensive comparison with the existing literature showcases the effectiveness of PAC-PAL against both conditional and unconditional PAL methods.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy analysis, we derive equations that describe the electrostatic potential and charge density within the solvent and at the boundary. Notably, our findings show that solvent effects significantly influence charge density at the boundary, but have minimal impact on bulk electrostatic properties. Additionally, our work introduces a flexible Redlich-Kwong model to model solvent behavior and evaluates its effectiveness.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers and practitioners. To this end, we employ BERT, a leading model utilizing BERT topology, to automatically extract requirements from textual documents in this paper. By converting textual documents into graphical representations and applying different models, we aim to develop an effective method for extracting requirements. The efficacy of our approach is validated through experiments using three distinct datasets, where we compare the performance of various models, including fine-tuned BERT models, against baseline approaches like graph-based methods and a heuristic technique proposed by VeriFlow. The outcome of our analysis reveals that our proposed solution significantly outperforms these competing approaches while also illustrating the importance of input representation in the requirement extraction process.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem. A generalized outer approximation algorithm is then applied to find a solution that simultaneously optimizes scheduling and power allocation, showing how to obtain the best possible energy efficiency gains by optimizing these two strategies. A comparison with a no network coding scheme shows that with a specific range of parameters, network coding can significantly improve energy efficiency when both scheduling and power allocation are optimized.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital-dependent density functional theory to account for the varied environments. By building upon the yield yield range, a quasi-one-dimensional Hamiltonian has been formulated and further developed into a semi-infinite tight-binding model. Using a self-consistent self-energy approach, reliable results have been obtained for impurities made of iron, chromium, and platinum on hydrogenated niobium and lead surfaces. These analyses have uncovered significant variations in the YSR resonance heights and widths, with external influences being more pronounced for impurities located near surface states. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the hybridized impurity-Host states exhibit unique spin-dependent behavior. This dependence stems from the distinct energy ranges and environments encountered by the impurity, rather than an intrinsic YSR state polarization. This novel mechanism for spin-dependent phenomena is anticipated to emerge in a wide range of materials with unconventional superconductors. These materials include recently discovered compounds such as iron-based materials and materials incorporating transition metals. These systems feature unique properties including a proximity effect, which involves the impurity's coupling to host and spin-orbit-induced effects. These properties are known to affect the behavior of localized magnetic impurities located within the material's bulk, a phenomenon that has been observed in the recently discovered Fe-chalcogen

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Although some models can learn key points and descriptors for distribution-based registration, they typically rely on localized, beam-based point sets which are costly to compute.  To address this issue, deep learning-based approaches are being explored that can learn a projection and descriptor extraction without relying on beam-based point sets.  To develop more effective deep learning-based approaches, new projection and descriptor metrics are proposed that can capture more natural distribution-based characteristics.  To evaluate the effectiveness of deep learning-based approaches, novel metrics are developed to assess their performance in a distribution-based context, rather than the point cloud-based measure of the traditional IQR.  Experimental results demonstrate that the introduced methods outperform traditional and deep learning-based approaches for distribution-to-distribution point cloud registration in dynamic scenes.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data. In 
the context of massive satellite datasets, securing sufficient computational 
resources and annotated data can become financially and logistically burdensome.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, though accurate spectral comparison necessitates an understanding of the influence of various factors, such as nonlinear absorption dynamics, radiation-induced sample alterations, and quantum mechanical processes stemming from the interaction with an intense X-ray field. Our experiment aimed to elucidate how absorption changes within the Ni K-edge of NiO upon being exposed to varying energy densities across a wide range of intensities. Our results reveal nonlinear effects prompting alterations in the white line and sub-valence region up to a certain point, beyond which the material undergoes radical structural modifications. Simultaneously, we discovered evidence of valence transition involving the 2p hole localization during excitation and an intense X-ray field-induced Stark effect affecting energy levels at the absorption edge.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject interference into the system without being detectable to the receiver. In our research, we use a specific type of attack, the Fast-Gradient-Sign method, to inject interference into a standard Wi-Fi system and classify the perturbed signals using different methods. We compared the classification accuracy of these methods, including one that uses a DNN-based AMC approach, on the perturbed signals and found that the DNN-based method was more resistant to perturbations than the other methods, which rely on manual parameters or pre-computed tables. This shows that the reliability of AMC systems can be compromised using specific types of attacks that target the radio frequency (RF) signal or the DNN used for classification.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using techniques based on fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs), but these approaches often fail because they don't account for the fact that some lesions aren't affected by the disease. We address this problem by modifying the loss function to ensure the network generates more conservative results. Additionally, we've developed a specialized training dataset that mimics non-lesional brain tissue, allowing the network to learn what normal brain tissue looks like. Our experiments show that using this tailored dataset alone leads to a small improvement in the network's performance. However, when combined, the gains are substantial - our method achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.8133 for non-lesional tissue classification, an Alasn value of 0.8455, and a Sorensen Dice coefficient of 0.8621 for lesion segmentation.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a measure and a distance function. 
This equivalence is shown for concave and convex functions, as well as for measures with 
polynomial growth. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the MTW condition yields 
upper bounds for the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data. To tackle this, we've developed an integrated framework that combines data-driven learning and domain knowledge to identify complex systems even with limited, noisy observations. This framework can be applied to different machine learning models, both continuous and discrete, and handles different types of model errors. 

Firstly, we've explored the impact of a specific type of error that isn't influenced by past events and proved that the accuracy of predictions is closely tied to the duration of the training data. 

For situations where remembering past events can be beneficial, we've developed two universal models for learning continuous-time systems, both with different memory capabilities. One model uses a simple sequence of memories, whereas the other retains information about the relative time intervals between memories. 

These two models share a common variation that can be used to tackle different types of errors, including situations where remembering past events may not be helpful. We've also conducted a thorough numerical analysis of these models, focusing on how their performance is affected by different factors, including the type of error, the model's capacity, the frequency of updates, and the size of the time intervals remembered. 

This work has significant implications because it shows that the accuracy of predictions largely depends on how we encode the time intervals remembered, especially when the complexity of the system increases. To demonstrate this, we've compared our continuous-time models with a widely-used discrete-time model that doesn't remember past events but consistently

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a result of mass accretion driven by the outflows.  Additionally, protostellar cores show a greater mass range compared to starless cores.  Notably, the mass spectrum of protostellar cores follows a power law with an index of -1.21, while the mass spectrum of starless cores exhibits a shallower slope at -0.35.  Our findings suggest that mass accretion via outflows is crucial for the removal of mass from cores and ultimately determines their disposal limit.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting these events, we analyzed PopSyCLE's data and found that a large number of these simulated black holes remain undetected. By considering various factors, we developed a probability model to estimate the likelihood of detecting these microlensing events as a percentage of all such events. Our calculation yields a probability range of 0.1-0.5 and suggests that a significant portion of these black holes remain undetected, which could explain why we have not seen the expected effects of dark matter in certain astronomical observations.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were determined by examining the dependence of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules in a specific area, as well as the angular dependence of the radial distribution functions for specific parameter values in a range that fosters various liquid crystalline orders. The observed results demonstrated that at low packing densities, the systems exhibited non-uniform layers and, at high packing densities, hexagonal arrangements. The uniaxial nematic and uniaxial rectangular invariant orders were identified in specific ranges of packing densities and for particular values of parameter $d$. The systems' transition diagrams were compared to existing empirical models and other numerical simulation results, as well as with experimental data obtained from systems consisting of molecules with fan-shaped molecules, where it was found that the systems could exhibit unique properties despite the inflexibility of these molecules, such as plastic crystal orders at low packing densities.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization on CoSAR and sentiment analysis on SST-2, all while requiring only 2.5% as many updated parameters as fine-tuning, and significantly fewer than other parameter-efficient methods.

This paper investigates a pre-trained BERT model as a baseline solution to determine if two mathematical expressions following addition of elements are equal, equitable in value, or neither equal nor coherent in meaning. The approach entails augmenting an Expression Transformer network, specifically an InclusionNet architecture, with a BERT model. InclusionNet, previously developed, utilizes a Comparison Transformer block to assess the outcome of mathematical operations on given input expressions. For this research, a BERT model was incorporated to refine InclusionNet's output by providing semantic context, thereby enhancing the accuracy of its predictions. Furthermore, the research involved assessing the performance of the integrated BERT-InclusionNet model, referred to as BERT-InclusionNet (BERT-IN), against strong competitors utilizing large public datasets. Human feedback was sought to validate the results and understand any discrepancies between the human and the machine's decisions. Overall, the research demonstrated that combining the strengths of pre-trained language models and tailored neural networks can lead to significant improvements in achieving state-of-the-art performance in specific task areas.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental data from Caruthers and Medvedev. This relationship enables us to reframe the generalized entropy theory for glass formation, combining the lattice cluster theory and Adam-Gibbs model, based on any of these properties to simplify the analysis. By utilizing thermodynamic scaling to assess correlations between properties and dynamics, we identified key thermodynamic characteristics related to dynamics and investigated the origin of this scaling through direct calculations and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of a polymer model. The convergence of lattice cluster theory and the generalized entropy model with simulated data allowed us to provide new insights into collective motion, the thermodynamic characteristics of the glass-forming process, and slow relaxation phenomena observed in these liquids.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their handling of this concept.

In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism is essential for selecting relevant source language information, but its dynamics and role are not well understood. We developed a novel attention analysis technique, called Attentive Attention, which models how target words are generated and how they impact the choice of source language elements. We demonstrated its utility in two studies: one examining the universality of attention weights and another investigating the conditions under which target words influence source words.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined using a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression based on elementary factors, while also providing an analogous formula for connection graph weights. Notably, we examine an exemplary case where the underlying symplectic manifold is the two-sphere, and discuss the connection between our findings and the recently introduced moduli spaces of framed bordered Poisson graphs.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+1, 4+1, and so on. Constant target space conditions create boundary conditions, effectively restricting the target space to a sphere. By analyzing the effect of this restriction, we find the entropy of the vacuum to be proportional to the volume of the sphere for any odd dimension. Furthermore, this limitation also applies to the entropy of quasi-normal modes, with their density corresponding to the volume of the sphere in the target space. Interestingly, the time evolution of these modes becomes a meritocratic system, where higher potential values result in faster propagation.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star clusters, supernova remnants, and other galactic objects may be causing this phenomenon. To understand the diffuse gamma-ray background, researchers analyzed data from the Fermi-LAT instrument, focusing on a specific region near the Milky Way's center. They then employed a model that takes into account various components including thermal gas, cosmic rays, ultra-high energy particles, and cosmic ray acceleration within galactic structures like star clusters and supernova remnants. These simulations revealed that a combination of galactic star clusters and supernova remnants could explain a significant portion of the diffuse gamma-ray background if they are highly concentrated in the Milky Way's center. The same effect could also be achieved if galactic magnetic fields were to redirect ultra-high energy particles towards the center of the galaxy. This phenomenon may also be responsible for polarization patterns in the galaxy's central gamma-ray spectrum. The same effect could also explain gamma-ray emissions associated with star collisions within the galaxy's bulge region. The required galactic magnetic fields are estimated to be tens of thousands of Gauss, corresponding with theoretical predictions of magnetic field behavior in the galaxy's core. The same effect could also account for gamma-ray emissions associated with the galaxy's disk region if the magnetic fields' strength declines with distance from the galaxy's center.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial distortions. First, we consider sub-Planckian oscillations that result from features in the inflationary potential, inducing massive field fluctuations at specific moments. We demonstrate that classical oscillations can induce a transient enhancement in the particle mass spectrum, lasting only during the oscillation period. The limitations of detecting these particles through the spectral index and equation of state are also examined. As a second scenario, we examine quantum primordial distortions born from rare occurrences during rapid roll inflation, where the rate of these occurrences is exponentially small. We show that the particle mass spectrum computed using the two-point correlation coefficient exhibits enrichment in frequencies exceeding the cut-off frequency of these distortions, where the corresponding particle masses exceed the Planck scale.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and we've identified a key property called interpretability that enables us to grasp the underlying decisions made by these models. Although there has been discussion about interpretability in computer vision, there is a lack of a unified definition and assessment method for models' interpretability. In response, we define and systematically evaluate different aspects of visual model interpretability, and we use a set of common, practical criteria for this purpose. Our analysis reveals that these criteria create trade-offs when assessing models, and we identify distinct types of interpretability, depending on whether we're looking for global or local explanations of the models. Our work aims to spark a conversation and provide a framework for clarifying what we mean by visual model interpretability and facilitating the evaluation of existing and future models.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we have discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling, which goes beyond standard models, significantly affects the interaction between neighboring electrons. Within reasonable limits of this interaction and phonon energy range, our model shows that high-dimensional microscopics can reduce to a simplified one-dimensional structure, closely related to Kondo lattice models. This finding enables us to better understand the relationship between high-dimensional and lower-dimensional systems and sheds light on the origin of single energy scales observed in cuprate materials. Moreover, our model demonstrates that the flux phase, related to hole doping, is linked to the relative phase between the electron's long-range interaction and a nearby hole's short-range hopping, thereby facilitating the formation of a charge gap within the system. Lastly, our simplified model offers a new interpretation of fracton bands observed in one-dimensional cuprate photoemission spectra, thereby reinforcing our hypothesis that the fracton mechanism significantly affects the physical properties of cuprate materials.

The rapid growth of India's Information and Communication Technologies sector has had a contrasting effect on the country's wide-spread HIV issue. Our research employs 10 years of data on HIV awareness and high-speed internet access from 2006 to 2015 for 21 states in India. Our findings indicate that there's a positive correlation between HIV awareness and female literacy, while there's a negative correlation between HIV awareness and male literacy. Additionally, we found a positive correlation between HIV awareness and the prevalence of high-speed internet access for females, while there's a negative correlation for males. These results suggest that access to high-speed internet may have a more significant impact on HIV awareness for women, while it may hinder it for men. These unexpected outcomes can be attributed to a higher number of effective online awareness campaigns for women and a higher propensity among male internet users to engage in behaviours that put them at a higher risk of contracting HIV.

In a chiral magnet with easy-plane anisotropy, at a temperature slightly higher than its three-dimensional transition point, a complex structure forms, composed of multiple layers. Each layer is a two-dimensional lattice of topological skyrmion structures. Two distinct conditions result in the creation of these structures: first, when the anisotropy is relatively strong, and second, when the system is at a temperature slightly higher than the point at which three-dimensional ordering occurs. Notably, the primary characteristics of this structure can be studied through the analysis of magnetic properties within a two-dimensional plane rather than the entire system.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types and their underlying structure, 
rather than estimation methodologies, aiming to highlight innovative 
research avenues and applicable areas which are still underdeveloped.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, can be considered a specific instance of this equilibrium problem. This paper aims to provide a detailed analysis of the Tikhonov regularized Tarski model for the equilibrium problem through the lens of strong convergence analysis in regularized Tarski geometries. It also proposes and examines the properties and stability of the set of regularized Tarski solutions, and derives specific criteria for identifying solutions of regularized equilibrium problems using different regularizing techniques. Furthermore, it interprets and generalizes regularized Tarski models through the application of reconfigurable Tarski geometries and extensive computational results that highlight the practical relevance of these regularized problems across various fields.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation across numerous scientific and technological fields. However, the field of engineering still heavily relies on traditional surrogate models. By integrating the perspectives of Bayesian deep learning, a framework that separates uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty can be formed. Aleatoric uncertainty represents inherent data variability, which can be characterized by noise, simultaneously, epistemic uncertainty emerges as a model's inherent limitation stemming from insufficient data, imperfect design, or other constraints. Traditionally, uncertainties have been addressed through classical statistical methods in computational fluid dynamics. In this study, a systematic review is performed to investigate the application of uncertainty quantification in CFD. Furthermore, a case study is conducted on turbulent flame propagation to distinguish between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties and demonstrate the application of uncertainty quantification in modeling.

The average values of turbulent transport coefficients are calculated in global α-effect simulations using the Induced Magnetohydrodynamics code. Local helicity flux and its relation to the α-effect are also investigated through direct numerical simulations of helical hydrodynamics. A critical aspect of these studies is validating the stationary transport coefficients by analyzing their time-averaged values, which is achieved by conducting simulations in the stationary regime. A mathematical derivation is also provided to express the global α-effect through a helicity flux, along with its associated error margins. Crucially, our results demonstrate the feasibility of local measurement of stationary α-effect and helicity flux without relying on global averages. Furthermore, the connection between helicity flux and the α-effect in the stationary state is established, which may have significant implications for geophysical and astrophysical fluid dynamics research.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas situated at the edges of an existing ionized outflow. Observations of line-of-sight velocities exceeding 450 km/s indicate outflow velocities exceeding 600 km/s in the fastest emitting plume. Most of these molecular gas outflows have counterparts in the emissions of HCN and HCO+. A proposed model suggests the molecular gas outflows have a cone-like geometry similar to ionized outflows and share the galaxy's rotation velocity when expelled. Using this model, it's possible to calculate the speed of ejected material and account for unobserved outflows due to confusion with the galaxy's disk. It's estimated that about 20 solar masses per year are lost from the galaxy, specifically in the 100 pc region near the galaxy's midplane, possibly driven by the starburst and the galaxy's active nucleus.
