Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be explained another way - by considering variations in orbital states rather than valley indices.  By replicating this phenomenon in a theoretical model, we reveal that the orbital Hall effect is actually a more general phenomenon than previously thought, and can be observed regardless of whether the valleys are coupled or not.  Additionally, we discovered that the orbital Hall effect is characterized by a specific physical quantity known as the orbital Chern number, and can be induced by a specific type of magnetic field variation at the boundaries of the material.  When a finite sample of the material is subjected to this varying magnetic field, we can predict a precise change in the orbital Chern number based on the applied stimulus.  Interestingly, this prediction holds true even in situations where the valleys and orbital states are not interconnected, providing a more nuanced understanding of this effect, and highlights the distinct physical properties of orbital states in graphene.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The direct application of existing methods in this domain is challenging due to differences between text and graph-based classifiers and the unique characteristics of graph data. This work aims to develop a comprehensive study on graph adversarial attacks and defenses, incorporating the existing state of knowledge as well as new findings, and introducing the Open Graph Classification Challenge, a benchmark dataset that showcases the sensitivity of graph classifiers.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve accuracy. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs to enhance the counterpart-matching process, leading to a substantial improvement in the assessment of matches. By including this photometric information, prior astrophysical knowledge can be omitted from the assessment, offering increased flexibility. Furthermore, this method accounts for the possibility that some sources have no counterparts or multiple potential matches. Two matching algorithms are discussed, and the assessment of matches is applied to a test involving ULAS J0015+0112 to examine potential inaccuracies in the catalog.

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C(k, m) if each subset of size k or larger includes at least m hyperedges. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that intersects with every edge at least once. A vertex cover is considered minimal if no proper subset fulfills this requirement. Furthermore, this property is denoted as property R(x, y)/R*(x, y), indicating that any subset of size x or larger, or a subset under size y, respectively, contains enough vertices to fulfill the requirement. The authors investigate the evolution of the minimum number, denoted as h(x, y)/h*(x, y), required to fulfill property R(x, y)/R*(x, y), with subsequent discussion on hypergraphs with property C(2, m). They also discuss the minimum number, denoted as c(x, y)/c*(x, y), required to fulfill property C(x, y)/C*(x, y), with subsequent discussion on hypergraphs with property C(k, 3).

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast knowledge bases with millions of interconnected concepts have been developed. These extensive knowledge bases can be challenging to work with, particularly when attempting to identify and highlight relevant parts. Various tools and interfaces have been designed to facilitate this process, though they are often restricted to particular applications or supported by particular philosophies. A more flexible approach seeks to provide a unified platform where users can create customized interfaces to suit their needs. By combining a comprehensive knowledge base with customizable visualizations, users can effectively pinpoint relevant concepts. These custom interfaces are made possible through web-based tools that enable users to create and manage visualizations with ease. A proposed platform, known as KOS, offers a scalable solution for point-of-need access to large knowledge bases. This solution emphasizes ease of use and provides a user-friendly web interface that allows users to create and manage their visualizations. A KOS implementation is demonstrated in the field of infectious diseases, where it is used to develop a point-of-need access system in conjunction with the Infectious Diseases Ontology. In order to allow others to replicate this approach and develop their own access systems, KOS has been made publicly available as an open-source platform. Additionally, open data sources for point-of-need access tools are also provided.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech representation across various speech processing tasks, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after transforming speech samples from one task domain to another. As a result, our proposed method effectively extracts task-agnostic speech features that can seamlessly be used for downstream tasks, ultimately leading to enhanced speech recognition accuracy. Extensive experiments were conducted on four distinct speech task domains, namely speech enhancement, speech separation, language identification, and bilingual translation. Moreover, our approach outperformed the current best baseline on Speech Recognition Corporations' benchmark scores in the speech separation domain and consistently achieved improvements of +0.8 to +3.4 CER relative to baseline models on other datasets.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in understanding human behavior, its applicability to other species remains uncertain. This research investigates active inference in zebrafish, a highly adaptable species suitable for studying in a controlled environment. Utilizing a task that requires both prediction and action, we demonstrate that zebrafish behavior aligns with the expectations of active inference. Moreover, our results reveal that the mental frameworks of both humans and zebrafish are characterized by similar dynamics, consistent with a hierarchical predictive model. This finding not only confirms the universal principles of active inference but also enables the cross-species evaluation of the theory.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational resource requirements pose significant barriers to their deployment. This paper presents an NLP model designed to score essays traditionally, but in a more scalable format, capable of assessing writing quality across a wide range of essay topics. The model consists of a lightweight transformer-based architecture, incorporating a reduced Number of Encoder-Decoder Layers, a minimal Hidden State Size in the Encoder, and a basic Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanism in the Decoder. The model was rigorously evaluated on large, real-world datasets extracted from real SAT exams, focusing on both individual trait assessment and overall score prediction and demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in both cases. Moreover, the research assesses the model's ability to generalize across time and domain boundaries by testing its performance on outdated and foreign language datasets. The results show the model's consistent high performance, suggesting its ability to extract essential, time-insensitive features. Additionally, the model achieves strong scores that directly compete with human scores and other prominent NLP models on multiple, highly dynamic writing datasets. The research's findings including full code, dataset samples, and model checkpoints are accessible via a publicly shared GitHub repository.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an efficient box re-ranking problem without the need for manual annotation.  A secondary challenge in box re-ranking arises from the absence of labeled validation data, which is why we introduced the self-supervised evaluation metric, box number alignment, to prevent over-specialization in the model and preserve true positive detection accuracy.  Our approach is supported by comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, including general benchmarks for unsupervised domain adaptive object detection.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo and compression flaws. A novel deep learning technique combines multiple types of data to repair these distortions, which commonly occur in live recordings and also affect music files shared online through mobile platforms. With sufficient training data, our approach yields highly effective results, a prerequisite for us to apply it to a range of common distortions with limited sample data available. Utilizing a neural network designed for image recognition but adapting it to process audio, we demonstrate the feasibility of restoring multiple types of distorted music files, which also includes samples generated synthetically to facilitate training. This new method is tested on a variety of real-world music recordings processed by common repair techniques and compared to models specifically designed to restore specific types of distortions, showing its clear advantages.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our research indicates that people generally overlook an error in the ball's motion as long as the Point of Release occurs relatively soon after the onset of the motion. However, when the Point of Release takes place later, people are more likely to notice such discrepancies. Furthermore, we discovered through our experiments that a significant majority of participants focus on the area where the ball is released rather than the arm's actual trajectory when evaluating the animations. Our findings also reveal that a considerable number of individuals are unable to distinguish between realistic and unrealistic animations, especially when the Point of Release occurs early. Interestingly, however, when the Point of Release takes place late, people are more divided in their judgment, with a greater preference for the more realistic animation in the correct ball path view. Our experiments also showed that a substantial number of participants preferred the more realistic animation in the late PoR condition, even though it deviates from physical laws, suggesting that other factors such as animation coherence contribute to their perception. Our study aims to provide further insights on this aspect, which we believe has the potential to enhance the creation of more realistic and engaging animations, especially those involving overarm throws.

To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called SeqPARS has been developed, which leverages sequence tagging and attachment styles to infuse syntax into translation. By assessing the compatibility of grammar rules and translation phrases using a designed score function, SeqPARS fuses syntax and semantics in a unified model. As an alternative to dependency parsing, the SeqPARS framework can be optimized to incorporate constituency parsing by adopting a binary parse tree structure. Experimental results demonstrate that SeqPARS consistently outperforms standard NMT systems across various metrics, encompassing translation quality, syntax adherence, and fluency. Notably, the syntax-guided SeqPARS model has proven to enhance translation quality, encompassing multiple NMT baseline approaches.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Tool to systematically evaluate and identify the binding energies of molecules in the universe. This tool uses a comprehensive database containing >1800 binding energy values from multiple sources, allowing for easy identification, verification, or calculation of binding energies related to specific molecular configurations. The tool also facilitates the determination of potential biases and uncertainties associated with existing datasets as well as the potential for completing or expanding existing datasets. We show that the BEET can be used to identify potential weaknesses or inaccuracies in existing datasets, enabling the development of more reliable methods for determining binding energies. The source code and database for this project are publicly available.

A multiplicative stochastic process is studied that follows a specific logarithmic pattern. This formulation often arises as the limit of a logistic map in a continuous context. Key aspects and statistical distributions of this process, specifically the lognormal and extreme value distributions, are examined and statistically checked for their applicability to 2006-2007 stock market closing prices.

We offer novel approaches to acquire in-depth knowledge about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement strategy that combines the capabilities of random Pauli measurements and random Clifford measurements. These can be viewed as the fundamental components of a more general randomized measurement scheme known as the probabilistic quantum Bernstein-Bernstein network (PQBB). Our main findings are two-fold. Firstly, we show that the randomness pattern of our practical measurement strategy is hierarchically structured, allowing us to apply a technique to control the probability of incorrect outcomes, thereby yielding a constant probability of misinterpreting the quantum state's depth. Secondly, we establish a relationship between the quantum state's depth and the distance between the measurement outcomes' distributions, resulting from analyzing the recurrence probability of a specific Markov chain associated with the PQBB. Our findings demonstrate that the measurement strategy is well-suited for states with high depth and highlight its utility in a variety of applications, such as estimating a quantum channel's $\ell_1$ norm, solving the quantum state estimation problem with maximal $\ell_1$ norm, and directly determining a quantum circuit's depth by sampling its outputs. Notably, our results improve and expand upon the recently proposed randomized Pauli measurements through a novel connection between the two measurement strategies. Additionally, the recurrence techniques utilized here can be used to establish an upper bound on the $\ell_1$ norm of a quantum circuit's output, representing a significant contribution

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related paper and applied it to the square array of wave guides in two dimensions, where they used this information to calculate the asymptotic behavior of the reflection coefficient when the frequency is very high.

The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that can vary class labels and lead to greater diversity in input data. To this end, we provide a systematic review of three prominent datasets for sentiment classification and highlight the benefits of developing custom NLP data transforms, designed to facilitate sibylvariance, such as the utilization of styles, languages, and semantic alterations. Through an in-depth analysis of the effects of data transforms on the characteristics of the datasets, we demonstrate their potential to broaden the range of input data, including both styled and semantic data. Moreover, we showcase the benefits of utilizing data transforms to enhance the robustness of machine learning models, including their ability to withstand various attacks and resilient in the face of corrupted labels. In line with the principles of sibylvariance, we propose a new class of data transforms, namely Bitplay, aimed at expanding the input range of data through semantic alterations, including the utilization of words, sentences, and semantic alterations.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features.

Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performing yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models for languages with scarce training data, specifically Hindi and Uzbek. It then details and compares two distillation techniques aimed at enhancing these models' performance: a task-oriented approach that improves the model's output for a particular task and a self-supervised method that refines the model's translation abilities when provided with target sentence contexts. The findings indicate that both techniques lead to improved performance and reduced model size, with task-oriented distillation yielding better results, while self-supervised distillation enables further improvements when implemented in an online setting, enabling adaptation of the model to novel vocabularly on the fly.

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the square of the number of vertices in the disjoint union of the complete graph K_r(n) and the graph F(n), denoted by pi(F) = lim(n to infinity) max{e(F(n) edge K_r(n)), over the square of the number of vertices in the disjoint union}. Recent breakthroughs by Gipson, Piercedale and Reed and Fu showed that the Turan number for 2K_2 plus 2-edge-free 4-uniform graphs can be determined and that this determines the extremal structure. We show that the extremal structure has an exact configuration - it is the disjoint union of the complete graph K_2 multiplied by K_2. Furthermore, this breakthrough allows us to show that the Turan number for r-uniform graphs with arbitrarily small profit can be determined for every fixed r, provided the profit is sufficiently small. In a follow-up paper, we show that the extremal structure of the r-uniform graphs with small profit converges to the disjoint union of the complete graph K_2 multiplied by K_r-2.

The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of data annotation. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labeled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of data with different image manipulation techniques applied, we demonstrate that using the original images or a single technique of rotating the images results in comparable performance to models trained on fully annotated data. The use of multiple image enhancement techniques actually decreases their collective value. Our findings indicate that fully automated data augmentation can be used not only to speed up model training on large, unlabeled datasets but also to transform labeled data into a form that is transferable across institutions.

Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a word embedding space, reducing the reliance on manual tuning and significantly enhancing the model's capabilities. At the inference stage, our model allows for the generation of custom caption styles by simply selecting the most suitable prompt, yielding outstanding results in COCO Karpathy and TextCaps benchmarks.

As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its capacity to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of Automatic Differentiation, a deep learning library powered by C++/Java/Python, expand the capabilities of Spark's ecosystem. The paper also outlines MMLSpark's architecture and key features, accompanied by a practical example that demonstrates how users can leverage the library to build advanced distributed deep learning models using Automatic Differentiation and Spark's data structures.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Recent advancements in zero-shot translation have focused primarily on written-to-written translation metrics such as BLEU. Unlike its written counterpart, zero-shot speech translation poses challenges in assessing its quality since verbal outputs are highly subjective. Existing methods for evaluating speech translation rely heavily on human judgment or external audio/video resources, which are often impractical. Speech translation can, however, leverage speech similarity metrics like BERT or BLAST. Building upon this idea, we propose a family of zero-shot speech translation metrics, dubbed SBLAST, which utilizes spoken language analysis, verbal context analysis, and verbal semantics analysis to gauge translation quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed metrics by showing they outperform existing zero-shot speech translation metrics in multiple languages. Specifically, we utilized publicly available speech translation datasets from five languages to test the performance of our proposed metrics. According to our results, our SBLAST metrics, particularly those utilizing BLAST or BLAST+, excel in several of these datasets, surpassing existing benchmarks by nearly 0.07. We also observed that our PERT-based SBLAST metrics outperformed others, with gains of up to 0.06. We note that our SBLAST metrics, like other verbal output evaluation methods, have inherent biases. We suggest combining our metrics with other metrics, such as semantic textual similarity metrics, which evaluate speech translation differently,  to  minimize  these  biases,  with

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated consumption like that of individual clients or small businesses, where a prolonged period of constant energy consumption often doesn't occur and is difficult to predict compared to aggregated consumption, where fluctuations tend to be smoother. The unpredictability of disaggregated consumption makes peak load forecasting more complex, resulting in a higher likelihood of unexpected network capacity requirements and costly infrastructure needs. One promising approach to improving peak load forecasting accuracy involves developing sophisticated data-driven statistical models that leverage past consumption data to forecast future loads, where incorporating spatial and temporal correlations can enhance the performance of such predictive models. However, such second-order autoregressive models are susceptible to convergence issues, which can be mitigated by incorporating spatiotemporal correlations into the predictive framework. In this research, we present a novel non-linear predictive model that combines non-linear net feedback auto-regressive characteristics with the incorporation of spatial and temporal correlations, which we evaluated using real data on Portuguese consumption and found that our proposed model, which we called NLNAR-STAR, demonstrated better performance and reliability compared to the 2nd-order autoregressive model and a linear reference model, with statistical significance.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient quality. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications.

Creating a reliable system for accurately segmenting COVID-19 infected areas in chest CT scans is crucial for developing effective algorithms to detect the disease. Since there is currently a shortage of labeled data for training a supervised segmentation model, unsupervised segmentation methods have become an essential option. In this research, we develop an advanced unsupervised segmentation technique that exploits pre-trained features to identify COVID-19 infected areas on a large scale. Specifically, we employ contrast-enhanced CT images, which helps to separate lung regions containing COVID-19 lesions from normal lung tissue. Our proposed unsupervised segmentation method relies on two deep learning models: the first generates contrast-enhanced fake images, and the second utilizes these images to produce detailed COVID-19 lesion masks without manual labeling. By evaluating this unsupervised segmentation approach on a large dataset, we found that it achieved an F1 score of 0.65, which is comparable to state-of-the-art results obtained from supervised segmentation methods. Moreover, we developed a simple model pruning technique that significantly reduced the memory consumption of the unsupervised segmentation system to 25% while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. Our hope is that this research will contribute towards the development of efficient and scalable systems for large-scale COVID-19 assessment.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility, adjacent body parts covering each other) make this task quite challenging. In this research, a quick and effective 2D-3D three-stage technique is introduced to accurately identify vertebrae. Firstly, body part localization is performed using ensemble methods and image features. Secondly, vertebrae detection is achieved through ensemble models and body part information. Thirdly, 3D pose estimation is established using the deep regression technique. We evaluated this approach using publicly available datasets from the 2019 Spine Challenge, comparing it to 25 other participating methods. Our results show that this technique is consistently superior to others in accuracy for localization and identification. However, while precision is also an important consideration, notable discrepancies were observed between the precision and recall of our approach, particularly for harder-to-spot cases, highlighting the potential for improved vertebrae detection using more advanced techniques.

Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a contained environment. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an entwined state confined at the center of the barrier. As an incoming electron's energy aligns with that of this confined state, it undergoes rapid, inelastic collision resulting in emission of a cavity-generated photon. This phenomenon is being researched as a potential method to produce unconventional light.

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, by directly teaching model-agnostic controllers to an actual biically-inspired robot using imitation learning. Our project centers around Zephyr, a biologically-inspired robot featuring the Actuation-by-Acceleration technique in its hips and knees. We successfully employ imitation learning to quickly train a central pattern generator to generate appropriate hip and knee movements for various tasks. Our results demonstrate that the adapted CPG can facilitate a range of locomotion gait and error resistance, and we also explore its ability to quickly learn new walking patterns alongside external distractions such as vibrations and external forces.

We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also use numerical methods to determine the closest separable states for maximally entangled multipartite X-states with three and four qubits in specific subspaces, and compare our algorithm's efficiency against existing separability verifiers. Our results demonstrate that VSV outclasses existing verifiers in solving some multipartite states, while exhibiting comparable performance for others. Our analysis suggests that VSV has the potential for further optimizations through faster convergence methods, particularly for X-states. Additionally, our analysis indicates that a purely classical optimization approach can achieve faster results than a quantum accelerated method when using sufficiently large particle numbers.

A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes small-scale magnetic reconnections, creating island coils. These modes are known to trigger the formation of magnetic islands. Our research extends this concept to 2D by using the reduced MHD model to analyze how electron temperature gradients drive island growth in both 2D and 3D geometries. In 2D, our study shows that island growth rates increase linearly with kinetic energy rates from electron temperature drive. We also discovered that 2D island structures respond to temperature gradients in plasma, altering their rotation speeds and accelerating their growth. Interestingly, in 3D, our simulations reveal a non-linear relationship between growth rates and kinetic energy rates, suggesting that 3D island geometry influences its growth rate, implying that faster magnetic reconnection in 3D contributes to faster island growth.

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in the industry, they remain understudied in academia. In this research, we tackle both tasks with a single backbone by introducing the MultiViewViewViewNet architecture. It consists of three view-modification blocks that simultaneously process image manipulation tasks within a multi-task framework. Moreover, we create advanced metrics for evaluating model performance and propose rules for assigning identities to fashion items. Our approach exhibits exceptional performance, with results on two benchmark datasets showcasing remarkable superiority over existing methods for fashion instance-level image retrieval and notable results for fashion attribute manipulation.

The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered for cases of incomplete data and noisy input. A dual gradient approach, though suffering from semi-convergence, can approximate the sought-after solution. Due to its underdetermined nature, the method requires an optimal stopping time, for which three rules – a priori estimation, the discrepancy principle, and an adaptive method – are examined, resulting in distinct convergence theorems. These theorems establish that convergence depends on the method's convergence rate in both the measurement space and the original space, which may vary independently. Our research aims to contribute a broader understanding of the methods' behavior, encompassing not only smooth $\R$ but also general strongly convex functions, and explores the applicability of minorizing functions in the minimization problem.

Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, typically denoted as $[pq, q(-1), pq+q, pq-q]$. However, this approach is associated with high computational costs and multiple data articulations. To resolve this issue, a new, straightforward, and efficient matching cost constructor is proposed in this paper. Utilizing convolution, the cost constructor is capable of generating matching cost in a linear time complexity, which is significantly more efficient than the traditional method. The proposed constructor also enhances matching cost's robustness by matching pixels across distinct sub-aperture images with various viewing angles. Evaluations conducted on four benchmark datasets reveal that the proposed constructor surpasses existing approaches in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, it achieves higher FSRCNN-xt's performance on the 13K light field dataset, while reducing the computation time by a massive 84.8 times. Similarly, it also reaches the highest performance of LID, while cutting the computation time by 92.7 times. Similarly, it even reaches the state-of-the-art performance of DeepLightNet, while cutting the computation time by 85.2 times. Moreover, it even reaches the state-of-the-art performance of DeepLightNet++, while cutting the computation time by 82.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations. By integrating multiple techniques, the research successfully obtains diverse solution patterns. These solutions, rich in structure, include double wavy solutions, solitary wave combinations, and waves with intrinsic Sech shape patterns. Furthermore, the study adapts an existing approach to obtain, for the first time, double rotor solutions. By extending the solution space, the research also discovers, for the first time, Fokas-Lenells equations with double wavy rotor solutions. To verify the validity of the obtained solutions, the study applies a consistency test. Lastly, the study visually illustrates the dynamic behavior of these novel solution patterns through Fokas-Lenells equations.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results.

To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve performance and efficiency.  The increasing requirements for applications such as virtual reality and high-quality video streaming drive this need.  One potential solution to address this challenge is to utilize the bandwidth of 6 GHz frequency, which offers large available spectra but with high interference and limited indoor reach, similar to the situation with the currently used 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequencies.  A possible solution to enhance performance is to implement millimeter wave (mmWave) technology using 3D beamforming for directional communication.  The main issue with mmWave technology, however, is its short range, which necessitates high update rates for directional information and victim channel state information (CSI).  These updates come with their own set of challenges, including potential timing discrepancies and phase shift fluctuations.  Our research focuses on addressing these challenges by incorporating scheduling into mmWave networks with 3D beamforming, as well as utilizing CSI reports on-demand instead of continuously.  Our proposed system combines these enhancements, including the use of timing adjustment to ensure accuracy despite existing timing discrepancies.  Our results, obtained from geometric probability analysis, confirm that incorporating mmWave technology with 3D beamforming can significantly improve network performance, and our low-complexity analytical model accurately predicts this performance enhancement, outperforming other available models.
